        /// tensors**. The result is an ordinary `Var`, so it can be squared, summed, added to a
        /// loss, and differentiated again.
        ///
        /// ---- WHAT IT IS FOR ----
        ///
        /// Gradient penalties. Every adversarial imitation method - AMP, ASE, ADD, HIL - trains
        /// its discriminator with a penalty on the gradient of its OUTPUT with respect to its
        /// INPUT, and then descends that penalty. Without it a discriminator converges toward a
        /// step function: near-perfect classification and a reward that is flat almost
        /// everywhere with a cliff at the boundary, so the policy gets no gradient over most of
        /// its state distribution. The symptom is not a crash - accuracy climbs, the style
        /// reward flattens, and the motion degenerates while every curve looks converged.
        ///
        /// ---- WHY IT NEEDED NO NEW BACKWARD ----
        ///
        /// Every rule below is written with operations that are ALREADY on the tape: a matmul's
        /// backward is a matmul against a transpose, a product rule is two multiplies. So the
        /// emitted graph is differentiable for free, and second-order support costs no
        /// third-order machinery.
        ///
        /// ---- STAGED, DELIBERATELY ----
        ///
        /// The ops below are the ones a discriminator is built from. Anything else returns
        /// `Error.Unsupported` rather than a wrong number, because a second-order implementation
        /// that silently falls back to first-order produces finite, plausible, stable values and
        /// a penalty that is a constant - which is the worst failure available here.
        pub fn gradientOf(self: *Self, output: Var, input: Var) Error!Var {
            if (self.values.items[output].size() != 1) {
                return Error.UnsupportedShape;
            }
            const count: usize = self.nodes.items.len;
            const seeds: []?Var = try self.gpa.alloc(?Var, count);
            defer self.gpa.free(seeds);
            @memset(seeds, null);

            const one: Tensor(T) = try ones(T, self.gpa, &.{ 1, 1 });
            seeds[output] = try self.constant(one);

            var i: usize = count;
            while (i > 0) {
                i -= 1;
                const seed: Var = seeds[i] orelse continue;
                const node: Node = self.nodes.items[i];
                switch (node.op) {
                    // A stop-gradient contributes nothing - exactly, by definition.
                    .detach => {},
                    .leaf => {},
                    .add => {
                        try self.seedInto(seeds, node.lhs, seed);
                        try self.seedInto(seeds, node.rhs, seed);
                    },
                    .sub_op => {
                        try self.seedInto(seeds, node.lhs, seed);
                        try self.seedInto(seeds, node.rhs, try self.scale(seed, -1));
                    },
                    .mul_op => {
                        // The product rule, and the reason this is worth doing symbolically: each
                        // side's gradient MENTIONS the other side, so it stays connected to the
                        // graph and can be differentiated again.
                        try self.seedInto(seeds, node.lhs, try self.mul(seed, node.rhs));
                        try self.seedInto(seeds, node.rhs, try self.mul(seed, node.lhs));
                    },
                    .scale_op => {
                        try self.seedInto(seeds, node.lhs, try self.scale(seed, node.scalar));
                    },
                    .matmul => {
                        try self.seedInto(seeds, node.lhs, try self.matmul(seed, try self.transpose(node.rhs)));
                        try self.seedInto(seeds, node.rhs, try self.matmul(try self.transpose(node.lhs), seed));
                    },
                    .relu_op => {
                        // ReLU's derivative is piecewise constant, so the mask is a genuine
                        // CONSTANT here rather than a simplification - its own derivative is zero
                        // everywhere the function is differentiable at all.
                        const source: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.lhs];
                        const mask: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(self.gpa, source.shape[0..source.rank]);
                        for (mask.data, source.data) |*m, v| {
                            m.* = if (v > 0) 1 else 0;
                        }
                        try self.seedInto(seeds, node.lhs, try self.mul(seed, try self.constant(mask)));
                    },
                    .sigmoid_op => {
                        // `s * (1 - s)` where `s` is this node's own output - which is already a
                        // Var, so the expression stays differentiable rather than freezing the
                        // derivative at today's values.
                        const s: Var = @intCast(i);
                        const unit: Var = try self.constant(try onesLike(T, self.gpa, self.values.items[i]));
                        const slope: Var = try self.mul(s, try self.sub(unit, s));
                        try self.seedInto(seeds, node.lhs, try self.mul(seed, slope));
                    },
                    .tanh_op => {
                        const t: Var = @intCast(i);
                        const unit: Var = try self.constant(try onesLike(T, self.gpa, self.values.items[i]));
                        const slope: Var = try self.sub(unit, try self.mul(t, t));
                        try self.seedInto(seeds, node.lhs, try self.mul(seed, slope));
                    },
                    .reduce_sum_rows_op => {
                        const source: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.lhs];
                        const wide: Tensor(T) = try ones(T, self.gpa, &.{ 1, source.shape[1] });
                        try self.seedInto(seeds, node.lhs, try self.matmul(seed, try self.constant(wide)));
                    },
                    .transpose_op => {
                        try self.seedInto(seeds, node.lhs, try self.transpose(seed));
                    },
                    // Not a fallback to first-order: an unsupported op returns an ERROR rather
                    // than a plausible number. A second-order implementation that silently
                    // degrades produces a penalty that is constant, a gradient that is zero, and
                    // an unregularised discriminator behind curves that all look fine.
                    else => return Error.UnsupportedShape,
                }
            }
            return seeds[input] orelse self.constant(try zeros(T, self.gpa, blk: {
                const v: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[input];
                break :blk v.shape[0..v.rank];
            }));
        }

        /// Accumulate a symbolic gradient into `seeds`, adding if one is already there.
        ///
        /// A value used twice receives a contribution from each use, exactly as `accumulate`
        /// sums into a gradient tensor - the difference is that this sums with a tape `add`, so
        /// the total stays differentiable.
        fn seedInto(
            self: *Self,
            seeds: []?Var,
            target: Var,
            contribution: Var,
        ) Error!void {
            if (seeds[target]) |existing| {
                seeds[target] = try self.add(existing, contribution);
            } else {
                seeds[target] = contribution;
            }
        }

        /// LayerNorm whose gain and bias are produced by a conditioning signal.
        ///
        /// ---- THIS IS HOW THE TIMESTEP REACHES THE NETWORK ----
        ///
        /// A diffusion transformer has to behave differently at every step of the chain. The
        /// obvious way to tell it which step it is on - concatenate the embedding onto the input
        /// - makes the condition one more thing competing for attention among the tokens.
        ///
        /// AdaLayerNorm instead lets the condition set the SCALE AND OFFSET of every normalised
        /// activation. That reaches the whole layer at once and costs two small projections, and
        /// it is what DiT uses. The same mechanism conditions a policy on a goal or a latent
        /// skill, which is why this is not filed with the diffusion code.
        ///
        /// ---- THE GAIN IS `1 + scale`, NOT `scale` ----
        ///
        /// So that a zero-initialised projection is the IDENTITY: at the start of training the
        /// block passes its input through untouched and the condition does nothing, rather than
        /// multiplying everything by zero and destroying the signal before any gradient has
        /// arrived. Networks that skip this are the ones that need a careful warmup.
        ///
        /// The two conditioning inputs are `[1, width]` - one vector for the whole batch,
        /// broadcast across rows the same way `diagGaussianLogProb` broadcasts a `log_std`. They
        /// are named `conditioning_gain` and `conditioning_bias` rather than `scale` and `shift`
        /// because this file exports a tensor `scale`, and because the names then say what they
        /// DO rather than which paper they came from.
        pub fn adaptiveLayerNorm(
            self: *Self,
            x: Var,
            conditioning_gain: Var,
            conditioning_bias: Var,
            epsilon: T,
        ) Error!Var {
            const value: Tensor(T) = self.valueOf(x);
            if (value.rank != 2) {
                return Error.UnsupportedShape;
            }
            const rows: usize = value.shape[0];
            const width: usize = value.shape[1];
            const gain_value: Tensor(T) = self.valueOf(conditioning_gain);
            const bias_value: Tensor(T) = self.valueOf(conditioning_bias);
            if (gain_value.rank != 2 or gain_value.shape[0] != 1 or gain_value.shape[1] != width) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }
            if (bias_value.rank != 2 or bias_value.shape[0] != 1 or bias_value.shape[1] != width) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }

            const row_ones: Var = try self.constant(try ones(T, self.gpa, &.{ rows, 1 }));
            const gain_wide: Var = try self.matmul(row_ones, conditioning_gain);
            const bias_wide: Var = try self.matmul(row_ones, conditioning_bias);

            const normed: Var = try self.layerNormRows(x, epsilon);
            const unit: Tensor(T) = try ones(T, self.gpa, &.{ rows, width });
            const gain: Var = try self.add(try self.constant(unit), gain_wide);
            return self.add(try self.mul(normed, gain), bias_wide);
        }

        /// Scaled dot-product attention: `softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)) V`.
        ///
        /// ---- COMPOSED, SO THERE IS NO NEW BACKWARD ----
        ///
        /// `matmul`, `transpose`, `scale` and `softmaxRows` are all already on the tape, so the
        /// whole of attention is an expression rather than a primitive. That was not obvious
        /// until it was checked: `Attention` exists in this file as a CPU type and cannot be
        /// trained through, which looked like a gap and was not.
        ///
        /// ---- THE `1/sqrt(d)` IS THE PART PEOPLE DROP ----
        ///
        /// `Q K^T` sums `d` products, so its variance grows with `d`. Without the scaling the
        /// scores reaching the softmax grow as the head widens, the softmax saturates toward
        /// one-hot, and **the gradient through it vanishes** - a wider model trains worse, which
        /// reads as a capacity problem and is an arithmetic one.
        ///
        /// It is a parameter rather than derived from the shape because multi-head attention
        /// scales by the HEAD dimension, not the model dimension, and the caller is the one who
        /// knows which it has just sliced.
        pub fn scaledDotProductAttention(
            self: *Self,
            query: Var,
            key: Var,
            value: Var,
            score_scale: T,
        ) Error!Var {
            const q: Tensor(T) = self.valueOf(query);
            const k: Tensor(T) = self.valueOf(key);
            const v: Tensor(T) = self.valueOf(value);
            if (q.rank != 2 or k.rank != 2 or v.rank != 2) {
                return Error.UnsupportedShape;
            }
            // Q and K must agree on the FEATURE width; K and V on the number of tokens. Checked
            // here rather than left to matmul, because a mismatch there reports the shapes of an
            // intermediate nobody wrote.
            if (q.shape[1] != k.shape[1] or k.shape[0] != v.shape[0]) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }
            const scores: Var = try self.matmul(query, try self.transpose(key));
            const weights: Var = try self.softmaxRows(try self.scale(scores, score_scale));
            return self.matmul(weights, value);
        }

        /// The projections and feed-forward weights of one encoder block.
        ///
        /// Named rather than passed loose because six `Var`s in a row is six chances to swap two
        /// of them, and swapping `wq` with `wk` produces a model that trains, converges slowly,
        /// and is computing attention backwards.
        pub const EncoderWeights = struct {
            /// Query, key and value projections, each `[model, head]`.
            wq: Var,
            wk: Var,
            wv: Var,
            /// Output projection, `[head, model]` - back to the residual stream's width.
            wo: Var,
            /// Feed-forward, `[model, hidden]` then `[hidden, model]`.
            w1: Var,
            w2: Var,
        };

        /// One pre-norm transformer encoder block.
        ///
        /// ---- PRE-NORM, AND WHY IT IS NOT A STYLE CHOICE ----
        ///
        /// `x + f(norm(x))` rather than `norm(x + f(x))`. The difference is what the residual
        /// stream carries: in pre-norm there is a path from input to output that passes through
        /// **no normalisation at all**, so a gradient reaches the first layer undiminished.
        /// Post-norm puts a LayerNorm on that path at every layer, and the gradient shrinks with
        /// depth - which is why post-norm transformers need a learning-rate warmup to train and
        /// pre-norm ones largely do not.
        ///
        /// At two layers, which is what HIL uses, either works. The reason to default to the one
        /// that survives depth is that nobody revisits this choice when they add layers.
        ///
        /// ---- THE RESIDUALS ARE NOT DECORATION ----
        ///
        /// They are two `add` calls and they are the difference between a block that trains and
        /// one that does not past a few layers. They get simplified away by someone getting the
        /// shapes right and never put back, because the failure is slow convergence rather than
        /// an error.
        pub fn encoderBlock(
            self: *Self,
            x: Var,
            w: EncoderWeights,
            score_scale: T,
            epsilon: T,
        ) Error!Var {
            const normed: Var = try self.layerNormRows(x, epsilon);
            const attended: Var = try self.scaledDotProductAttention(
                try self.matmul(normed, w.wq),
                try self.matmul(normed, w.wk),
                try self.matmul(normed, w.wv),
                score_scale,
            );
            const mixed: Var = try self.add(x, try self.matmul(attended, w.wo));

            const normed_again: Var = try self.layerNormRows(mixed, epsilon);
            const hidden: Var = try self.relu(try self.matmul(normed_again, w.w1));
            return self.add(mixed, try self.matmul(hidden, w.w2));
        }

        /// `KL(p || q)` between two diagonal Gaussians, per row, ON THE TAPE: `p` is given by the graph values `mean`
        /// and `log_std` (a policy, being trained), `q` by the tensors `reference_mean` and `reference_log_std` (a
        /// reference the policy is pulled toward, which training must never move). The result is [rows, 1].
        ///
        /// ---- WHAT THE NUMBER MEANS ----
        ///
        /// KL(p || q) = E over x drawn from p of [log p(x) - log q(x)]: drawing from p, how much less likely q finds
        /// the draws than p does - on average, in nats. It is zero exactly when the two are the same distribution, and
        /// positive otherwise. One dimension has a closed form, and a diagonal Gaussian's dimensions are independent,
        /// so its KL is the SUM of its dimensions' KLs:
        ///
        ///     KL = sum over d of [ log(s_q / s_p) + (s_p^2 + (m_p - m_q)^2) / (2 s_q^2) - 1/2 ]
        ///
        /// Three pieces: the gap between the centres, measured in q's variance, (m_p - m_q)^2 / (2 s_q^2); p's own
        /// spread measured the same way, s_p^2 / (2 s_q^2); and the log of the width ratio. With the -1/2, the width
        /// part is (r - 1 - log r) / 2 for the variance ratio r = s_p^2 / s_q^2 - never negative, and zero only when
        /// r = 1. So the whole divergence is zero exactly when both the centres and the widths agree.
        ///
        /// ---- THE DIRECTION IS A DESIGN DECISION ----
        ///
        /// KL is not symmetric, and which distribution goes first changes what the policy learns:
        ///
        ///   * KL(policy || target) - this function's order - is MODE-SEEKING. The average is taken under the POLICY,
        ///     so the policy pays for putting probability where the target has little, and hardly at all for missing
        ///     part of the target. A narrow policy inside a wide target is cheap - KL(N(0, 1) || N(0, 2^2)) = 0.318 -
        ///     while a wide policy around a narrow target is dear - KL(N(0, 2^2) || N(0, 1)) = 0.807 (the known answers
        ///     pin both numbers). Given a target with two modes, the policy settles on one of them.
        ///   * KL(target || policy) is MASS-COVERING: the policy pays for missing any part of the target, so it spreads
        ///     to cover all of it - and, given two modes, puts its centre in the gap between them.
        ///
        /// BMPC's code distills its planner into its policy with KL(policy || planner) - this order - although its
        /// paper writes KL(planner || policy); the code is what produced the results. PPO's trust region and a motion
        /// prior use the same order: the policy is the thing being judged against a fixed reference.
        ///
        /// ---- THE REFERENCE IS DATA ----
        ///
        /// It is passed as tensors, not graph values: the planner's target (BMPC), a recorded pose (a motion prior),
        /// the old policy (a trust region) - none of them is something the optimiser may move. Passing them as tensors
        /// makes that structural: there is no way to train the reference to agree with the policy, which would lower
        /// the loss beautifully and learn nothing. The tensors are wrapped, not copied: refill them and `recompute` to
        /// score the next batch against its own targets.
        ///
        /// ---- SHAPES: ONE SPREAD PER DIMENSION, OR ONE PER ROW ----
        ///
        /// `mean` and `reference_mean` are [rows, dims]. Each log standard deviation is either [1, dims] - one spread
        /// per dimension, shared by every row: a state-independent policy's (PPO's), a motion prior's fixed variance -
        /// or [rows, dims] - one per row: a STATE-DEPENDENT policy's (BMPC's, whose network outputs a spread for every
        /// state), the planner's target (whose spread differs at every replayed state). A shared spread is copied to
        /// every row by an exact product with a column of ones; from there on the arithmetic is the same either way.
        ///
        /// ---- A SUM, NOT A MEAN; AND THE SAFE DOMAIN ----
        ///
        /// The result is the true KL, SUMMED over dimensions. BMPC averages over the action's dimensions instead -
        /// `scale` by 1 / dims to match it. The composition exponentiates 2 log s_p and -2 log s_q, which stays finite
        /// at f32 for |log s| up to about 44 - far beyond BMPC's bounds (the policy's log-std in [-3, 1], the planner's
        /// std in [0.05, 2]). Composed from existing ops, so there is no new backward to get wrong.
        pub fn klGaussianDiag(
            self: *Self,
            mean: Var,
            log_std: Var,
            reference_mean: Tensor(T),
            reference_log_std: Tensor(T),
        ) Error!Var {
            const policy_mean_value: Tensor(T) = self.valueOf(mean);
            if (policy_mean_value.rank != 2 or reference_mean.rank != 2) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }
            const row_count: usize = policy_mean_value.shape[0];
            const dimension_count: usize = policy_mean_value.shape[1];
            if (reference_mean.shape[0] != row_count or reference_mean.shape[1] != dimension_count) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }
            const policy_spread_is_shared: bool = try logStdIsShared(self.valueOf(log_std), row_count, dimension_count);
            const reference_spread_is_shared: bool = try logStdIsShared(reference_log_std, row_count, dimension_count);

            // Every quantity as [rows, dims]: a shared spread copied to each row, a per-row one taken as it is.
            const reference_mean_rows: Var = try self.constant(reference_mean);
            const reference_log_std_given: Var = try self.constant(reference_log_std);
            const policy_log_std_rows: Var = if (policy_spread_is_shared)
                try self.copyToEveryRow(log_std, row_count)
            else
                log_std;
            const reference_log_std_rows: Var = if (reference_spread_is_shared)
                try self.copyToEveryRow(reference_log_std_given, row_count)
            else
                reference_log_std_given;

            // 1. The gap between the centres, squared: (m_p - m_q)^2.
            const mean_gap: Var = try self.sub(mean, reference_mean_rows);
            const squared_mean_gap: Var = try self.mul(mean_gap, mean_gap);
            // 2. The policy's variance, s_p^2 = exp(2 log s_p), and 1 / (2 s_q^2) = 0.5 exp(-2 log s_q).
            const policy_variance: Var = try self.exp(try self.scale(policy_log_std_rows, 2));
            const inverse_reference_variance: Var = try self.exp(try self.scale(reference_log_std_rows, -2));
            const half_inverse_reference_variance: Var = try self.scale(inverse_reference_variance, 0.5);
            // 3. The policy's spread and the centres' gap, measured in the reference's variance.
            const spread_plus_squared_gap: Var = try self.add(policy_variance, squared_mean_gap);
            const in_reference_variances: Var = try self.mul(spread_plus_squared_gap, half_inverse_reference_variance);
            // 4. The log of the width ratio: log s_q - log s_p.
            const log_std_gap: Var = try self.sub(reference_log_std_rows, policy_log_std_rows);
            // 5. Each dimension's divergence (without its -1/2), summed over the dimensions.
            const per_dimension: Var = try self.add(log_std_gap, in_reference_variances);
            const summed_over_dimensions: Var = try self.reduceRows(per_dimension, .sum);
            // 6. The -1/2 of every dimension, folded into one constant per row.
            const minus_half_per_dimension: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(self.gpa, &.{ row_count, 1 });
            @memset(minus_half_per_dimension.data, -0.5 * @as(T, @floatFromInt(dimension_count)));
            return self.add(summed_over_dimensions, try self.constant(minus_half_per_dimension));
        }

        /// A log standard deviation for `klGaussianDiag`: `true` when it is [1, dims] - one per dimension, shared by
        /// every row - and `false` when it is [rows, dims] - one per row. Anything else is refused.
        fn logStdIsShared(
            log_std: Tensor(T),
            row_count: usize,
            dimension_count: usize,
        ) Error!bool {
            if (log_std.rank != 2 or log_std.shape[1] != dimension_count) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }
            if (log_std.shape[0] == 1) {
                return true;
            }
            if (log_std.shape[0] == row_count) {
                return false;
            }
            return Error.ShapeMismatch;
        }

        /// A [1, dims] value copied to every one of `row_count` rows - `ones[rows, 1] . value`, an exact copy (each
        /// entry is 1 * x) that the tape already knows how to differentiate: the gradient of the copy is summed back
        /// over the rows, as a shared parameter's must be. How a per-feature parameter (a layer norm's gain, a shared
        /// log-std) meets a batch wherever an op wants equal shapes (`mul` does; `add` broadcasts by itself).
        pub fn copyToEveryRow(self: *Self, value: Var, row_count: usize) Error!Var {
            const column_of_ones: Var = try self.constant(try ones(T, self.gpa, &.{ row_count, 1 }));
            return self.matmul(column_of_ones, value);
        }

        /// A [rows, 1] column copied to every one of `column_count` columns - `column . ones[1, columns]`, an exact
        /// copy (each entry is x * 1): `copyToEveryRow`'s twin, along the other axis. The gradient of the copy is
        /// summed back across the columns. How a per-row weight - a 0 / 1 mask of the rows that count - meets a
        /// [rows, width] value wherever an op wants equal shapes (`mul` does).
        pub fn copyToEveryColumn(
            self: *Self,
            column: Var,
            column_count: usize,
        ) Error!Var {
            const row_of_ones: Var = try self.constant(try ones(T, self.gpa, &.{ 1, column_count }));
            return self.matmul(column, row_of_ones);
        }

        /// The differential ENTROPY of a diagonal Gaussian, per row, ON THE TAPE - `DiagGaussian.entropy`'s twin:
        ///
        ///       entropy = sum over d of ( log s_d + log(2 pi e) / 2 )
        ///
        /// In nats. It measures the Gaussian's SPREAD, so the mean never enters: shifting a Gaussian moves it without
        /// changing its shape. `log_std` is [rows, dims] - a spread per row, as a state-dependent policy has - or
        /// [1, dims], one shared spread; the result is [rows, 1]. Its gradient is exactly 1 for every log std (making
        /// any dimension e times wider adds one nat), so an entropy BONUS in a policy loss, `- coefficient *
        /// entropy`, pushes every log std up by the same steady amount - all it is meant to do: keep a policy from
        /// collapsing to a point before its targets justify it.
        pub fn diagGaussianEntropy(self: *Self, log_std: Var) Error!Var {
            const log_std_value: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[log_std];
            if (log_std_value.rank != 2 or log_std_value.shape[1] == 0) {
                return Error.UnsupportedShape;
            }
            const row_count: usize = log_std_value.shape[0];
            const dimension_count: T = @as(T, @floatFromInt(log_std_value.shape[1]));
            const summed_log_std: Var = try self.reduceRows(log_std, .sum);
            // The part that does not depend on the spread - log(2 pi e) / 2 per dimension - one constant per row.
            const shape_free_part: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(self.gpa, &.{ row_count, 1 });
            @memset(shape_free_part.data, dimension_count * (DiagGaussian(T).half_log_tau + 0.5));
            return self.add(summed_log_std, try self.constant(shape_free_part));
        }

        /// The log-probability a diagonal Gaussian assigns to each action, ON THE TAPE.
        ///
        /// ---- WHY THIS HAS TO EXIST FOR CONTINUOUS CONTROL ----
        ///
        /// `PpoClipLoss` takes the new log-probabilities as a `Var`, because the gradient has to
        /// flow back through them to the policy. `DiagGaussian.logProb` works on Tensors and is
        /// therefore a dead end: it gives the right number and no gradient, so a continuous
        /// policy could be evaluated and never trained. This is the missing link between a
        /// network that outputs `mean` and `log_std` and a loss that can be descended.
        ///
        /// ---- COMPOSED, NOT PRIMITIVE ----
        ///
        /// Every step is an existing differentiable op, so there is no new backward to get
        /// wrong. Two of them are doing a job their names do not suggest:
        ///
        ///   `matmul(ones[N,1], log_std[1,D])` BROADCASTS the per-dimension log_std across the
        ///   batch, because `mul` requires identical shapes here.
        ///   `matmul(per_dim[N,D], ones[D,1])` SUMS each row, because the tape has no axis
        ///   reduction. A Gaussian's log density is a sum over dimensions, so this is the step
        ///   that makes it one number per action rather than one per component.
        ///
        /// Both are differentiable by construction - a matmul against a constant is just a
        /// linear map, and the tape already knows its gradient.
        ///
        /// `actions` is a CONSTANT: they were drawn by the acting policy and are not something
        /// the update may move. Attaching them as a parameter instead would let the optimiser
        /// change history to lower the loss.
        pub fn diagGaussianLogProb(
            self: *Self,
            mean: Var,
            log_std: Var,
            actions: Tensor(T),
        ) Error!Var {
            const mean_value: Tensor(T) = self.valueOf(mean);
            if (mean_value.rank != 2 or actions.rank != 2) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }
            const rows: usize = mean_value.shape[0];
            const dims: usize = mean_value.shape[1];
            if (actions.shape[0] != rows or actions.shape[1] != dims) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }
            // `[1, D]`, not `[D]`. The broadcast across the batch is a matmul, and matmul needs
            // rank 2 - whereas `DiagGaussian.logProb` indexes with `at1` and wants rank 1. The
            // two spellings describe the same distribution; this one is what the tape can use.
            const std_value: Tensor(T) = self.valueOf(log_std);
            if (std_value.rank != 2 or std_value.shape[0] != 1 or std_value.shape[1] != dims) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }

            const ones_rows: Tensor(T) = try ones(T, self.gpa, &.{ rows, 1 });

            const row_ones: Var = try self.constant(ones_rows);
            const act: Var = try self.constant(actions);

            // log_std, one row per sample.
            const std_wide: Var = try self.matmul(row_ones, log_std);
            // (a - mu) / sigma, with sigma = exp(log_std).
            const centred: Var = try self.sub(act, mean);
            const inv_std: Var = try self.exp(try self.scale(std_wide, -1));
            const z: Var = try self.mul(centred, inv_std);
            // 0.5 * z^2 + log_std, per dimension.
            const half_sq: Var = try self.scale(try self.mul(z, z), 0.5);
            const per_dim: Var = try self.add(half_sq, std_wide);
            // Sum over dimensions, then the constant term, then negate.
            const summed: Var = try self.reduceRows(per_dim, .sum);
            const constant_term: T = @as(T, @floatCast(DiagGaussian(T).half_log_tau)) *
                @as(T, @floatFromInt(dims));
            const shifted: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(self.gpa, &.{ rows, 1 });
            @memset(shifted.data, constant_term);
            const offset: Var = try self.constant(shifted);
            return self.scale(try self.add(summed, offset), -1);
        }

        pub fn crossEntropy(self: *Self, logits: Var, labels: []const usize) Error!Var {
            const out: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(self.gpa, &.{ 1, 1 });
            out.data[0] = try crossEntropyRows(T, self.values.items[logits], labels);
            return self.push(
                out,
                .{ .op = .cross_entropy, .lhs = logits, .labels = labels },
                self.wants_grad.items[logits],
            );
        }

        /// SOFT-LABEL CROSS-ENTROPY of `logits` against the target DISTRIBUTION `targets` - both [rows, atoms] -
        /// averaged over the rows: the loss a categorical critic trains on (the math, and why it is computed in log
        /// space: `zimrnum.softCrossEntropyRows`). A single value, like every loss here.
        ///
        /// THE TARGET IS DATA, as in `mseLoss`: no gradient flows into it. A categorical critic's target is built
        /// from frozen target networks and a projection, and training must move the prediction toward it - never it
        /// toward the prediction. Refill the target's constant each update and `recompute`.
        pub fn softCrossEntropy(self: *Self, logits: Var, targets: Var) Error!Var {
            const predicted_logits: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[logits];
            const target_distribution: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[targets];
            const loss_value: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(self.gpa, &.{ 1, 1 });
            loss_value.data[0] = try softCrossEntropyRows(T, predicted_logits, target_distribution);
            // The target is recorded in `target` (read by the backward pass and `recompute`) but asks for no gradient:
            // only the logits decide whether this node wants one.
            const node: Node = .{ .op = .soft_cross_entropy, .lhs = logits, .target = targets };
            return self.push(loss_value, node, self.wants_grad.items[logits]);
        }

        /// Row-wise softmax of a rank-2 value.
        pub fn softmaxRows(self: *Self, a: Var) Error!Var {
            const va: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[a];
            const out: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(self.gpa, va.shape[0..va.rank]);
            try zimrnum.softmaxRows(T, out, va);
            return self.push(out, .{ .op = .softmax_op, .lhs = a }, self.wants_grad.items[a]);
        }

        /// SimNorm of a rank-2 value: a softmax within each consecutive group of `group` features - the last step of
        /// TD-MPC's encoder and dynamics (the math, and why a world model wants it: `zimrnum.simNormRows`). `group`
        /// equal to the width is `softmaxRows`. The group size travels in the node's `geometry[0]`, where the
        /// backward pass and `recompute` read it.
        pub fn simNorm(self: *Self, a: Var, group: usize) Error!Var {
            const input_value: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[a];
            const normalised: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(self.gpa, input_value.shape[0..input_value.rank]);
            try simNormRows(T, normalised, input_value, group);
            var geometry: [4]usize = @splat(0);
            geometry[0] = group;
            const node: Node = .{ .op = .sim_norm, .lhs = a, .geometry = geometry };
            return self.push(normalised, node, self.wants_grad.items[a]);
        }

        /// Row-wise layer normalisation of a rank-2 value.
        pub fn layerNormRows(self: *Self, a: Var, epsilon: T) Error!Var {
            const va: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[a];
            const out: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(self.gpa, va.shape[0..va.rank]);
            try zimrnum.layerNormRows(T, out, va, epsilon);
            return self.push(
                out,
                .{ .op = .layernorm_op, .lhs = a, .scalar = epsilon },
                self.wants_grad.items[a],
            );
        }

        /// 2-D convolution of a rank-2 value with a learned kernel.
        ///
        /// THE BACKWARD PASS IS THE FORWARD LOOP WITH THE ACCUMULATION REVERSED
        ///
        /// Forward, each output reads a window: `y[i][j] += x[i*s+a-p][j*s+b-p] * k[a][b]`. Both
        /// gradients fall out of that one line by moving what is read and what is written:
        ///
        /// dx[i*s+a-p][j*s+b-p] += g[i][j] * k[a][b]
        /// dk[a][b]             += g[i][j] * x[i*s+a-p][j*s+b-p]
        ///
        /// So the backward rule is the SAME loop nest with the same bounds and the same
        /// in-range test - which is why it is written as one pass producing both, rather than as
        /// the "full correlation with a flipped kernel" the textbooks give. That form is correct
        /// and is a second thing to get right; this one cannot disagree with the forward pass
        /// about which taps are in range, because it asks the identical question.
        pub fn conv2d(
            self: *Self,
            input: Var,
            kernel: Var,
            stride: [2]usize,
            pad: [2]usize,
        ) Error!Var {
            const x: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[input];
            const k: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[kernel];
            if (x.rank != 2 or k.rank != 2) {
                return Error.UnsupportedShape;
            }
            if (stride[0] == 0 or stride[1] == 0) {
                return Error.DomainError;
            }
            const out_h: usize = (x.shape[0] + 2 * pad[0] - k.shape[0]) / stride[0] + 1;
            const out_w: usize = (x.shape[1] + 2 * pad[1] - k.shape[1]) / stride[1] + 1;
            const out: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(self.gpa, &.{ out_h, out_w });
            try zimrnum.conv2d(T, out, x, k, stride, pad);
            return self.push(
                out,
                .{
                    .op = .conv2d_op,
                    .lhs = input,
                    .rhs = kernel,
                    .geometry = .{ stride[0], stride[1], pad[0], pad[1] },
                },
                self.wants_grad.items[input] or self.wants_grad.items[kernel],
            );
        }

        /// A contiguous run along one axis, as a differentiable operation.
        ///
        /// THE VIEW ALREADY EXISTS; WHAT IS NEW IS THE GRADIENT
        ///
        /// `Tensor.slice` gives a strided view for free, but a view carries no gradient, so
        /// slicing a computed value needs this node: multi-head attention splitting a projection,
        /// an LSTM slicing four fused gates out of one matmul.
        ///
        /// The backward is a scatter: the gradient lands in the rows the slice took and every
        /// other row gets zero, because a row nobody read cannot have influenced anything.
        pub fn slice(
            self: *Self,
            a: Var,
            axis: usize,
            start: usize,
            len: usize,
        ) Error!Var {
            const source: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[a];
            if (axis >= source.rank or start + len > source.shape[axis]) {
                return Error.OutOfRange;
            }
            var shape: [max_rank]usize = source.shape;
            shape[axis] = len;
            const out: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(self.gpa, shape[0..source.rank]);
            try materialise(T, out, try source.slice(axis, start, len));
            return self.push(
                out,
                .{ .op = .slice_op, .lhs = a, .geometry = .{ axis, start, len, 0 } },
                self.wants_grad.items[a],
            );
        }

        /// Two values joined along one axis, as a differentiable operation.
        ///
        /// The backward is the slice's, read in the other direction: each input gets back the
        /// part of the gradient that came from its own rows.
        pub fn concat(self: *Self, a: Var, b: Var, axis: usize) Error!Var {
            const first: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[a];
            const second: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[b];
            if (first.rank != second.rank or axis >= first.rank) {
                return Error.UnsupportedShape;
            }
            var shape: [max_rank]usize = first.shape;
            shape[axis] = first.shape[axis] + second.shape[axis];
            const out: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(self.gpa, shape[0..first.rank]);
            try zimrnum.concat(T, out, first, second, axis);
            return self.push(
                out,
                .{
                    .op = .concat_op,
                    .lhs = a,
                    .rhs = b,
                    .geometry = .{ axis, first.shape[axis], 0, 0 },
                },
                self.wants_grad.items[a] or self.wants_grad.items[b],
            );
        }

        /// Gather rows of a table by index: `out[i] = table[rows[i]]`.
        ///
        /// `rows` reuses the node's `labels` field, and here that is not a borrow - an
        /// embedding's indices ARE the same kind of thing as a classifier's labels: positions
        /// into a first axis, with no gradient of their own.
        ///
        /// The gradient is a SCATTER-ADD, and `+=` is the whole point: a token appearing three
        /// times in a batch must accumulate three contributions into one row of the table. A
        /// scatter that assigned would train on the last occurrence and silently discard the
        /// rest.
        pub fn embedding(self: *Self, table: Var, rows: []const usize) Error!Var {
            const t: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[table];
            if (t.rank != 2) {
                return Error.UnsupportedShape;
            }
            for (rows) |r| {
                if (r >= t.shape[0]) {
                    return Error.OutOfRange;
                }
            }
            const out: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(self.gpa, &.{ rows.len, t.shape[1] });
            try gatherRows(T, out, t, rows);
            return self.push(
                out,
                .{ .op = .embedding_op, .lhs = table, .labels = rows },
                self.wants_grad.items[table],
            );
        }

        /// The transpose of a rank-2 value, MATERIALISED.
        ///
        /// A view would be free on the CPU, but a value of the graph must be a tensor a later
        /// `matmul` can read and a later `recompute` can overwrite in place - and a transposed
        /// view of another value's storage is neither. The copy is the price of the tape owning
        /// every value it records. Its gradient is the transpose of the incoming one.
        pub fn transpose(self: *Self, a: Var) Error!Var {
            const va: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[a];
            if (va.rank != 2) {
                return Error.UnsupportedShape;
            }
            const out: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(self.gpa, &.{ va.shape[1], va.shape[0] });
            try materialise(T, out, try va.transpose(0, 1));
            return self.push(out, .{ .op = .transpose_op, .lhs = a }, self.wants_grad.items[a]);
        }

        /// THE CHOSEN COLUMNS OF EVERY ROW, DIFFERENTIABLY: out[r][k] = input[r][columns[k]] - `gatherColumns` on the
        /// graph, for a policy that watches only part of the state (an asymmetric observation).
        ///
        /// No new op: a product with a constant 0/1 SELECTION MATRIX S, [width, chosen], whose column k holds a single
        /// 1, in row columns[k]:
        ///
        ///       out = input . S          S for columns = { 3, 0 } of a width-4 input:     [ 0  1 ]
        ///                                                                                  [ 0  0 ]
        ///                                                                                  [ 0  0 ]
        ///                                                                                  [ 1  0 ]
        ///
        /// It is EXACT, not approximate: each output is one input times 1 plus every other times 0, and adding zeros
        /// changes nothing - so choosing every column in order gives back the input, equal as numbers (a negative zero
        /// comes back as zero: -0 + 0 is +0). The gradient returns through matmul's own backward, grad . S^T: each
        /// chosen column gets its output's gradient (both, summed, if chosen twice) and every other exactly zero.
        ///
        /// S is the one-hot ROWS of `columns` (`oneHotRows`), transposed. The input must be finite - 0 * infinity is
        /// NaN, so one infinite feature, chosen or not, would spoil its row. The product costs rows * width * chosen,
        /// where a dedicated gather would cost rows * chosen; for observations a few hundred wide on the CPU that is
        /// cheap, and needs no backward of its own (a dedicated gather belongs to the GPU kit).
        pub fn gatherColumns(self: *Self, input: Var, columns: []const usize) Error!Var {
            const input_value: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[input];
            if (input_value.rank != 2) {
                return Error.UnsupportedShape;
            }
            const input_width: usize = input_value.shape[1];
            for (columns) |column| {
                if (column >= input_width) {
                    return Error.OutOfRange;
                }
            }
            const picks_by_row: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(self.gpa, &.{ columns.len, input_width });
            try oneHotRows(T, picks_by_row, columns);
            const picks_by_row_var: Var = try self.constant(picks_by_row);
            const selection_matrix: Var = try self.transpose(picks_by_row_var);
            return self.matmul(input, selection_matrix);
        }

        /// `out = a * factor`.
        pub fn scale(self: *Self, a: Var, factor: T) Error!Var {
            const va: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[a];
            const out: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(self.gpa, va.shape[0..va.rank]);
            try zimrnum.scale(T, out, va, factor);
            return self.push(
                out,
                .{ .op = .scale_op, .lhs = a, .scalar = factor },
                self.wants_grad.items[a],
            );
        }

        /// Inverted dropout: each element is kept with probability `1 - rate` and scaled by
        /// `1 / (1 - rate)`, so the expected value is unchanged.
        ///
        /// THE MASK IS DRAWN ONCE AND STORED
        ///
        /// A dropout that redrew its mask on every `recompute` would be a different function each
        /// time - `checkGradient` would compare a derivative against a finite difference of
        /// something else and report noise. The mask is a value of the graph, fixed until
        /// `resampleDropout` is called, which a training loop does once per step.
        ///
        /// Inverted scaling means nothing changes at inference: dropping the operation from the
        /// graph is exactly equivalent to `rate = 0`, with no `1 - rate` factor to remember.
        ///
        /// ONE GENERATOR PER NODE
        ///
        /// The mask is a function of `rng` and each element's index alone, so two dropout nodes of
        /// one shape given the same generator draw the SAME mask. Give each its own split - one per
        /// network, per step, per head - as `resampleDropout` does for every node.
        pub fn dropout(self: *Self, a: Var, rate: T, rng: Rng) Error!Var {
            if (rate < 0 or rate >= 1) {
                return Error.DomainError;
            }
            const va: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[a];
            const shape: []const usize = va.shape[0..va.rank];
            const mask: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(self.gpa, shape);
            const keep: T = 1 - rate;
            fillDropoutMask(T, mask, rng, keep);
            const mask_var: Var = try self.constant(mask);
            const out: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(self.gpa, shape);
            try zimrnum.mul(T, out, va, mask);
            return self.push(
                out,
                .{ .op = .dropout_op, .lhs = a, .mask = mask_var, .scalar = keep },
                self.wants_grad.items[a],
            );
        }

        /// Draw fresh masks for every dropout node, from a new generator: each node from its own
        /// split of it, `rng.split(node index)`, so no two nodes share a mask - two value heads, or
        /// one head at two steps of a rollout, drop independently, as separate forward passes would
        /// - and the masks are reproducible from the generator.
        pub fn resampleDropout(self: *Self, rng: Rng) void {
            for (self.nodes.items, 0..) |node, node_index| {
                if (node.op == .dropout_op) {
                    const node_rng: Rng = rng.split(@intCast(node_index));
                    fillDropoutMask(T, self.values.items[node.mask], node_rng, node.scalar);
                }
            }
        }

        /// Mean squared error against `target`, as a 1x1 value so it is a `Var` like any other.
        pub fn mseLoss(self: *Self, a: Var, target: Var) Error!Var {
            const out: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(self.gpa, &.{ 1, 1 });
            out.data[0] = try zimrnum.mseLoss(T, self.values.items[a], self.values.items[target]);
            return self.push(
                out,
                .{ .op = .mse, .lhs = a, .target = target },
                self.wants_grad.items[a],
            );
        }

        /// TD4'S PRE-ACTIVATION PENALTY: how far a tanh policy's pre-activations `u` ([rows, actions]) stray outside
        /// [-1, 1], squared - a [1, 1] value:
        ///
        ///       penalty = mean over rows of  sum over columns of  relu(u - 1)^2 + relu(-u - 1)^2
        ///
        ///       one value's share:    (|u| - 1)^2 outside [-1, 1], nothing inside
        ///
        ///             \                                   /
        ///              \                                 /
        ///               '.                             .'
        ///       ___________'-..___________________..-'___________  u
        ///                       -1               1
        ///
        /// A tanh actor saturates: once |u| is large, tanh(u) is flat, the critic's gradient barely reaches the
        /// weights, and the action sticks at its bound. The penalty pulls u back toward the range where tanh still
        /// responds, and costs nothing inside it. Written as two relus rather than relu(|u| - 1): an absolute value
        /// would put a kink at u = 0 on the tape, where each relu's kink sits at +-1, where the penalty is zero
        /// anyway. The actor's loss adds it with a small coefficient (TD4's; off in their benchmark).
        pub fn preActivationPenalty(self: *Self, pre_activation: Var) Error!Var {
            const pre_activation_value: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[pre_activation];
            if (pre_activation_value.rank != 2) {
                return Error.UnsupportedShape;
            }
            const column_count: usize = pre_activation_value.shape[1];
            // One row of -1s; `add` broadcasts it over every row, so u + (-1) is u - 1 everywhere.
            const minus_one_row: Var = try self.constant(try full(T, self.gpa, &.{ 1, column_count }, -1));
            const excess_above_one: Var = try self.relu(try self.add(pre_activation, minus_one_row));
            const negated_pre_activation: Var = try self.scale(pre_activation, -1);
            const excess_below_minus_one: Var = try self.relu(try self.add(negated_pre_activation, minus_one_row));
            // Per row, the sum of both excesses squared: [rows, 1].
            const above_per_row: Var = try self.squaredRowNorm(excess_above_one);
            const below_per_row: Var = try self.squaredRowNorm(excess_below_minus_one);
            const penalty_per_row: Var = try self.add(above_per_row, below_per_row);
            // The mean over rows: the column of per-row values laid on its side, then averaged across.
            const penalty_per_row_as_one_row: Var = try self.transpose(penalty_per_row);
            return self.reduceRows(penalty_per_row_as_one_row, .mean);
        }

        /// Propagate a gradient of 1 from `loss` back to every parameter.
        ///
        /// THE SEED IS 1, AND THAT IS WHY `loss` MUST BE A SINGLE VALUE. Differentiating a
        /// tensor with respect to parameters gives a Jacobian, not a gradient; reverse mode
        /// answers "how does THIS ONE NUMBER change", so the entry point takes a scalar and
        /// seeds it with its own derivative with respect to itself.
        pub fn backward(self: *Self, loss: Var) Error!void {
            // One pass's temporaries (see `scratch`): last pass's are dead by now.
            _ = self.scratch.reset(.retain_capacity);
            const temp: Allocator = self.scratch.allocator();
            if (self.values.items[loss].size() != 1) {
                return Error.UnsupportedShape;
            }
            for (self.grads.items, self.wants_grad.items) |g, wants| {
                if (wants) {
                    g.fill(0);
                }
            }
            self.grads.items[loss].fill(1);

            var i: usize = self.nodes.items.len;
            while (i > 0) {
                i -= 1;
                if (!self.wants_grad.items[i]) {
                    continue;
                }
                const node: Node = self.nodes.items[i];
                const g: Tensor(T) = self.grads.items[i];
                switch (node.op) {
                    .leaf => {},
                    .add => {
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, g);
                        try self.accumulate(node.rhs, g);
                    },
                    .sub_op => {
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, g);
                        const shape: []const usize = g.shape[0..g.rank];
                        const negated: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, shape);
                        try neg(T, negated, g);
                        try self.accumulate(node.rhs, negated);
                    },
                    .reduce_sum_rows_op => {
                        // Every element of a row contributed equally, so each receives the row's
                        // whole incoming gradient. A broadcast, not a division - `mean` gets its
                        // `1/D` from the `scale` it is composed with.
                        const in: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.lhs];
                        const rows: usize = in.shape[0];
                        const cols: usize = in.shape[1];
                        const scratch: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, &.{ rows, cols });
                        for (0..rows) |r| {
                            const share: T = g.data[g.base + r];
                            for (0..cols) |c| {
                                scratch.data[scratch.base + r * cols + c] = share;
                            }
                        }
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, scratch);
                    },
                    .reduce_max_rows_op => {
                        // The mask says which element the value came from, so this is the same
                        // broadcast as `.sum` with the losers zeroed. No argmax is computed here
                        // - see `reduceRows` for why re-deriving it would be a second decision.
                        const in: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.lhs];
                        const mask: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.mask];
                        const rows: usize = in.shape[0];
                        const cols: usize = in.shape[1];
                        const scratch: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, &.{ rows, cols });
                        for (0..rows) |r| {
                            const share: T = g.data[g.base + r];
                            for (0..cols) |c| {
                                const at: usize = r * cols + c;
                                scratch.data[scratch.base + at] = share * mask.data[mask.base + at];
                            }
                        }
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, scratch);
                    },
                    .min_op => {
                        // ---- THE GRADIENT GOES TO WHICHEVER SIDE WON ----
                        //
                        // `min` is not differentiable where the two inputs are equal, and that
                        // is not a corner case to be clever about: the convention is to route
                        // the whole gradient to ONE side and zero to the other. Splitting it
                        // evenly at ties would be defensible in isolation and wrong in context -
                        // DroQ takes the min over dropout masks of the SAME network, so the two
                        // inputs are frequently equal early in training when dropout has not yet
                        // diversified them, and a half-gradient to each would quietly halve the
                        // effective learning rate exactly when the critic is furthest from right.
                        //
                        // Ties go to the LEFT, matching `@min`'s own behaviour and the
                        // lowest-index rule `Categorical.greedy` uses: decided, not better.
                        const left: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.lhs];
                        const right: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.rhs];
                        const shape: []const usize = g.shape[0..g.rank];
                        const to_left: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, shape);
                        const to_right: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, shape);
                        for (g.data, left.data, right.data, 0..) |grad, l, r, k| {
                            const left_wins: bool = l <= r;
                            to_left.data[k] = if (left_wins) grad else 0;
                            to_right.data[k] = if (left_wins) 0 else grad;
                        }
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, to_left);
                        try self.accumulate(node.rhs, to_right);
                    },
                    .mul_op => {
                        // Each side's gradient is the OTHER side's value times the incoming one.
                        const shape: []const usize = g.shape[0..g.rank];
                        const scratch: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, shape);
                        try zimrnum.mul(T, scratch, g, self.values.items[node.rhs]);
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, scratch);
                        const other: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, shape);
                        try zimrnum.mul(T, other, g, self.values.items[node.lhs]);
                        try self.accumulate(node.rhs, other);
                    },
                    // A stop-gradient: whatever arrived here goes no further.
                    .detach => {},
                    .relu_op => {
                        // reluGrad takes the forward INPUT, which is what `lhs` holds.
                        const in: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.lhs];
                        const shape: []const usize = in.shape[0..in.rank];
                        const scratch: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, shape);
                        try reluGrad(T, scratch, in, g);
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, scratch);
                    },
                    .sigmoid_op => {
                        // sigmoidGrad takes the forward OUTPUT, which is this node's value.
                        const out: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[i];
                        const shape: []const usize = out.shape[0..out.rank];
                        const scratch: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, shape);
                        try sigmoidGrad(T, scratch, out, g);
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, scratch);
                    },
                    .cross_entropy => {
                        const in: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.lhs];
                        const shape: []const usize = in.shape[0..in.rank];
                        const scratch: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, shape);
                        try crossEntropyRowsGrad(T, scratch, in, node.labels);
                        try zimrnum.scale(T, scratch, scratch, g.data[g.base]);
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, scratch);
                    },
                    .soft_cross_entropy => {
                        // d loss / d logits = (target mass * predicted - target) / rows, the row's target mass being
                        // the sum of its target - predicted - target for a target that is a distribution, and exactly
                        // zero for an all-zero target row (how WorldModelLoss leaves out a finished window) - times
                        // the gradient arriving from above (1 when this IS the loss; anything else when the loss was
                        // scaled or summed on top of it). Nothing flows into the target: it is data.
                        const predicted_logits: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.lhs];
                        const shape: []const usize = predicted_logits.shape[0..predicted_logits.rank];
                        const logit_gradient: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, shape);
                        const target_distribution: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.target];
                        try softCrossEntropyRowsGrad(T, logit_gradient, predicted_logits, target_distribution);
                        try zimrnum.scale(T, logit_gradient, logit_gradient, g.data[g.base]);
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, logit_gradient);
                    },
                    .softmax_op => {
                        // dx = y * (g - sum(g * y)) per row: the Jacobian of a softmax applied
                        // to g, without forming it.
                        const y: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[i];
                        const scratch: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, y.shape[0..y.rank]);
                        try softmaxBackward(T, scratch, y, g);
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, scratch);
                    },
                    .sim_norm => {
                        // A softmax's backward, group by group, from this node's OUTPUT (as softmax's is).
                        const normalised_output: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[i];
                        const shape: []const usize = normalised_output.shape[0..normalised_output.rank];
                        const input_gradient: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, shape);
                        const group: usize = node.geometry[0];
                        try simNormRowsGrad(T, input_gradient, normalised_output, g, group);
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, input_gradient);
                    },
                    .layernorm_op => {
                        const y: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[i];
                        const x: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.lhs];
                        const scratch: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, y.shape[0..y.rank]);
                        try layerNormRowsBackward(T, scratch, x, g, node.scalar);
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, scratch);
                    },
                    .conv2d_op => {
                        const x: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.lhs];
                        const k: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.rhs];
                        const dx: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, x.shape[0..2]);
                        const dk: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, k.shape[0..2]);
                        dx.fill(0);
                        dk.fill(0);
                        try conv2dBackward(T, dx, dk, x, k, g, node.geometry);
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, dx);
                        try self.accumulate(node.rhs, dk);
                    },
                    .embedding_op => {
                        const t: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.lhs];
                        const dt: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, t.shape[0..2]);
                        dt.fill(0);
                        try scatterAddRows(T, dt, g, node.labels);
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, dt);
                    },
                    .transpose_op => {
                        const in: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.lhs];
                        const scratch: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, in.shape[0..in.rank]);
                        try materialise(T, scratch, try g.transpose(0, 1));
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, scratch);
                    },
                    .exp_op => {
                        // `d/dx exp(x)` is `exp(x)` - the value already computed, so the
                        // backward reads the forward's output rather than recomputing it.
                        const value: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[i];
                        const scratch: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(
                            temp,
                            value.shape[0..value.rank],
                        );
                        try zimrnum.mul(T, scratch, g, value);
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, scratch);
                    },
                    .log_op => {
                        // `d/dx log(x)` is `1/x`, and `x` is the INPUT - the one case here where
                        // the output is not enough.
                        const source: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.lhs];
                        const scratch: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(
                            temp,
                            source.shape[0..source.rank],
                        );
                        try zimrnum.div(T, scratch, g, source);
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, scratch);
                    },
                    .softplus_op => {
                        // `d/dx softplus(x)` is exactly `sigmoid(x)` - no branch and nothing to
                        // derive, which is what makes a dedicated node cheap despite the stable
                        // forward being more than one line.
                        const source: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.lhs];
                        const scratch: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(
                            temp,
                            source.shape[0..source.rank],
                        );
                        try zimrnum.sigmoid(T, scratch, source);
                        try zimrnum.mul(T, scratch, g, scratch);
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, scratch);
                    },
                    .elu_op => {
                        // `1` above zero, `alpha * exp(x)` below - read from the INPUT, because
                        // only the input says which side of the branch a value was on.
                        const source: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.lhs];
                        const scratch: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(
                            temp,
                            source.shape[0..source.rank],
                        );
                        var walk: Walk = .over(source.shape[0..source.rank]);
                        while (walk.next()) |at| {
                            const x: T = try source.at(at);
                            const slope: T = if (x > 0) 1 else node.scalar * @exp(x);
                            try scratch.setAt(at, (try g.at(at)) * slope);
                        }
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, scratch);
                    },
                    .mish_op => {
                        // The slope read from the INPUT, one exponential per element (`zm.mishSlope`).
                        const source: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.lhs];
                        const scratch: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(
                            temp,
                            source.shape[0..source.rank],
                        );
                        var walk: Walk = .over(source.shape[0..source.rank]);
                        while (walk.next()) |at| {
                            const slope: T = zm.mishSlope(try source.at(at));
                            try scratch.setAt(at, (try g.at(at)) * slope);
                        }
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, scratch);
                    },
                    .slice_op => {
                        // A SCATTER: the gradient lands where the slice read, and every other
                        // row gets zero - a row nobody read influenced nothing.
                        const source: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.lhs];
                        const scratch: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(
                            temp,
                            source.shape[0..source.rank],
                        );
                        scratch.fill(0);
                        const window: Tensor(T) = try scratch.slice(
                            node.geometry[0],
                            node.geometry[1],
                            node.geometry[2],
                        );
                        var walk: Walk = .over(g.shape[0..g.rank]);
                        while (walk.next()) |at| {
                            try window.setAt(at, try g.at(at));
                        }
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, scratch);
                    },
                    .concat_op => {
                        // The slice's backward read the other way: each input takes back the
                        // part of the gradient that came from its own rows.
                        const axis: usize = node.geometry[0];
                        const split: usize = node.geometry[1];
                        const left: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.lhs];
                        const right: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.rhs];
                        const left_grad: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(
                            temp,
                            left.shape[0..left.rank],
                        );
                        try materialise(T, left_grad, try g.slice(axis, 0, split));
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, left_grad);
                        const right_grad: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(
                            temp,
                            right.shape[0..right.rank],
                        );
                        try materialise(T, right_grad, try g.slice(axis, split, right.shape[axis]));
                        try self.accumulate(node.rhs, right_grad);
                    },
                    .scale_op => {
                        const scratch: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, g.shape[0..g.rank]);
                        try zimrnum.scale(T, scratch, g, node.scalar);
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, scratch);
                    },
                    .dropout_op => {
                        // The same mask that scaled the forward pass scales the gradient.
                        const scratch: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, g.shape[0..g.rank]);
                        try zimrnum.mul(T, scratch, g, self.values.items[node.mask]);
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, scratch);
                    },
                    .matmul => try self.matmulBackward(node, g),
                    .tanh_op => {
                        const out: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[i];
                        const shape: []const usize = out.shape[0..out.rank];
                        const scratch: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, shape);
                        try tanhGrad(T, scratch, out, g);
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, scratch);
                    },
                    .mse => {
                        const a: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.lhs];
                        const shape: []const usize = a.shape[0..a.rank];
                        const scratch: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(temp, shape);
                        try zimrnum.sub(T, scratch, a, self.values.items[node.target]);
                        const n: T = @floatFromInt(a.size());
                        try zimrnum.scale(T, scratch, scratch, 2 * g.data[g.base] / n);
                        try self.accumulate(node.lhs, scratch);
                    },
                }
            }
        }

        /// Replay the recorded operations forward, refreshing every computed value.
        ///
        /// WHAT MAKES THE TAPE A MODEL RATHER THAN A ONE-SHOT
        ///
        /// Without this a graph is single-use: a training loop would have to rebuild it every
        /// step, allocating the whole tape again for a forward pass that differs only in the
        /// numbers. Replaying instead writes new values into the buffers already allocated.
        ///
        /// It is also what makes `checkGradient` possible. Verifying a derivative numerically
        /// means evaluating the SAME function at a perturbed input, and "the same function" is
        /// exactly what the tape is a record of.
        ///
        /// Leaves are skipped: their values are whatever the caller last wrote, which is how a
        /// new batch of inputs enters an existing graph.
        pub fn recompute(self: *Self) Error!void {
            for (self.nodes.items, 0..) |node, i| {
                const out: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[i];
                switch (node.op) {
                    .leaf => {},
                    .add => try zimrnum.add(
                        T,
                        out,
                        self.values.items[node.lhs],
                        self.values.items[node.rhs],
                    ),
                    .sub_op => try zimrnum.sub(
                        T,
                        out,
                        self.values.items[node.lhs],
                        self.values.items[node.rhs],
                    ),
                    .mul_op => try zimrnum.mul(
                        T,
                        out,
                        self.values.items[node.lhs],
                        self.values.items[node.rhs],
                    ),
                    .min_op => try zimrnum.minimum(
                        T,
                        out,
                        self.values.items[node.lhs],
                        self.values.items[node.rhs],
                    ),
                    .matmul => try zimrnum.matmul(
                        T,
                        out,
                        self.values.items[node.lhs],
                        self.values.items[node.rhs],
                    ),
                    .tanh_op => try zimrnum.tanh(T, out, self.values.items[node.lhs]),
                    .detach => try zimrnum.scale(T, out, self.values.items[node.lhs], 1),
                    .relu_op => try zimrnum.relu(T, out, self.values.items[node.lhs]),
                    .sigmoid_op => try zimrnum.sigmoid(T, out, self.values.items[node.lhs]),
                    .softmax_op => try zimrnum.softmaxRows(T, out, self.values.items[node.lhs]),
                    .sim_norm => try simNormRows(T, out, self.values.items[node.lhs], node.geometry[0]),
                    .layernorm_op => try zimrnum.layerNormRows(
                        T,
                        out,
                        self.values.items[node.lhs],
                        node.scalar,
                    ),
                    .conv2d_op => try zimrnum.conv2d(
                        T,
                        out,
                        self.values.items[node.lhs],
                        self.values.items[node.rhs],
                        .{ node.geometry[0], node.geometry[1] },
                        .{ node.geometry[2], node.geometry[3] },
                    ),
                    .embedding_op => try gatherRows(
                        T,
                        out,
                        self.values.items[node.lhs],
                        node.labels,
                    ),
                    .transpose_op => try materialise(
                        T,
                        out,
                        try self.values.items[node.lhs].transpose(0, 1),
                    ),
                    .exp_op => try zimrnum.exp(T, out, self.values.items[node.lhs]),
                    .log_op => try zimrnum.log(T, out, self.values.items[node.lhs]),
                    .softplus_op => try zimrnum.softplus(T, out, self.values.items[node.lhs]),
                    .elu_op => try zimrnum.elu(T, out, self.values.items[node.lhs], node.scalar),
                    .mish_op => try zimrnum.mish(T, out, self.values.items[node.lhs]),
                    .slice_op => try materialise(T, out, try self.values.items[node.lhs].slice(
                        node.geometry[0],
                        node.geometry[1],
                        node.geometry[2],
                    )),
                    .concat_op => try zimrnum.concat(
                        T,
                        out,
                        self.values.items[node.lhs],
                        self.values.items[node.rhs],
                        node.geometry[0],
                    ),
                    .scale_op => try zimrnum.scale(T, out, self.values.items[node.lhs], node.scalar),
                    .reduce_sum_rows_op => {
                        const in: Tensor(T) = self.values.items[node.lhs];
                        const cols: usize = in.shape[1];
                        for (0..in.shape[0]) |r| {
                            var total: CompensatedSum(T) = .{};
                            for (0..cols) |c| {
                                total.add(in.data[in.base + r * cols + c]);
                            }
                            out.data[out.base + r] = total.value();
                        }
                    },
                    .reduce_max_rows_op => fillRowMaxAndMask(
                        T,
                        out,
                        self.values.items[node.mask],
                        self.values.items[node.lhs],
                    ),
                    .dropout_op => try zimrnum.mul(
                        T,
                        out,
                        self.values.items[node.lhs],
                        self.values.items[node.mask],
                    ),
                    .cross_entropy => out.data[out.base] = try crossEntropyRows(
                        T,
                        self.values.items[node.lhs],
                        node.labels,
                    ),
                    .soft_cross_entropy => out.data[out.base] = try softCrossEntropyRows(
                        T,
                        self.values.items[node.lhs],
                        self.values.items[node.target],
                    ),
                    .mse => out.data[out.base] = try zimrnum.mseLoss(
                        T,
                        self.values.items[node.lhs],
                        self.values.items[node.target],
                    ),
                }
            }
        }

        /// The largest disagreement between the tape's gradient for `param` and a central finite
        /// difference of `loss`, over every element of `param`.
        ///
        /// THE ONE CHECK THAT DOES NOT REPEAT THE DERIVATION
        ///
        /// A hand-written backward pass and a tape rule can both be wrong in the same way,
        /// because the same person derived them. A finite difference does not know the
        /// derivative at all - it only evaluates the function twice - so agreement between the
        /// two is evidence about the derivative rather than about the deriver.
        ///
        /// CENTRAL, NOT FORWARD. `(f(x+h) - f(x-h)) / 2h` has error O(h^2) where
        /// `(f(x+h) - f(x)) / h` has O(h); at a usable `h` that is the difference between
        /// agreeing to six digits and to three, which decides whether a real error is visible
        /// above the noise.
        ///
        /// Every value is restored and the graph recomputed before returning, so calling this
        /// leaves the model exactly as it found it.
        pub fn checkGradient(self: *Self, loss: Var, param: Var, h: T) Error!T {
            comptime requireFloat(T);
            if (h <= 0) {
