    var pair: Walk2 = .over(prediction.shape[0..prediction.rank], truth.shape[0..truth.rank]);
    while (pair.next()) |at| {
        const predicted: T = try prediction.at(at.first);
        const observed: T = try truth.at(at.second);
        residual.add((observed - predicted) * (observed - predicted));
        total.add((observed - mean) * (observed - mean));
    }
    const denominator: T = total.value();
    if (denominator == 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    return 1 - residual.value() / denominator;
}
cosineSimilarity
/// The cosine of the angle between two tensors read as vectors.
///
/// `DomainError` for a zero vector, which has no direction to compare. Returning 0 would mean
/// "perpendicular", and a zero vector is not perpendicular to anything - it is undefined, and
/// silently calling it orthogonal is how a degenerate embedding becomes a plausible-looking
/// similarity score.
pub fn cosineSimilarity(comptime T: type, a: Tensor(T), b: Tensor(T)) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    if (a.size() != b.size()) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }
    const norm_a: T = try norm(T, a);
    const norm_b: T = try norm(T, b);
    if (norm_a == 0 or norm_b == 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    return (try dotAll(T, a, b)) / (norm_a * norm_b);
}
hingeLoss
/// Hinge loss for binary labels in `{-1, +1}`: `mean(max(0, 1 - label * score))`.
///
/// The margin is 1, not 0: a sample classified correctly but only just still contributes, which
/// is what pushes the boundary away from the data rather than merely onto the right side of it.
/// That margin is the whole difference between a hinge loss and a step function.
pub fn hingeLoss(comptime T: type, scores: Tensor(T), labels: Tensor(T)) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const n: usize = scores.size();
    if (n != labels.size()) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }
    if (n == 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    var total: CompensatedSum(T) = .{};
    var pair: Walk2 = .over(scores.shape[0..scores.rank], labels.shape[0..labels.rank]);
    while (pair.next()) |at| {
        const score: T = try scores.at(at.first);
        const label: T = try labels.at(at.second);
        total.add(@max(0, 1 - label * score));
    }
    return total.value() / @as(T, @floatFromInt(n));
}

Precision is "of everything called class k, how much was". If the model never predicted k at all, that denominator is zero and the quantity is genuinely undefined — there is no fraction of predictions that were right when there were no predictions. This returns 0, as scikit-learn does, because a macro average has to average something. But 0 is a lie in a specific way: it says every prediction of this class was wrong, when the truth is that there were none.

So ClassScore carries precision_undefined and recall_undefined alongside the numbers. The average uses the plain zeros; a caller who cares can tell the two kinds of zero apart. The test is built around a class that occurs once in the truth and is never predicted, so recall is a real zero — the model missed it — while precision's zero describes nothing.

r2Score can be negative, and that is information. The name says "R squared" and squares are not negative, which misleads nearly everyone who meets it. 1 − ss_res/ss_tot goes below zero whenever the model does worse than predicting the mean, which happens and is exactly what you want to be told. Clamping at zero would turn "worse than a constant" into "explains nothing", and those are different. A constant truth is DomainError: there is no variation to explain.

cosineSimilarity refuses a zero vector rather than returning 0. Zero would mean "perpendicular", and a zero vector is not perpendicular to anything — silently calling it orthogonal is how a degenerate embedding becomes a plausible-looking similarity score.

10.12 Chain, and the quietest bug in the file#

const Net = zn.Chain(f64, struct {
    first:  zn.Dense(f64),
    second: zn.Dense(f64),
});
const run = try net.attach(&graph, x);
var opt = try zn.Optimizer(f64).init(gpa, &graph, &run.parameters, .{ .adam = ... });
Chain
/// Layers run in order, with their parameters collected for you.
///
/// COLLECTING THE PARAMETERS IS THE POINT; RUNNING THEM IN ORDER IS THE EASY HALF
///
/// Writing the forward pass by hand is fine - three calls, three named intermediates, and the
/// names help when a shape is wrong. What is NOT fine is the line after it:
///
///     &.{ a1.weight, a1.bias, a2.weight, a2.bias }
///
/// That list is written by hand today, and **a parameter left out of it silently never trains**.
/// The loss still falls, because the other parameters compensate; the network is simply worse
/// than it should be, and nothing anywhere says so. It is the quietest bug in the file.
///
/// A `Chain` holds its layers in a tuple and hands back every parameter it attached, in order,
/// so the list cannot disagree with the network. It carries a tuple and a count: the graph already
/// composes layers, so no table of fused activations is needed.
pub fn Chain(comptime T: type, comptime Layers: type) type {
    return struct {
        layers: Layers,

        const Self = @This();
        const info = @typeInfo(Layers).@"struct";

        /// Every parameter this chain attached, in the order the layers were listed.
        ///
        /// A fixed array rather than a slice: the size is known at comptime from the layer list,
        /// so there is nothing to allocate and nothing to free.
        pub const Parameters = [parameterCount()]Var;

        /// What `attach` hands back: the last layer's output, and every parameter on the way.
        pub const Run = struct {
            out: Var,
            parameters: Parameters,
        };

        /// How many `Var`s `attach` will produce, counted at comptime from the layer types.
        ///
        /// Every layer declares `pub const Attached`, whose fields are `out` plus one per
        /// parameter - so the count is the field count less one, and it comes from the layer
        /// ITSELF rather than from a table here that could fall out of step with it.
        fn parameterCount() usize {
            var total: usize = 0;
            for (info.field_types) |Layer| {
                total += @typeInfo(Layer.Attached).@"struct".field_names.len - 1;
            }
            return total;
        }

        /// Run every layer in order and collect what they attached.
        pub fn attach(self: Self, graph: *Graph(T), input: Var) Error!Run {
            var current: Var = input;
            var collected: Parameters = undefined;
            comptime var next: usize = 0;
            inline for (info.field_names) |layer_name| {
                const Layer: type = @FieldType(Layers, layer_name);
                const attached: Layer.Attached = try @field(self.layers, layer_name).attach(graph, current);
                current = attached.out;
                inline for (@typeInfo(@TypeOf(attached)).@"struct".field_names) |slot| {
                    if (comptime !eql(u8, slot, "out")) {
                        collected[next] = @field(attached, slot);
                        next += 1;
                    }
                }
            }
            return .{ .out = current, .parameters = collected };
        }
    };
}
Dense
pub fn Dense(comptime T: type) type {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    return struct {
        const Self = @This();

        weight: Tensor(T),
        bias: Tensor(T),

        /// Allocate and initialise. `He` for a layer feeding a rectifier, `Xavier` otherwise.
        pub fn init(
            gpa: Allocator,
            rng: Rng,
            fan_in: usize,
            fan_out: usize,
            scheme: InitScheme,
        ) Error!Self {
            const weight: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(gpa, &.{ fan_in, fan_out });
            errdefer gpa.free(weight.data);
            const bias: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(gpa, &.{ 1, fan_out });
            switch (scheme) {
                .xavier => try initXavier(T, weight, rng, fan_in, fan_out),
                .he => try initHe(T, weight, rng, fan_in),
                .small_normal => try initNormal(T, weight, rng, small_normal_deviation),
            }
            // Biases start at zero. A random bias adds nothing a random weight does not already
            // provide, and a non-zero one shifts every unit's activation before any data is seen.
            bias.fill(0);
            return .{ .weight = weight, .bias = bias };
        }

        /// What `attach` hands back: the output, and handles for the two parameters.
        ///
        /// RETURNING ONLY THE OUTPUT IS NOT ENOUGH, which a first attempt at a training loop
        /// showed immediately: the loop needs the parameter handles to read their gradients, and
        /// with the layer holding no `Var` there is nowhere else to get them. Returning all three
        /// keeps the layer graph-agnostic AND gives the caller what a step requires.
        pub const Attached = struct {
            out: Var,
            weight: Var,
            bias: Var,
        };

        /// Record `input @ weight + bias` onto `graph`, the weight and bias TRAINED (as parameters).
        pub fn attach(self: Self, graph: *Graph(T), input: Var) Error!Attached {
            return self.attachAs(graph, input, .trained);
        }

        /// Record `input @ weight + bias` onto `graph`, the weight and bias entering as `binding` says: `.trained`
        /// (parameters - what `attach` does) or `.frozen` (constants over the SAME tensors - the live weights, read at
        /// every `recompute`, never differentiated: how a planner or a target reads a network that another graph is
        /// training; `Params` tells the whole story).
        pub fn attachAs(
            self: Self,
            graph: *Graph(T),
            input: Var,
            binding: Binding,
        ) Error!Attached {
            const weight_value: Var = try bindTensor(T, graph, self.weight, binding);
            const bias_value: Var = try bindTensor(T, graph, self.bias, binding);
            return .{
                .out = try applyBound(graph, weight_value, bias_value, input),
                .weight = weight_value,
                .bias = bias_value,
            };
        }

        /// The layer's ARITHMETIC alone - `input @ weight + bias` - over handles already bound (`attachAs` binds, or a
        /// `Params.bind`). Binding once and applying many times is how ONE set of weights serves every step of a
        /// rollout: a tensor bound twice would be two parameters to the graph, each with half the gradient.
        pub fn applyBound(
            graph: *Graph(T),
            weight: Var,
            bias: Var,
            input: Var,
        ) Error!Var {
            const weighted_input: Var = try graph.matmul(input, weight);
            return graph.add(weighted_input, bias);
        }
    };
}
Optimizer
/// An optimiser bound to a set of a graph's parameters, owning whatever state the algorithm
/// needs per parameter.
///
/// THE STATE LIVES HERE, NOT WITH THE CALLER
///
/// `sgdMomentum` needs a velocity per parameter and `adamStep` needs two moments; without this,
/// a caller training four parameters with Adam allocates and threads eight extra tensors by
/// hand, and a mistake - one moment buffer shared between two parameters - trains silently
/// wrong. Binding the state to the parameter list at construction makes that mistake
/// unrepresentable.
///
/// ONE TYPE, THREE ALGORITHMS. The choice is a field, not a type parameter, so a training loop
/// can be written once and the algorithm changed at one call site. The state buffers for an
/// algorithm that does not use them are never allocated.
///
/// `step` reads gradients through the graph and writes updates into the graph's parameter
/// tensors, so the next `recompute` sees them with no further bookkeeping.
pub fn Optimizer(comptime T: type) type {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    return struct {
        const Self = @This();

        pub const Kind = union(enum) {
            sgd: struct { rate: T },
            momentum: struct { rate: T, momentum: T },
            adam: Adam,
        };

        kind: Kind,
        params: []const Var,
        /// Per parameter: one buffer for momentum, two for Adam, none for SGD.
        state: []Tensor(T),
        /// Adam's 1-based step counter.
        steps: usize,

        pub fn init(
            gpa: Allocator,
            graph: *const Graph(T),
            params: []const Var,
            kind: Kind,
        ) Error!Self {
            const per: usize = switch (kind) {
                .sgd => 0,
                .momentum => 1,
                .adam => 2,
            };
            // THE PARAMETER LIST IS COPIED, NOT RETAINED
            //
            // The first version stored the caller's slice. Every test passed, because a test
            // writes `&.{ a, b, c }` in the same frame that calls `step`. The GPU training example
            // built its optimiser in `init` and stepped it from `update`, and the array literal
            // was gone - an out-of-bounds read inside `valueOf`, on the first frame. A type that
            // outlives the call that made it owns what it needs.
            const owned: []Var = try gpa.alloc(Var, params.len);
            @memcpy(owned, params);
            const state: []Tensor(T) = try gpa.alloc(Tensor(T), params.len * per);
            for (params, 0..) |v, i| {
                const shape: []const usize = graph.valueOf(v).shape[0..graph.valueOf(v).rank];
                var k: usize = 0;
                while (k < per) : (k += 1) {
                    state[i * per + k] = try Tensor(T).alloc(gpa, shape);
                    state[i * per + k].fill(0);
                }
            }
            return .{ .kind = kind, .params = owned, .state = state, .steps = 0 };
        }

        /// Apply one update to every bound parameter, from the gradients `backward` left.
        pub fn step(self: *Self, graph: *const Graph(T)) Error!void {
            self.steps += 1;
            for (self.params, 0..) |v, i| {
                const weight: Tensor(T) = graph.valueOf(v);
                const grad: Tensor(T) = try graph.gradOf(v);
                switch (self.kind) {
                    .sgd => |h| try sgdStep(T, weight, weight, grad, h.rate),
                    .momentum => |h| try sgdMomentum(
                        T,
                        weight,
                        weight,
                        grad,
                        self.state[i],
                        h.rate,
                        h.momentum,
                    ),
                    .adam => |h| try adamStep(
                        T,
                        weight,
                        weight,
                        grad,
                        self.state[i * 2],
                        self.state[i * 2 + 1],
                        h,
                        self.steps,
                    ),
                }
            }
        }
    };
}

Writing the forward pass by hand is fine — three calls, three named intermediates, and the names help when a shape is wrong. The line after it is not:

&.{ a1.weight, a1.bias, a2.weight, a2.bias }

That list is written by hand, and a parameter missing from it silently never trains. The loss still falls — the other parameters compensate — so the network is simply worse than it should be and nothing anywhere says so. It is the quietest bug in this library, and it is the reason Chain exists. Running the layers in order is the easy half.

The count comes from each layer's own pub const Attached, whose fields are out plus one per parameter. So adding a layer changes the count without anyone editing a table, and a layer that gained a parameter would be counted correctly the day it did.

Parameters is a fixed array, not a slice: the size is known at comptime from the layer list, so there is nothing to allocate and nothing to free.

The test checks two things beyond the count. Every collected Var must be distinct — a chain handing back the same one twice would train one parameter twice and another never, which is the same bug arriving by a different route. And the collected list is compared against attaching the same layers by hand on a fresh graph, so "in order" is asserted rather than assumed.

A Chain carries a tuple and a count: the graph already composes layers, so there is nothing more for the chain to know.

10.13 BatchNorm, and a mode you cannot forget#

const h = try bn.attach(&graph, x, .training);   // batch stats
const h = try bn.attach(&graph, x, .inference);  // running stats
try bn.observe(batch);                           // move the running stats

A mode stored on the struct and defaulting to .training, as PyTorch's model.train() / model.eval() do, invites one of the most common bugs: forget to flip it before evaluating and the network silently normalises by whatever batch it is looking at.

On a large evaluation batch the numbers look plausible. On a batch of one they are exactly zero for every feature, because a single sample has no variance — the output carries no information at all. The model "works in training and breaks in production", and nothing anywhere reported a mistake. The test makes that visible rather than describing it: it pushes one row through .training and asserts every output is erased, then pushes the same row through .inference and asserts it survives.

Here use is a required argument. There is no state to forget, no default to inherit, and the call site says which statistics it wants. A caller cannot reach the single-row disaster by omission — only by asking for it.

observe is separate from attach for the same reason. attach only reads; folding the running-statistics update into the forward pass would make building the graph mutate the layer, and a caller who recomputes a graph twice would age the statistics twice. Two attaches leave the running mean at zero, and only observe moves it.

Batch norm is layer norm transposed

Layer norm normalises each row across its features; batch norm normalises each column across the batch. That is the same arithmetic on the transpose — verified to 2.2e-16 against a direct per-column implementation — so the forward pass and its gradient both come from the pair that already exists: attach transposes, calls layerNormRows, and transposes back. Both transposes are views, so the cost is strided access rather than a copy.

10.14 LstmCell, and a one-line change worth 44x#

const cell = try zn.LstmCell(f64).init(gpa, rng, input_size, hidden_size);
const s = try cell.step(&graph, x, hidden, cell_state);
// s.hidden, s.cell, s.parameters
LstmCell
/// One LSTM timestep: four gates deciding what to keep, what to add, and what to show.
///
/// THE FORGET BIAS STARTS AT ONE, AND THAT IS THE DIFFERENCE THAT MATTERS
///
/// PyTorch zeroes every bias. A zero forget bias means `sigmoid(0) = 0.5` on
/// the first step, so **the cell halves its memory every timestep before it has learned
/// anything**: after ten steps 0.1% of the original signal survives, and the gradient that would
/// teach it to remember has to travel back through all that decay.
///
/// Starting the forget bias at one makes `sigmoid(1) = 0.73` instead. Measured over ten steps
/// with no input at all, the cell retains **4.3% against 0.1% - forty times more** - which is the
/// difference between a gradient that arrives and one that does not. The result is Gers's, from
/// 1999, and it is still absent from most implementations.
///
/// Every other bias starts at zero, for the usual reason: a random or nonzero bias adds nothing a
/// weight does not already provide.
///
/// FOUR WEIGHT PAIRS, NOT ONE FUSED MATRIX
///
/// PyTorch fuses the four gates into one `(4*hidden, input)` matrix and slices the result, which
/// is one matmul instead of four. When this cell was written the tape had no differentiable
/// slice, so fusing was not available and the note said so.
///
/// **That is no longer true** - `Graph.slice` and `Graph.concat` both exist now, with backwards
/// checked against a numerical derivative. So the fused form is buildable, and the reason it has
/// not been built is now a cost argument rather than a missing primitive: it saves three matmuls
/// per timestep on a cell whose cost is dominated by the sequence loop and the gate
/// nonlinearities, and it costs the gate-per-field naming that makes `forget_gate.bias` the
/// thing you set to one. Worth measuring before worth doing.
pub fn LstmCell(comptime T: type) type {
    return struct {
        /// How much of the new candidate to let in.
        input_gate: Gate,
        /// How much of the existing cell to keep. Its bias starts at ONE - see above.
        forget_gate: Gate,
        /// The new value proposed for the cell, before the input gate scales it.
        candidate: Gate,
        /// How much of the cell to expose as the hidden state.
        output_gate: Gate,

        const Self = @This();

        /// The four gates, in the order `Bound.all` and `Stepped.parameters` use. One list, so
        /// `init`, `bind` and `stepBound` cannot disagree about which index is the forget gate.
        const gate_names = [_][]const u8{ "input_gate", "forget_gate", "candidate", "output_gate" };

        /// One gate's two weight matrices and its bias.
        ///
        /// Every gate reads BOTH the current input and the previous hidden state, which is the
        /// whole idea: `from_input` is what the world says, `from_hidden` is what the cell
        /// remembers, and the gate is their sum.
        pub const Gate = struct {
            from_input: Tensor(T),
            from_hidden: Tensor(T),
            bias: Tensor(T),
        };

        /// What one step produces. **Two states, not one** - `hidden` is what the next layer
        /// sees, `cell` is the memory that carries forward, and confusing them is the classic
        /// LSTM mistake.
        pub const Stepped = struct {
            hidden: Var,
            cell: Var,
            parameters: [12]Var,
        };

        pub fn init(
            gpa: Allocator,
            rng: Rng,
            input_size: usize,
            hidden_size: usize,
        ) Error!Self {
            var made: Self = undefined;
            inline for (gate_names, 0..) |name, i| {
                const from_input: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(gpa, &.{ input_size, hidden_size });
                const from_hidden: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(gpa, &.{ hidden_size, hidden_size });
                const bias: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(gpa, &.{ 1, hidden_size });
                try initXavier(T, from_input, rng.split(@intCast(i * 2)), input_size, hidden_size);
                try initXavier(T, from_hidden, rng.split(@intCast(i * 2 + 1)), hidden_size, hidden_size);
                // The forget gate is index 1, and it is the one that starts at one.
                bias.fill(if (i == 1) 1 else 0);
                @field(made, name) = .{
                    .from_input = from_input,
                    .from_hidden = from_hidden,
                    .bias = bias,
                };
            }
            return made;
        }

        /// One gate's three parameter nodes, already on the tape.
        pub const BoundGate = struct {
            from_input: Var,
            from_hidden: Var,
            bias: Var,
        };

        /// The twelve parameter nodes of this cell, bound to a graph ONCE.
        ///
        /// WHY THIS TYPE EXISTS - IT IS THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN BPTT AND A SILENT BUG
        ///
        /// `graph.parameter` pushes a NEW leaf on every call; it does not look up a tensor it
        /// has already seen. So a sequence loop that calls `step` at each timestep binds the
        /// same twelve tensors once per step, and `gradOf` on any one of them then returns
        /// THAT STEP'S gradient rather than the sum over the sequence. The weights are shared
        /// in memory and unshared on the tape: the model trains on one timestep's worth of
        /// signal, the loss still falls because the last step is still the loss, and nothing
        /// anywhere reports a mistake.
        ///
        /// Binding once and stepping with the bound vars is what makes the gradient accumulate
        /// across time, which is the whole content of "backpropagation through time".
        /// `LSTM.run` does exactly that, and `zn LSTM: binding once is what makes it BPTT`
        /// measures the difference rather than asserting it.
        pub const Bound = struct {
            input_gate: BoundGate,
            forget_gate: BoundGate,
            candidate: BoundGate,
            output_gate: BoundGate,
            /// The same twelve nodes as a flat list, for the optimiser.
            all: [12]Var,
        };

        /// Put this cell's twelve weights on the tape, once.
        pub fn bind(self: Self, graph: *Graph(T)) Error!Bound {
            var made: Bound = undefined;
            var next: usize = 0;
            inline for (gate_names) |name| {
                const gate: Gate = @field(self, name);
                const bound: BoundGate = .{
                    .from_input = try graph.parameter(gate.from_input),
                    .from_hidden = try graph.parameter(gate.from_hidden),
                    .bias = try graph.parameter(gate.bias),
                };
                @field(made, name) = bound;
                made.all[next] = bound.from_input;
                made.all[next + 1] = bound.from_hidden;
                made.all[next + 2] = bound.bias;
                next += 3;
            }
            return made;
        }

        /// Advance one timestep using weights ALREADY on the tape. Built entirely from tape
        /// operations, so the gradient is the tape's and nothing here needs a backward of its
        /// own.
        pub fn stepBound(
            self: Self,
            graph: *Graph(T),
            bound: Bound,
            input: Var,
            hidden: Var,
            cell: Var,
        ) Error!Stepped {
            _ = self;
            var summed: [4]Var = undefined;
            inline for (gate_names, 0..) |name, i| {
                const gate: BoundGate = @field(bound, name);
                const world: Var = try graph.matmul(input, gate.from_input);
                const memory: Var = try graph.matmul(hidden, gate.from_hidden);
                summed[i] = try graph.add(try graph.add(world, memory), gate.bias);
            }
            const keep: Var = try graph.sigmoid(summed[1]);
            const admit: Var = try graph.sigmoid(summed[0]);
            const proposed: Var = try graph.tanh(summed[2]);
            const show: Var = try graph.sigmoid(summed[3]);
            // The cell is what survives plus what is admitted; the hidden state is the cell seen
            // through the output gate. Keeping these two lines apart is the point of the type.
            const next_cell: Var = try graph.add(
                try graph.mul(keep, cell),
                try graph.mul(admit, proposed),
            );
            const next_hidden: Var = try graph.mul(show, try graph.tanh(next_cell));
            return .{ .hidden = next_hidden, .cell = next_cell, .parameters = bound.all };
        }

        /// Advance one timestep, binding the weights as it goes.
        ///
        /// Correct for a SINGLE step and for a single step only. Over a sequence, use
        /// `LSTM.run`, or `bind` once and call `stepBound` - see the note on `Bound` for what
        /// goes wrong otherwise.
        pub fn step(
            self: Self,
            graph: *Graph(T),
            input: Var,
            hidden: Var,
            cell: Var,
        ) Error!Stepped {
            return self.stepBound(graph, try self.bind(graph), input, hidden, cell);
        }
    };
}

The forget bias starts at one. PyTorch zeroes every bias, and a zero forget bias means sigmoid(0) = 0.5, so the cell halves its memory every timestep before it has learned anything. Ten steps in, 0.1% of the original signal survives, and the gradient that would teach it to remember has to travel back through all that decay.

Starting at one gives sigmoid(1) = 0.73. with every weight zeroed so only the biases decide and the input gate shut so nothing but decay happens:

forget bias 0    0.000977   (0.5^10,  as it must be)
forget bias 1    0.043604   (0.73^10)

Forty-four times the signal, and with it forty-four times the gradient. The result is Gers's, from 1999, and it is still absent from most implementations. The test asserts the exact powers rather than just the ratio, so it measures the gate and not the arithmetic around it — and it separately asserts that init produces this default, because a default nobody checks is a default that drifts.

Two states, and confusing them is the classic mistake

step returns hidden and cell. The hidden state is what the next layer sees; the cell is the memory that carries forward. A type returning one value could not stop you mixing them, so this one returns both, and they are different vars.

Four weight pairs, not one fused matrix

PyTorch fuses the four gates into one (4·hidden, input) matrix and slices the result — one matmul instead of four. That needs a graph-level slice with a backward, and this tape has none. Fusing would mean building tape machinery to save three matmuls on a cell whose cost is dominated by the sequence loop around it, so the fusion is a note here rather than a half-built abstraction.

The twelve tensors of an LSTM (w_ii, w_hi, b_i, and so on) are grouped into four Gates with from_input and from_hidden, because that grouping is the idea: every gate reads both what the world says and what the cell remembers.

Every operation in step is already on the tape — matmul, sigmoid, tanh, add, mul — so the gradient is the tape's and nothing here needs a backward of its own.

10.15 LSTM, and the one line that makes it BPTT#

const layer = try zn.LSTM(f64).init(gpa, rng, input_size, hidden_size);
const h0 = try graph.constant(try layer.zeroState(gpa, batch));
const c0 = try graph.constant(try layer.zeroState(gpa, batch));
const r = try layer.run(&graph, steps, h0, c0, null);
// r.last_hidden, r.last_cell, r.parameters
LSTM
/// An `LstmCell` run over a sequence, with the gradient flowing back through every step.
///
/// WHAT THIS ADDS OVER THE CELL, WHICH IS THE ONLY REASON IT EXISTS
///
/// The cell is one timestep. Running a sequence is a loop, and the loop has exactly one subtle
/// part: **the weights must be bound to the tape once and reused, not re-bound per step.** See
/// the note on `LstmCell.Bound`. Written the obvious way - `for (steps) |x| cell.step(...)` -
/// the model gets one timestep's gradient instead of the sum over the sequence, and it still
/// trains, just badly and for a reason nothing reports. That loop is this type.
///
/// THE STATE IS THREADED, NOT STORED
///
/// `run` takes the initial hidden and cell states and returns the final ones, rather than
/// keeping them in the struct. A layer that remembers its own state across calls is a layer
/// that carries a hidden dependency on call ORDER, and truncated BPTT - where the next window
/// starts from the previous window's final state - becomes indistinguishable from a leak when
/// it is wrong. Here the caller passes what it means and gets back what it needs.
///
/// ZERO IS A CHOICE AND IT IS THE RIGHT ONE. `zeroState` gives the usual start. A learned
/// initial state is one more parameter for the benefit of the first few timesteps, and on any
/// sequence long enough to need an LSTM the gates have overwritten it.
pub fn LSTM(comptime T: type) type {
    return struct {
        cell: LstmCell(T),
        input_size: usize,
        hidden_size: usize,

        const Self = @This();

        /// What a sequence produces. `last_hidden` is what a classifier reads; `last_cell` is
        /// what the next window continues from under truncated BPTT.
        pub const Run = struct {
            last_hidden: Var,
            last_cell: Var,
            /// The cell's twelve weights, bound ONCE for the whole sequence.
            parameters: [12]Var,
        };

        pub fn init(
            gpa: Allocator,
            rng: Rng,
            input_size: usize,
            hidden_size: usize,
        ) Error!Self {
            return .{
                .cell = try LstmCell(T).init(gpa, rng, input_size, hidden_size),
                .input_size = input_size,
                .hidden_size = hidden_size,
            };
        }

        /// A `(batch, hidden)` tensor of zeros, for the start of a sequence.
        pub fn zeroState(self: Self, gpa: Allocator, batch: usize) Error!Tensor(T) {
            const made: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(gpa, &.{ batch, self.hidden_size });
            made.fill(0);
            return made;
        }

        /// Run the cell over `steps`, each a `(batch, input_size)` value already on the tape.
        ///
        /// If `out_hidden` is given it must be exactly `steps.len` long and receives each step's
        /// hidden state - what a sequence-to-sequence head reads. Pass null when only the final
        /// state matters, which is the classifier case.
        pub fn run(
            self: Self,
            graph: *Graph(T),
            steps: []const Var,
            hidden0: Var,
            cell0: Var,
            out_hidden: ?[]Var,
        ) Error!Run {
            if (steps.len == 0) {
                return Error.OutOfRange;
            }
            if (out_hidden) |slot| {
                if (slot.len != steps.len) {
                    return Error.ShapeMismatch;
                }
            }
            // ONCE, before the loop. This line is the whole point of the type.
            const bound: LstmCell(T).Bound = try self.cell.bind(graph);
            var hidden: Var = hidden0;
            var cell: Var = cell0;
            for (steps, 0..) |x, i| {
                const stepped: LstmCell(T).Stepped =
                    try self.cell.stepBound(graph, bound, x, hidden, cell);
                hidden = stepped.hidden;
                cell = stepped.cell;
                if (out_hidden) |slot| {
                    slot[i] = hidden;
                }
            }
            return .{ .last_hidden = hidden, .last_cell = cell, .parameters = bound.all };
        }
    };
}

steps is a slice of values already on the tape, one per timestep, each (batch, input_size). Pass a slice as the last argument instead of null and it receives every step's hidden state, which is what a sequence-to-sequence head reads.

The loop is four lines, and exactly one of them is subtle. Graph.parameter pushes a new leaf on every call — it does not look up a tensor it has already seen. So the obvious sequence loop, calling cell.step once per timestep, binds the same twelve weight tensors once per step, and each binding then collects only that step's gradient. The weights are shared in memory and unshared on the tape.

Nothing reports this. The forward values are identical either way, the gradients are all finite, and the loss still falls — because the loss is still the loss. The model simply trains on a fraction of the signal. Measured over four timesteps: the last step alone carries 49% of the total gradient on the recurrent matrix, and the first step carries exactly zero, because hidden0 is zeros and the gradient of matmul(hidden0, from_hidden) with respect to from_hidden is zero however large the upstream gradient is.

So run calls cell.bind(graph) once, before the loop, and steps with those bound vars. Summing the gradient across timesteps is the entire content of “backpropagation through time”, and that one hoisted line is where it happens. LstmCell.step still exists and is still correct — for a single step.

The state is threaded rather than stored: run takes the initial states and returns the final ones. A layer that keeps its own state across calls carries a hidden dependency on call order, and truncated BPTT — where the next window continues from the previous window's final state — becomes indistinguishable from a leak when it is wrong.

The test is a learning curve rather than a gradient check: eight timesteps of noise where the target is the value shown at step zero. Nothing in the last seven inputs carries it, so a model reading any fixed window that excludes the first cannot beat predicting the mean. The target's variance is 1.016, the loss starts at 1.232 and ends at 0.033 — 3.2% of the variance.

10.16 GRU: the same capability from a different shape#

const layer = try zn.GRU(f64).init(gpa, rng, input_size, hidden_size);
const ran = try layer.run(&graph, &seq, h0, null);   // one state, not two
GRU
/// A GRU over a sequence: `LSTM`'s loop, with one state to thread instead of two.
///
/// Everything `LSTM`'s note says about binding once and threading the state applies here
/// unchanged; the only difference is that there is no cell line to carry.
pub fn GRU(comptime T: type) type {
    return struct {
        cell: GruCell(T),
        input_size: usize,
        hidden_size: usize,

        const Self = @This();

        /// What a sequence produces.
        pub const Run = struct {
            last_hidden: Var,
            /// The cell's nine weights, bound ONCE for the whole sequence.
            parameters: [9]Var,
        };

        pub fn init(
            gpa: Allocator,
            rng: Rng,
            input_size: usize,
            hidden_size: usize,
        ) Error!Self {
            return .{
                .cell = try GruCell(T).init(gpa, rng, input_size, hidden_size),
                .input_size = input_size,
                .hidden_size = hidden_size,
            };
        }

        /// A `(batch, hidden)` tensor of zeros, for the start of a sequence.
        pub fn zeroState(self: Self, gpa: Allocator, batch: usize) Error!Tensor(T) {
            const made: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(gpa, &.{ batch, self.hidden_size });
            made.fill(0);
            return made;
        }

        /// Run the cell over `steps`, each a `(batch, input_size)` value already on the tape.
        ///
        /// If `out_hidden` is given it must be exactly `steps.len` long and receives each step's
        /// hidden state. Pass null when only the final state matters.
        pub fn run(
            self: Self,
            graph: *Graph(T),
            steps: []const Var,
            hidden0: Var,
            out_hidden: ?[]Var,
        ) Error!Run {
            if (steps.len == 0) {
                return Error.OutOfRange;
            }
            if (out_hidden) |slot| {
                if (slot.len != steps.len) {
                    return Error.ShapeMismatch;
                }
            }
            // ONCE, before the loop. This line is the whole point of the type.
            const bound: GruCell(T).Bound = try self.cell.bind(graph);
            var hidden: Var = hidden0;
            for (steps, 0..) |x, i| {
                const stepped: GruCell(T).Stepped =
                    try self.cell.stepBound(graph, bound, x, hidden);
                hidden = stepped.hidden;
                if (out_hidden) |slot| {
                    slot[i] = hidden;
                }
            }
            return .{ .last_hidden = hidden, .parameters = bound.all };
        }
    };
}

An LSTM keeps a cell line whose update is f*c + i*g — a gated sum, which is what lets a gradient travel back through time multiplied by roughly one. A GRU gets the same property from a different shape: h' = (1-z)*n + z*h is an interpolation, so when the update gate sits near one the hidden state is carried forward almost unchanged and the path back is again near-multiplicative-by-one.

The saving is real — nine weight tensors against twelve, and one state to thread instead of two. The cost is that the thing the unit remembers and the thing it emits are now the same vector. An LSTM can hold something in c without showing it in h; a GRU cannot.

The reset gate multiplies the hidden projection, not the hidden state. n = tanh(W_in x + r * (W_hn h) + b_n), with r applied after the matmul. Applying it to h first is the other published form and it is a different model — it also makes the fused single-matmul implementation impossible, which is presumably why the framework everyone compares against chose this one.

No gate is biased open here, and the asymmetry with LstmCell is deliberate. The LSTM's forget gate starts at one so the cell line survives by default. The GRU's update gate sits on both sides of an interpolation: biasing it open would not just preserve memory, it would shut the candidate out, and the unit would start unable to learn anything new. Zero leaves it balanced.

The test runs the LSTM test's exact task, seeds, optimiser and schedule, against the same bars rather than looser ones, so the two are directly comparable. If the GRU ever needs a longer schedule to pass, that is a finding about the unit and it belongs in a comment rather than in a tuned constant.

It did not need one, and the measurement is worth stating. On the identical task, seeds and 400 steps: the target's variance is 1.016, the loss falls from 1.206 to 0.0835 — 8.2% of the variance, where the LSTM reaches 3.2%. The GRU is behind at the point where both are measured.

Run past the bar, though, and it reaches 7.8e-4 by 800 steps and zero by 1600, well below where the LSTM stands at 400. That makes this convergence speed on this task rather than a ceiling on what the unit can represent — the one-state shape is costing steps here, not capability. Neither number would exist if the test had been handed a schedule long enough to hide the difference.

10.17 BiLSTM and StackedLSTM: the two loops left#

const bi = try zn.BiLSTM(f64).init(gpa, rng, input_size, hidden_size);
var joined: [steps]zn.Var = undefined;
const r = try bi.run(&graph, gpa, &seq, zero, &joined); // joined[t] is 2*hidden wide

const tower = try zn.StackedLSTM(f64).init(gpa, rng, input_size, hidden_size, depth);
var params: [24]zn.Var = undefined;                        // tower.parameterCount()
const s = try tower.run(&graph, gpa, &seq, zero, &params);
BiLSTM
/// An LSTM read in both directions, so every position sees the whole sequence.
///
/// WHAT IT BUYS, AND THE TEST THAT MAKES THE CLAIM CHECKABLE
///
/// A forward LSTM's state at position `t` has seen steps `0..t` and nothing after. That is the
/// right shape for anything that must run as the data arrives, and the wrong shape for anything
/// that gets the whole sequence up front and needs per-position output - tagging a word by its
/// context, scoring a frame by what follows it. The backward pass supplies exactly the half the
/// forward pass cannot have.
///
/// `zn BiLSTM: position zero can see the end, and a forward LSTM cannot` asks for the LAST step's
/// value from the FIRST position's output, and runs a forward-only LSTM against the same task as
/// a control. The control has no path to the answer, and measurably fails.
///
/// TWO CELLS, NOT ONE RUN TWICE. The directions learn different things and must not share
/// weights: a single cell applied both ways would be forced to one set of gates for two jobs.
/// Hence 24 parameters, twelve per direction.
///
/// `out_hidden` IS REQUIRED, unlike `LSTM.run`'s. A bidirectional summary that throws away the
/// per-position outputs has spent a whole extra pass on a vector the forward one nearly had; if
/// only the ends matter, an `LSTM` is the honest choice.
pub fn BiLSTM(comptime T: type) type {
    return struct {
        /// Reads `steps` front to back.
        forward: LstmCell(T),
        /// Reads the same `steps` back to front. Its own weights - see above.
        backward: LstmCell(T),
        input_size: usize,
        /// Per DIRECTION. Each position's output is `2 * hidden_size` wide.
        hidden_size: usize,

        const Self = @This();

        pub const Run = struct {
            /// The two directions' final states joined: the forward pass at the last position and
            /// the backward pass at the first. What a whole-sequence classifier reads.
            summary: Var,
            /// Forward's twelve then backward's twelve.
            parameters: [24]Var,
        };

        pub fn init(
            gpa: Allocator,
            rng: Rng,
            input_size: usize,
            hidden_size: usize,
        ) Error!Self {
            return .{
                .forward = try LstmCell(T).init(gpa, rng.split(0), input_size, hidden_size),
                .backward = try LstmCell(T).init(gpa, rng.split(1), input_size, hidden_size),
                .input_size = input_size,
                .hidden_size = hidden_size,
            };
        }

        /// A `(batch, hidden_size)` tensor of zeros - ONE direction's state.
        pub fn zeroState(self: Self, gpa: Allocator, batch: usize) Error!Tensor(T) {
            const made: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(gpa, &.{ batch, self.hidden_size });
            made.fill(0);
            return made;
        }

        /// Run both directions over `steps` and join them per position.
        ///
        /// `out_hidden` must be `steps.len` long; entry `t` is `concat(forward_t, backward_t)`,
        /// `(batch, 2 * hidden_size)` wide. `gpa` is scratch for the two per-direction state
        /// lists and is released before returning - nothing it allocates outlives the call.
        pub fn run(
            self: Self,
            graph: *Graph(T),
            gpa: Allocator,
            steps: []const Var,
            zero: Var,
            out_hidden: []Var,
        ) Error!Run {
            if (steps.len == 0) {
                return Error.OutOfRange;
            }
            if (out_hidden.len != steps.len) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }
            const forward_bound: LstmCell(T).Bound = try self.forward.bind(graph);
            const backward_bound: LstmCell(T).Bound = try self.backward.bind(graph);

            const scratch: []Var = try gpa.alloc(Var, steps.len * 2);
            defer gpa.free(scratch);
            const going: []Var = scratch[0..steps.len];
            const coming: []Var = scratch[steps.len..];

            var hidden: Var = zero;
            var cell: Var = zero;
            for (steps, 0..) |x, t| {
                const stepped: LstmCell(T).Stepped =
                    try self.forward.stepBound(graph, forward_bound, x, hidden, cell);
                hidden = stepped.hidden;
                cell = stepped.cell;
                going[t] = hidden;
            }

            // Back to front. `t` counts down so `coming[t]` is indexed by POSITION, not by order
            // of computation - which is what makes the join below a per-position pairing rather
            // than a reversal nobody would notice was missing.
            var back_hidden: Var = zero;
            var back_cell: Var = zero;
            var t: usize = steps.len;
            while (t > 0) {
                t -= 1;
                const stepped: LstmCell(T).Stepped =
                    try self.backward.stepBound(graph, backward_bound, steps[t], back_hidden, back_cell);
                back_hidden = stepped.hidden;
                back_cell = stepped.cell;
                coming[t] = back_hidden;
            }

            for (out_hidden, going, coming) |*slot, f, b| {
                slot.* = try graph.concat(f, b, 1);
            }

            var both: [24]Var = undefined;
            @memcpy(both[0..12], &forward_bound.all);
            @memcpy(both[12..24], &backward_bound.all);
            return .{
                // The forward pass at the end, the backward pass at the start: each direction's
                // most-informed state, which is not the same as `out_hidden`'s first or last.
                .summary = try graph.concat(going[steps.len - 1], coming[0], 1),
                .parameters = both,
            };
        }
    };
}
Var
/// A handle to a value inside a `Graph`. An index, not a pointer.
///
/// WHY VALUES ARE INDICES AND NOT TENSORS
///
/// The obvious design keys gradients off the tensor itself - its `data.ptr`, say. That breaks
/// immediately here, because a view SHARES `data.ptr` with its parent: `w` and
/// `w.transpose(0,1)` would be the same key while being different values in the graph. Worse, a
/// tensor is copied by value throughout this library, so there is no stable address to key on at
/// all.
///
/// An index into the graph's own arrays sidesteps both. The graph owns the correspondence between
/// a value, its tensor, and its gradient, and nothing about `Tensor` has to change to support it.
pub const Var = u32;
StackedLSTM
/// LSTM layers stacked, each reading the one below it.
///
/// Depth here is not width. One layer with twice the hidden size has more parameters and still
/// computes one transformation per timestep; two layers compute a transformation OF a
/// transformation, and the second can read features the first only just produced. That is the
/// same argument depth always makes, and it applies per timestep rather than across the sequence.
///
/// THE SHAPES ARE FIXED BY THE STACK, WHICH REMOVES THE COMMON MISTAKE. Layer 0 takes
/// `input_size`; every layer above takes `hidden_size`, because that is what the layer below
/// emits. A stack that let each layer be sized independently would let a caller build one whose
/// widths do not meet, and the error would arrive from a matmul several frames away.
///
/// THE PARAMETER COUNT IS NOT COMPTIME, so `run` fills a caller-supplied slice rather than
/// returning an array. `parameterCount` says how long it must be, and a wrong length is an error
/// rather than a truncation.
pub fn StackedLSTM(comptime T: type) type {
    return struct {
        /// Bottom first. `layers[0]` reads the input; `layers[k]` reads `layers[k-1]`.
        layers: []LstmCell(T),
        input_size: usize,
        hidden_size: usize,

        const Self = @This();

        pub const Run = struct {
            /// The TOP layer's final hidden state. The lower layers' states are intermediate.
            last_hidden: Var,
        };

        pub fn init(
            gpa: Allocator,
            rng: Rng,
            input_size: usize,
            hidden_size: usize,
            depth: usize,
        ) Error!Self {
            if (depth == 0) {
                return Error.OutOfRange;
            }
            const layers: []LstmCell(T) = try gpa.alloc(LstmCell(T), depth);
            for (layers, 0..) |*slot, i| {
                slot.* = try LstmCell(T).init(
                    gpa,
                    rng.split(@intCast(i)),
                    if (i == 0) input_size else hidden_size,
                    hidden_size,
                );
            }
            return .{ .layers = layers, .input_size = input_size, .hidden_size = hidden_size };
        }

        /// Twelve per layer.
        pub fn parameterCount(self: Self) usize {
            return self.layers.len * 12;
        }

        /// A `(batch, hidden_size)` tensor of zeros. Every layer starts from one.
        pub fn zeroState(self: Self, gpa: Allocator, batch: usize) Error!Tensor(T) {
            const made: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(gpa, &.{ batch, self.hidden_size });
            made.fill(0);
            return made;
        }

        /// Run the whole stack over `steps`.
        ///
        /// `out_parameters` must be exactly `parameterCount()` long and comes back holding every
        /// layer's twelve, bottom layer first. `gpa` is scratch for the inter-layer sequences and
        /// is released before returning.
        pub fn run(
            self: Self,
            graph: *Graph(T),
            gpa: Allocator,
            steps: []const Var,
            zero: Var,
            out_parameters: []Var,
        ) Error!Run {
            if (steps.len == 0) {
                return Error.OutOfRange;
            }
            if (out_parameters.len != self.parameterCount()) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }
            // Two buffers, swapped: what this layer reads, and what it writes for the next.
            const scratch: []Var = try gpa.alloc(Var, steps.len * 2);
            defer gpa.free(scratch);
            var reading: []Var = scratch[0..steps.len];
            var writing: []Var = scratch[steps.len..];
            @memcpy(reading, steps);

            var top: Var = zero;
            for (self.layers, 0..) |layer, i| {
                // ONCE PER LAYER, before its loop - the same rule `LstmCell.Bound` documents.
                const bound: LstmCell(T).Bound = try layer.bind(graph);
                @memcpy(out_parameters[i * 12 ..][0..12], &bound.all);
                var hidden: Var = zero;
                var cell: Var = zero;
                for (reading, 0..) |x, t| {
                    const stepped: LstmCell(T).Stepped =
                        try layer.stepBound(graph, bound, x, hidden, cell);
                    hidden = stepped.hidden;
                    cell = stepped.cell;
                    writing[t] = hidden;
                }
                top = hidden;
                const swap: []Var = reading;
                reading = writing;
                writing = swap;
            }
            return .{ .last_hidden = top };
        }
    };
}

Both are loops over the cell that already exists, and both bind once per direction or per layer for the reason 11.15 gives.

A forward LSTM's state at position t has seen steps 0..t and nothing after. That is right for anything that must run as data arrives and wrong for anything handed the whole sequence that needs per-position output. The backward pass supplies exactly the half the forward pass cannot have, and the two directions get separate weights — one cell applied both ways would be forced to use one set of gates for two jobs.

The test asks for the last step's value from the first position's output, and runs a forward-only LSTM on the identical task as a control, because a control that does not apply looks exactly like a test that cannot fail. Target variance 0.295. Bidirectional: 0.573 → 0.0119, 4.0% of the variance. Forward-only: 0.628 → 0.276 — 93.6% of the variance, which is to say it learned little beyond answering with the mean, since from position zero the answer is not a function of anything it has seen. A 23× gap.

out_hidden is required on BiLSTM.run, unlike LSTM.run's optional one. A bidirectional summary that discards the per-position outputs has spent a whole extra pass on a vector the forward model nearly had; if only the ends matter, an LSTM is the honest choice.

For the stack, layer 0 takes input_size and every layer above takes hidden_size, because that is what the layer below emits — the stack fixes the widths rather than trusting the caller, so they cannot fail to meet. The parameter count is not comptime, so run fills a caller-supplied slice and a wrong length is an error rather than a truncation.

That test was written expecting to show only that a stack composes and trains; the sequence looked too easy for depth to matter. It measured 0.00516, 0.51% of the variance, against the single layer's 3.2% on identical seeds and budget — a 6× improvement. Worth stating what it does not show: the stack also carries twice the parameters, so this is depth-plus-capacity against neither, and separating them needs a parameter-matched single layer. Recorded as measured rather than explained.

10.18 Dataset, DataLoader and fit: the loop, written once#

const data = try zn.Dataset(f64).init(inputs, targets);
var loader = try zn.DataLoader(f64).init(gpa, data, .{ .batch = 2, .seed = 9 });
const report = try zn.fit(f64, .{
    .graph = &graph, .input = x, .target = y, .loss = loss,
    .weights = &.{ hidden.weight, hidden.bias, out.weight, out.bias },
    .parameters = &.{ h.weight, h.bias, o.weight, o.bias },
}, &loader, gpa, .{ .epochs = 600, .hyper = .{ .rate = 0.05 } });
Dataset
/// Rows of inputs paired with rows of targets. Nothing more.
///
/// A dataset here does not own its tensors, decode a file, or know what a "sample" means beyond
/// "row `i` of both". Everything a real loader eventually grows - augmentation, lazy decode,
/// sharding - is a transformation of rows that a caller can write, and none of it belongs behind
/// this type until something needs it.
///
/// THE ROW COUNTS ARE CHECKED AT CONSTRUCTION, which is the only mistake this type can prevent.
/// Mismatched inputs and targets otherwise surface as a garbage loss with no error anywhere: the
/// batches still fill, the shapes still multiply, and the model trains against the wrong answers.
pub fn Dataset(comptime T: type) type {
    return struct {
        /// `(rows, in_features)`.
        inputs: Tensor(T),
        /// `(rows, out_features)`.
        targets: Tensor(T),

        const Self = @This();

        pub fn init(inputs: Tensor(T), targets: Tensor(T)) Error!Self {
            if (inputs.rank != 2 or targets.rank != 2) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }
            if (inputs.shape[0] != targets.shape[0]) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }
            return .{ .inputs = inputs, .targets = targets };
        }

        pub fn rows(self: Self) usize {
            return self.inputs.shape[0];
        }
    };
}
DataLoader
/// A dataset walked in batches, reshuffled per epoch.
///
/// THE LAST PARTIAL BATCH IS DROPPED, AND THAT IS NOT A PREFERENCE
///
/// The graph is built once, and the tensors it holds for the input and the target are allocated
/// once with a fixed first dimension. `fit` feeds a batch by writing THROUGH those tensors - so
/// every batch must be exactly `batch` rows, because there is nowhere to put a shorter one.
/// Five rows with `batch = 2` gives two batches and the fifth row sits out the epoch; with
/// shuffling on it is a different row that sits out each time.
///
/// Frameworks make this a `drop_last` flag because their graphs are rebuilt per batch. Here it
/// falls out of the tape, so it is a documented consequence rather than a choice, and
/// `numBatches` reports the truncated count rather than rounding up to a batch that cannot run.
pub fn DataLoader(comptime T: type) type {
    return struct {
        data: Dataset(T),
        batch: usize,
        /// The row order for this epoch. Shuffling permutes THIS, never the data itself - the
        /// caller's tensors are not the loader's to rearrange.
        order: []usize,
        cursor: usize,
        rng: Rng,
        shuffle: bool,
        /// Which epoch's permutation to draw. `Rng` is INDEXED rather than a stream - it has no
        /// `next` - so a fresh order per epoch comes from a fresh label, not from advancing
        /// hidden state. Same seed and same epoch is the same order, every run.
        epoch: u32,

        const Self = @This();

        pub fn init(gpa: Allocator, data: Dataset(T), opts: LoaderOptions) Error!Self {
            if (opts.batch == 0 or opts.batch > data.rows()) {
                return Error.OutOfRange;
            }
            const order: []usize = try gpa.alloc(usize, data.rows());
            for (order, 0..) |*slot, i| {
                slot.* = i;
            }
            var made: Self = .{
                .data = data,
                .batch = opts.batch,
                .order = order,
                .cursor = 0,
                .rng = Rng.init(opts.seed),
                .shuffle = opts.shuffle,
                .epoch = 0,
            };
            if (opts.shuffle) {
                made.reshuffle();
            }
            return made;
        }

        /// Whole batches only. A partial tail is not counted because it cannot be run.
        pub fn numBatches(self: Self) usize {
            return self.data.rows() / self.batch;
        }

        /// Start an epoch: rewind, and reorder if shuffling was asked for.
        pub fn reshuffle(self: *Self) void {
            self.cursor = 0;
            if (!self.shuffle) {
                return;
            }
            // Fisher-Yates, backwards. `i` reaches 1 and stops: swapping element 0 with itself is
            // the only thing a final iteration could do.
            const stream: Rng = self.rng.split(self.epoch);
            self.epoch += 1;
            var i: usize = self.order.len;
            while (i > 1) {
                i -= 1;
                const j: usize = stream.intBelow(@intCast(i), @intCast(i + 1));
                const held: usize = self.order[i];
                self.order[i] = self.order[j];
                self.order[j] = held;
            }
        }

        /// Fill `out_inputs` and `out_targets` with the next batch; false when the epoch is done.
        ///
        /// The two tensors are written THROUGH, not replaced, because they are the graph's own
        /// leaf tensors. Their first dimension must be exactly `batch`.
        pub fn next(
            self: *Self,
            out_inputs: Tensor(T),
            out_targets: Tensor(T),
        ) Error!bool {
            if (self.cursor + self.batch > self.data.rows()) {
                return false;
            }
            if (out_inputs.shape[0] != self.batch or out_targets.shape[0] != self.batch) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }
            const in_width: usize = self.data.inputs.shape[1];
            const out_width: usize = self.data.targets.shape[1];
            if (out_inputs.shape[1] != in_width or out_targets.shape[1] != out_width) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }
            for (0..self.batch) |b| {
                const row: usize = self.order[self.cursor + b];
                for (0..in_width) |c| {
                    out_inputs.setAt2(b, c, try self.data.inputs.at(&.{ row, c }));
                }
                for (0..out_width) |c| {
                    out_targets.setAt2(b, c, try self.data.targets.at(&.{ row, c }));
                }
            }
            self.cursor += self.batch;
            return true;
        }
    };
}
fit
/// Train `what` on `loader` for `opts.epochs` epochs of AdamW.
///
/// This is the loop every test in this file had been writing by hand: recompute, backward, step
/// each parameter, repeat. Three lines at a call site instead of twenty, and - more to the point
/// - ONE place where "step every parameter" is written down. A hand-rolled loop that steps the
/// head and forgets a gate still shows a falling loss, because the head alone can fit a good deal
/// of anything; nothing about the curve says a layer was never trained.
pub fn fit(
    comptime T: type,
    what: Fitting(T),
    loader: *DataLoader(T),
    gpa: Allocator,
    opts: Fit,
) Error!FitReport {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    if (what.weights.len != what.parameters.len) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }
    if (loader.numBatches() == 0) {
        return Error.OutOfRange;
    }
    const graph: *Graph(T) = what.graph;
    const batch_inputs: Tensor(T) = graph.valueOf(what.input);
    const batch_targets: Tensor(T) = graph.valueOf(what.target);

    const moments: []Tensor(T) = try gpa.alloc(Tensor(T), what.weights.len);
    defer gpa.free(moments);
    const velocities: []Tensor(T) = try gpa.alloc(Tensor(T), what.weights.len);
    defer gpa.free(velocities);
    for (moments, velocities, what.weights) |*m, *v, w| {
        m.* = try Tensor(T).alloc(gpa, w.shape[0..w.rank]);
        v.* = try Tensor(T).alloc(gpa, w.shape[0..w.rank]);
        m.*.fill(0);
        v.*.fill(0);
    }

    const decay: T = @floatCast(opts.weight_decay);
    var first: f64 = 0;
    var seen_first: bool = false;
    var last: f64 = 0;
    var epoch_total: f64 = 0;
    var epoch_count: usize = 0;
    var step: usize = 1;

    var epoch: usize = 0;
    while (epoch < opts.epochs) : (epoch += 1) {
        loader.reshuffle();
        epoch_total = 0;
        epoch_count = 0;
        while (try loader.next(batch_inputs, batch_targets)) {
            try graph.recompute();
            if (!seen_first) {
                first = @floatCast(graph.valueOf(what.loss).data[0]);
                seen_first = true;
            }
            try graph.backward(what.loss);
            for (what.weights, what.parameters, moments, velocities) |w, v, m, vel| {
                try adamWStep(T, w, w, try graph.gradOf(v), m, vel, opts.hyper, decay, step);
            }
            step += 1;
            // Read AFTER the step, so the number reflects the weights that will be carried
            // forward rather than the ones just replaced.
            try graph.recompute();
            last = @floatCast(graph.valueOf(what.loss).data[0]);
            epoch_total += last;
            epoch_count += 1;
        }
    }
    return .{
        .first_loss = first,
        .final_loss = last,
        .final_epoch_mean = if (epoch_count == 0) last else epoch_total / float64(epoch_count),
        .steps = step - 1,
    };
}

Every test in this file had been writing this loop by hand: recompute, backward, step each parameter, repeat. The reason to have it once is not brevity. A hand-rolled loop that steps the head and forgets a gate still shows a falling loss — the read-out alone fits a good deal of anything — and nothing about the curve says a layer was never trained.

input and target must be leaves, graph.constant results, because fit feeds each batch by writing through their tensors rather than rebuilding the graph. Pass a computed value and it gets overwritten by the next recompute, and the model trains on whatever the last batch left behind.

That is also why the last partial batch is dropped. The graph's leaf tensors are allocated once with a fixed first dimension, so every batch must be exactly that many rows — there is nowhere to put a shorter one. Five rows with batch = 2 gives two batches and one row sits out, a different row each epoch once shuffling is on. Frameworks make this a drop_last flag because they rebuild per batch; here it falls out of the tape, so numBatches reports the truncated count rather than rounding up to a batch that cannot run.

Shuffling permutes an index array, never the caller's data. And Rng is indexed rather than a stream — it has no next — so a fresh order per epoch comes from a fresh label, not from advancing hidden state: same seed and same epoch is the same order, every run.

XOR is the test because it cannot be fitted by the read-out alone. It is not linearly separable, so the forgot-a-layer bug lands at 0.25 and stays. Measured: 1200 steps, first batch 1.885, final epoch mean exactly zero.

Exactly zero is alarming, and an MSE of 0.0 usually means a test is comparing something to itself — so it was checked rather than accepted. Re-run with targets of 0.3 and 0.7 instead of 0 and 1 and the loss lands at 1.04e-21, predictions reading 0.29999999995 and 0.69999999999. The difference is that 0 and 1 are exactly representable in binary and 0.3 is not: the optimiser reaches machine precision either way, and only one of the two target sets can show it as a clean number.

10.19 eig: the eigenvalue that is not there#

var values: [n]zn.ComplexNumber(f64) = undefined;
try zn.eig(f64, &values, m); // m is OVERWRITTEN
ComplexNumber
/// A complex number, as a pair.
///
/// `ComplexNumber` rather than `Complex`, which is a reserved name - `zm` has its own, of a different
/// shape. `extern` so an array of them is exactly interleaved re/im, which
/// is the layout every FFT library and every GPU buffer expects.
pub fn ComplexNumber(comptime T: type) type {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    return extern struct {
        const Self = @This();

        re: T = 0,
        im: T = 0,

        pub fn add(a: Self, b: Self) Self {
            return .{ .re = a.re + b.re, .im = a.im + b.im };
        }

        pub fn sub(a: Self, b: Self) Self {
            return .{ .re = a.re - b.re, .im = a.im - b.im };
        }

        pub fn mul(a: Self, b: Self) Self {
            return .{
                .re = a.re * b.re - a.im * b.im,
                .im = a.re * b.im + a.im * b.re,
            };
        }

        pub fn magnitude(a: Self) T {
            return @sqrt(a.re * a.re + a.im * a.im);
        }
    };
}
eig
/// Eigenvalues of a general REAL square matrix, by Hessenberg reduction then shifted QR.
///
/// `a` is `(n, n)` and is OVERWRITTEN. `out` receives the `n` eigenvalues, in no particular
/// order, each with a real and an imaginary part.
///
/// THE COMPLEX PAIR IS THE WHOLE DIFFICULTY, AND IT IS WHY `eigh` CANNOT BE REUSED
///
/// A symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues, and `eigh` finds them by Jacobi rotations that drive
/// the off-diagonal to zero. A non-symmetric real matrix need not have any real eigenvalue at
/// all: `[[0, -1], [1, 0]]` is a rotation by a quarter turn, and its eigenvalues are `+i` and
/// `-i`. No sequence of real similarity transforms will ever make that matrix diagonal, because
/// a real triangular matrix has real eigenvalues on its diagonal and this matrix has none.
///
/// So the iteration cannot aim for triangular. It aims for **real Schur form** - quasi-triangular,
/// with 1x1 blocks on the diagonal for real eigenvalues and 2x2 blocks for conjugate pairs. Each
/// surviving 2x2 block is solved by the quadratic formula, and a negative discriminant IS the
/// complex pair. That is why the shift is a DOUBLE shift: the two shifts of a conjugate pair are
/// conjugates of each other, and taking them together keeps every intermediate matrix real.
///
/// EIGENVALUES ONLY, NOT VECTORS. Eigenvectors of a non-symmetric matrix are a separate problem
/// with its own hazards - a defective matrix has fewer independent eigenvectors than eigenvalues,
/// so a routine returning `n` columns has to decide what to put in the missing ones, and every
/// answer is misleading. Stated rather than half-built.
///
/// `DomainError` if the iteration fails to converge, rather than a silently unconverged answer.
pub fn eig(comptime T: type, out: []ComplexNumber(T), a: Tensor(T)) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    if (a.rank != 2) {
        return Error.UnsupportedShape;
    }
    const n: usize = a.shape[0];
    if (a.shape[1] != n or out.len != n) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }
    if (n == 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    try hessenberg(T, a);

    // The convergence test is relative to this, for the reason `eigh`'s note gives at length: a
    // fixed threshold declares any sufficiently small matrix already converged, and returns its
    // untouched diagonal as the eigenvalues.
    var anorm: T = 0;
    for (0..n) |i| {
        for (0..n) |j| {
            anorm += @abs(try a.at(&.{ i, j }));
        }
    }
    if (anorm == 0) {
        for (out) |*slot| {
            slot.* = .{};
        }
        return;
    }
    const eps: T = zm.floatEps(T);

    // SIGNED INDICES, DELIBERATELY. The published form of this algorithm is written for 1-based
    // arrays, where `l - 1` and `hi - 2` are always in range. Translated to 0-based `usize` they
    // underflow and the routine crashes rather than answering - which is exactly what the first
    // version of this did. Signed arithmetic here costs a cast per index and removes the whole
    // class.
    const ni: isize = @intCast(n);
    var hi: isize = ni - 1;
    var t: T = 0;
    while (hi >= 0) {
        var its: usize = 0;
        while (true) {
            // Find the first negligible subdiagonal entry: everything below it has deflated.
            var l: isize = hi;
            while (l > 0) : (l -= 1) {
                const lu_: usize = @intCast(l);
                var s: T = @abs(try a.at(&.{ lu_ - 1, lu_ - 1 })) + @abs(try a.at(&.{ lu_, lu_ }));
                if (s == 0) {
                    s = anorm;
                }
                if (@abs(try a.at(&.{ lu_, lu_ - 1 })) <= eps * s) {
                    a.setAt2(lu_, lu_ - 1, 0);
                    break;
                }
            }
            const h: usize = @intCast(hi);
            var x: T = try a.at(&.{ h, h });
            if (l == hi) {
                // ONE real eigenvalue has deflated off the bottom.
                out[h] = .{ .re = x + t, .im = 0 };
                hi -= 1;
                break;
            }
            var y: T = try a.at(&.{ h - 1, h - 1 });
            var w: T = (try a.at(&.{ h, h - 1 })) * (try a.at(&.{ h - 1, h }));
            if (l == hi - 1) {
                // A 2x2 BLOCK, solved by the quadratic formula. The SIGN OF THE DISCRIMINANT is
                // what decides between two real roots and the conjugate pair, and it is the only
                // place in this routine where a complex number is ever formed.
                const p0: T = 0.5 * (y - x);
                const q0: T = p0 * p0 + w;
                const z0: T = @sqrt(@abs(q0));
                x += t;
                if (q0 >= 0) {
                    const zs: T = if (p0 >= 0) p0 + z0 else p0 - z0;
                    out[h - 1] = .{ .re = x + zs, .im = 0 };
                    out[h] = if (zs != 0) .{ .re = x - w / zs, .im = 0 } else .{ .re = x + zs, .im = 0 };
                } else {
                    out[h - 1] = .{ .re = x + p0, .im = z0 };
                    out[h] = .{ .re = x + p0, .im = -z0 };
                }
                hi -= 2;
                break;
            }
            if (its == 30) {
                return Error.DomainError;
            }
            if (its == 10 or its == 20) {
                // EXCEPTIONAL SHIFT. The usual shift can cycle on a matrix whose symmetry the
                // iteration keeps reproducing; a deliberately ad-hoc one breaks the cycle.
                // Without it the routine reaches 30 and reports failure on a matrix that is fine.
                t += x;
                for (0..h + 1) |i| {
                    a.setAt2(i, i, (try a.at(&.{ i, i })) - x);
                }
                const s: T = @abs(try a.at(&.{ h, h - 1 })) + @abs(try a.at(&.{ h - 1, h - 2 }));
                x = 0.75 * s;
                y = x;
                w = -0.4375 * s * s;
            }
            its += 1;

            // Look for two consecutive small subdiagonal entries, which is where the bulge can
            // be started without disturbing what has already converged.
            var p: T = 0;
            var q: T = 0;
            var r: T = 0;
            var m: isize = hi - 2;
            while (true) {
                const mu: usize = @intCast(m);
                const z: T = try a.at(&.{ mu, mu });
                const rr: T = x - z;
                const ss: T = y - z;
                p = (rr * ss - w) / (try a.at(&.{ mu + 1, mu })) + (try a.at(&.{ mu, mu + 1 }));
                q = (try a.at(&.{ mu + 1, mu + 1 })) - z - rr - ss;
                r = try a.at(&.{ mu + 2, mu + 1 });
                const bulge_scale: T = @abs(p) + @abs(q) + @abs(r);
                if (bulge_scale != 0) {
                    p /= bulge_scale;
                    q /= bulge_scale;
                    r /= bulge_scale;
                }
                if (m == l) {
                    break;
                }
                const u: T = @abs(try a.at(&.{ mu, mu - 1 })) * (@abs(q) + @abs(r));
                const v: T = @abs(p) * (@abs(try a.at(&.{ mu - 1, mu - 1 })) + @abs(z) +
                    @abs(try a.at(&.{ mu + 1, mu + 1 })));
                if (u <= eps * v) {
                    break;
                }
                m -= 1;
            }
            {
                var i: isize = m + 2;
                while (i <= hi) : (i += 1) {
                    const iu: usize = @intCast(i);
                    a.setAt2(iu, iu - 2, 0);
                    if (i != m + 2) {
                        a.setAt2(iu, iu - 3, 0);
                    }
                }
            }

            // Chase the bulge back down the subdiagonal with Householder reflections.
            var k: isize = m;
            while (k <= hi - 1) : (k += 1) {
                const ku: usize = @intCast(k);
                if (k != m) {
                    p = try a.at(&.{ ku, ku - 1 });
                    q = try a.at(&.{ ku + 1, ku - 1 });
                    r = if (k != hi - 1) try a.at(&.{ ku + 2, ku - 1 }) else 0;
                    x = @abs(p) + @abs(q) + @abs(r);
                    if (x == 0) {
                        continue;
                    }
                    p /= x;
                    q /= x;
                    r /= x;
                }
                const root: T = @sqrt(p * p + q * q + r * r);
                const sgn: T = if (p >= 0) root else -root;
                if (sgn == 0) {
                    continue;
                }
                if (k == m) {
                    if (l != m) {
                        a.setAt2(ku, ku - 1, -(try a.at(&.{ ku, ku - 1 })));
                    }
                } else {
                    a.setAt2(ku, ku - 1, -sgn * x);
                }
                p += sgn;
                const px: T = p / sgn;
                const py: T = q / sgn;
                const pz: T = r / sgn;
                const qn: T = q / p;
                const rn: T = r / p;
                var j: usize = ku;
                while (j <= @as(usize, @intCast(hi))) : (j += 1) {
                    var sum: T = (try a.at(&.{ ku, j })) + qn * (try a.at(&.{ ku + 1, j }));
                    if (k != hi - 1) {
                        sum += rn * (try a.at(&.{ ku + 2, j }));
                        a.setAt2(ku + 2, j, (try a.at(&.{ ku + 2, j })) - sum * pz);
                    }
                    a.setAt2(ku + 1, j, (try a.at(&.{ ku + 1, j })) - sum * py);
                    a.setAt2(ku, j, (try a.at(&.{ ku, j })) - sum * px);
                }
                const last: isize = if (hi < k + 3) hi else k + 3;
                var i: isize = l;
                while (i <= last) : (i += 1) {
                    const iu: usize = @intCast(i);
                    var sum: T = px * (try a.at(&.{ iu, ku })) + py * (try a.at(&.{ iu, ku + 1 }));
                    if (k != hi - 1) {
                        sum += pz * (try a.at(&.{ iu, ku + 2 }));
                        a.setAt2(iu, ku + 2, (try a.at(&.{ iu, ku + 2 })) - sum * rn);
                    }
                    a.setAt2(iu, ku + 1, (try a.at(&.{ iu, ku + 1 })) - sum * qn);
                    a.setAt2(iu, ku, (try a.at(&.{ iu, ku })) - sum);
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

A symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues, and eigh finds them by driving the off-diagonal to zero. A non-symmetric real matrix need not have a single real eigenvalue. [[0,-1],[1,0]] is a quarter-turn rotation; its eigenvalues are +i and -i, and no sequence of real similarity transforms will ever make it triangular — a real triangular matrix wears its eigenvalues on the diagonal, and this one has none to put there.

So the iteration cannot aim for triangular. It aims for real Schur form: quasi-triangular, 1×1 blocks for real eigenvalues and 2×2 blocks for conjugate pairs. Each surviving 2×2 is solved by the quadratic formula, and a negative discriminant is the complex pair. That is also why the shift is a double shift: the two shifts of a conjugate pair are conjugates of each other, so taking them together keeps every intermediate matrix real. No complex number is formed anywhere until that last quadratic.

Hessenberg reduction comes first, and it is not an optimisation.
