QR converges on any matrix, but a sweep on a full one costs O(n³) and the whole solve O(n⁴); on a Hessenberg one a sweep is O(n²), because there are only n-1 nonzeros to chase — and Hessenberg form is preserved by a QR step. One O(n³) reduction turns the iteration from unusable into the standard method.

The reflections go on from both sides, A ← P A P. Applying from one side gives a perfectly Hessenberg matrix with the wrong eigenvalues, and no amount of staring at the zeros reveals it — which is why the test checks trace and determinant, the similarity invariants, rather than the shape alone.

The published form of this algorithm is written for 1-based arrays, where l-1 and hi-2 are always in range. Translated to 0-based usize they underflow, and the first version here crashed instead of answering. The indices are signed now: a cast per access, and the whole class is gone.

Four checks, because a spectrum is easy to get plausibly wrong: the rotation's exact ±i; the companion matrix of (x-1)(x²+1), so one 1×1 and one 2×2 deflate from the same matrix; trace and determinant against the sum and product of the eigenvalues on a random 6×6, whose imaginary parts must cancel exactly because the pairs are conjugate; and agreement with eigh on a symmetric matrix, where two implementations sharing no code have to reach the same numbers.

Eigenvalues only, not vectors. Eigenvectors of a non-symmetric matrix are a separate problem: a defective matrix has fewer independent eigenvectors than eigenvalues, so a routine returning n columns must decide what to put in the missing ones, and every answer misleads. Stated rather than half-built.

10.20 Attention, and a mask you cannot forget#

try attention.attach(&graph, x, .everywhere);     // encoder: all positions
try attention.attach(&graph, x, .backward_only);  // decoder: no peeking ahead

Same shape as BatchNorm.Use, and the consequence is worse. A language model trained without a causal mask can see the answer it is predicting: the loss drops to near zero, the training curve looks superb, and the model generates nonsense the moment it has to predict something it has not been shown. Nothing fails, nothing warns, and the metric that would tell you is the one that looks best.

So look is required at every call. There is no default to inherit and no field to forget.

The test perturbs the future and watches the past

Inspecting the mask would only confirm the mask is the one intended. Instead, replacing the last position with a large value and measures how much every earlier output moves:

.backward_only   largest shift  EXACTLY 0
.everywhere      largest shift  > 0.1

Not "small" — zero. A causal mask that let through a millionth would be a causal mask with a bug, and a tolerance would hide it. The unmasked run is what proves the zero came from the mask rather than from the input being ignored.

Two smaller choices

The scale is derived, not passed. Dot products grow with the width they are summed over, so without 1/sqrt(width) the softmax saturates and the gradient vanishes. Passing the wrong dimension is a quiet, common mistake; here it comes from the projection's own shape and cannot disagree with the tensors it scales.

The mask adds a large negative, not -inf. Negative infinity is exactly right in algebra and produces inf - inf = NaN the moment a row is entirely masked — which the first row of a causal mask never is, but a padded batch would be. A number the exponential flushes to zero says the same thing and survives.

Multi-head, and what the name hides

try zn.Attention(f64).init(gpa, rng, model_dim, width, heads);
Attention
/// Scaled dot-product attention: every position reads every position it is allowed to see.
///
/// WHETHER IT CAN SEE THE FUTURE IS AN ARGUMENT, NOT A SETTING
///
/// The same lesson as `BatchNorm.Use`, and the consequence is worse. A language model trained
/// without a causal mask **can see the answer it is predicting**: the loss drops to near zero,
/// the training curve looks superb, and the model generates nonsense the moment it has to predict
/// something it has not been shown. Nothing fails, nothing warns, and the metric that would tell
/// you is the one that looks best.
///
/// So `look` is required at every call:
///
///     try attention.attach(&graph, x, .everywhere);     // encoder: all positions
///     try attention.attach(&graph, x, .backward_only);  // decoder: no peeking ahead
///
/// THE SCALE IS DERIVED, NOT PASSED
///
/// Dot products grow with the width they are summed over, so without `1/sqrt(width)` the softmax
/// saturates and the gradient vanishes - and passing the wrong dimension is a quiet, common
/// mistake. Here it comes from the projection's own shape, so it cannot disagree with the tensors
/// it scales.
///
/// SINGLE HEAD. Multiple heads need the projection split and the results concatenated. When this
/// was written the tape had neither operation with a backward, and the note recorded that limit
/// rather than half-building around it.
///
/// **The limit is gone** - `Graph.slice` and `Graph.concat` both exist now, with backwards
/// checked against a numerical derivative, so multi-head is buildable from what is already here.
/// It has not been built yet; `heads` is carried and used for the scale, and splitting the
/// projection is the remaining work. Recorded as owed rather than as impossible.
pub fn Attention(comptime T: type) type {
    return struct {
        /// What each position is looking for.
        query: Tensor(T),
        /// What each position offers as a label.
        key: Tensor(T),
        /// What each position hands over when chosen.
        value: Tensor(T),
        /// How many independent attention patterns share the projection width.
        heads: usize,

        const Self = @This();

        /// Which positions a query may attend to. **Required** - see the note above.
        pub const Look = enum {
            /// Every position, in both directions. What an encoder wants.
            everywhere,
            /// Only positions at or before this one. What a decoder MUST have.
            backward_only,
        };

        pub const Attached = struct {
            out: Var,
            query: Var,
            key: Var,
            value: Var,
        };

        /// `heads` independent attention patterns sharing one projection of `width` columns.
        ///
        /// `heads = 1` is ordinary attention. More heads do not widen anything - they DIVIDE the
        /// same width, so each head attends in a narrower subspace and the cost is unchanged.
        /// That is the part the name hides: multi-head is not more capacity, it is the same
        /// capacity spent on several patterns instead of one.
        pub fn init(
            gpa: Allocator,
            rng: Rng,
            model_dim: usize,
            width: usize,
            heads: usize,
        ) Error!Self {
            if (heads == 0 or width % heads != 0) {
                return Error.UnsupportedShape;
            }
            const query: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(gpa, &.{ model_dim, width });
            const key: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(gpa, &.{ model_dim, width });
            const value: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(gpa, &.{ model_dim, width });
            try initXavier(T, query, rng.split(0), model_dim, width);
            try initXavier(T, key, rng.split(1), model_dim, width);
            try initXavier(T, value, rng.split(2), model_dim, width);
            return .{ .query = query, .key = key, .value = value, .heads = heads };
        }

        pub fn attach(
            self: Self,
            graph: *Graph(T),
            input: Var,
            look: Look,
        ) Error!Attached {
            const x: Tensor(T) = graph.valueOf(input);
            if (x.rank != 2 or x.shape[1] != self.query.shape[0]) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }
            const positions: usize = x.shape[0];
            const width: usize = self.query.shape[1];

            const wq: Var = try graph.parameter(self.query);
            const wk: Var = try graph.parameter(self.key);
            const wv: Var = try graph.parameter(self.value);
            const q: Var = try graph.matmul(input, wq);
            const k: Var = try graph.matmul(input, wk);
            const v: Var = try graph.matmul(input, wv);

            // RANK 2 THROUGHOUT, ONE HEAD AT A TIME
            //
            // The usual way splits heads by reshaping to rank 4 and permuting: `[rows, D]` becomes
            // `[B, S, H, d]` becomes `[B, H, S, d]`. That needs a differentiable reshape AND
            // permute, and it makes every line afterwards reason about four axes.
            //
            // With `graph.slice` and `graph.concat` the same thing is a loop: take each head's
            // columns, attend, and join the results. Every tensor stays rank 2 and each iteration
            // reads exactly like the single-head maths, because it IS the single-head maths.
            //
            // The cost: `heads` separate matmuls where a batched form would do one. For the head
            // counts a rank-2 tape sees that is a fair trade for not having two more tape ops and
            // four axes to track - and it is stated here rather than discovered.
            const head_width: usize = width / self.heads;
            const scale_by: T = 1.0 / @sqrt(@as(T, @floatFromInt(head_width)));
            var joined: ?Var = null;
            for (0..self.heads) |head| {
                const from: usize = head * head_width;
                const qh: Var = try graph.slice(q, 1, from, head_width);
                const kh: Var = try graph.slice(k, 1, from, head_width);
                const vh: Var = try graph.slice(v, 1, from, head_width);
                const raw_head: Var = try graph.matmul(qh, try graph.transpose(kh));
                const scaled_head: Var = try graph.scale(raw_head, scale_by);
                const allowed: Var = try applyLook(graph, scaled_head, look, positions);
                const attended: Var = try graph.matmul(try graph.softmaxRows(allowed), vh);
                joined = if (joined) |so_far|
                    try graph.concat(so_far, attended, 1)
                else
                    attended;
            }
            return .{ .out = joined.?, .query = wq, .key = wk, .value = wv };
        }

        /// The mask, or nothing, depending on `look`.
        fn applyLook(
            graph: *Graph(T),
            scores: Var,
            look: Look,
            positions: usize,
        ) Error!Var {
            if (look == .everywhere) {
                return scores;
            }
            // A LARGE NEGATIVE, NOT AN INFINITY. `-inf` would be exactly right in algebra and
            // produces `inf - inf = NaN` the moment a row is entirely masked, which the first row
            // of a causal mask never is but a padded batch would be. A number the exponential
            // flushes to zero says the same thing and survives.
            const mask: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(graph.gpa, &.{ positions, positions });
            for (0..positions) |row| {
                for (0..positions) |col| {
                    try mask.setAt(&.{ row, col }, if (col > row) -1.0e30 else 0);
                }
            }
            return graph.add(scores, try graph.constant(mask));
        }
    };
}

More heads do not widen anything — they divide the same width. Two heads over a width of 8 produce exactly the same output shape and the same parameter count as one head over 8; each simply attends in a narrower subspace. That is the part "multi-head" hides, and this is exact for it: same shape, different numbers.

The scale then comes from the head's width, not the projection's. Splitting 8 into two heads means each sums over 4, so the scale is 1/sqrt(4). Getting that wrong is invisible in the shapes and quiet in the output — it just saturates the softmax a little more than it should. The test pins it by checking that one head over 4 and two heads over 8 share a scale, where a projection-wide scale would have made them differ.

A width that does not divide by the head count is refused rather than silently dropping a column.

Rank 2 throughout, one head at a time

The usual way splits heads by reshaping to rank 4 and permuting: [rows, D] becomes [B, S, H, d] becomes [B, H, S, d]. That needs a differentiable reshape and permute, and every line afterwards reasons about four axes.

With graph.slice and graph.concat the same thing is a loop: take each head's columns, attend, join the results. Every tensor stays rank 2, and each iteration reads exactly like the single-head maths — because it is the single-head maths.

The cost is heads separate matmuls where a batched form would do one. For the head counts a rank-2 tape sees, that is a fair trade for not carrying two more tape ops and four axes, and it is stated here rather than discovered.

10.21 TransformerBlock, and why pre-norm#

h = x + attention(norm(x))
y = h + feedForward(norm(h))

The block normalises before each sublayer and adds the result to the untouched input. The original transformer did it the other way — sublayer, add, then normalise — and that version cannot be trained without a learning-rate warmup, because the normalisation sits on the residual path and rescales the gradient at every block.

Pre-norm leaves the path clear: the gradient reaches the input carrying a component of exactly one from each residual, whatever the depth, so no element of the input gradient collapses.

A fresh block is close to the identity. The sublayers start small against the residual, so depth you have not trained yet does nothing rather than something arbitrary. That is what makes stacking blocks safe before any training has happened, and there is a bound on how far the output can move from its input.

Causality survives composition, and that is worth checking separately

The mask lives inside Attention. But a residual carries the input forward around the attention, so composition is exactly where a leak would appear — the block could route the future past its own mask. The same perturbation test therefore runs again at this level: disturb the last position, and every earlier output must be bit-identical.

The seven parameters are collected the same way Chain does it, for the same reason: one missing from that list would silently never train.

The feed-forward is chosen at init, because the gate changes a shape

try zn.TransformerBlock(f64).init(gpa, rng, model_dim, hidden, heads, eps, .swiglu);
TransformerBlock
/// One transformer block: attention and a feed-forward pair, each behind a residual.
///
/// PRE-NORM, AND THE RESIDUAL IS WHY
///
/// The block normalises BEFORE each sublayer and adds the result to the untouched input:
///
///     h = x + attention(norm(x))
///     y = h + feedForward(norm(h))
///
/// The original transformer did it the other way - sublayer, add, then normalise - and that
/// version **cannot be trained without a learning-rate warmup**, because the normalisation sits
/// on the residual path and rescales the gradient every block. Pre-norm leaves the path clear:
/// the gradient reaches the input with a component of exactly one from each residual, whatever
/// the depth. The test below asserts the consequence rather than the arrangement.
///
/// The sublayers begin small relative to the residual, so a fresh block is close to the identity.
/// That is the point: depth you have not trained yet should do nothing, not something arbitrary.
pub fn TransformerBlock(comptime T: type) type {
    return struct {
        /// Reads across positions.
        attention: Attention(T),
        /// The first half of the position-wise pair, widening.
        widen: Dense(T),
        /// The second half, narrowing back so the residual still fits.
        narrow: Dense(T),
        /// Added under the square root in both norms.
        epsilon: T,
        /// Which feed-forward this block was built with - it decided `widen`'s shape.
        feed_forward: FeedForward,

        const Self = @This();

        pub const Attached = struct {
            out: Var,
            /// Everything the block attached, ready for the optimiser - the same argument as
            /// `Chain`: a parameter missing from this list would silently never train.
            parameters: [7]Var,
        };

        /// Which feed-forward the block uses. **Chosen at `init`, not at `attach`.**
        ///
        /// THE GATE CHANGES A LAYER'S SHAPE, NOT JUST THE ACTIVATION BETWEEN TWO
        ///
        /// It looks like an activation swap and is not. SwiGLU consumes half its input as a gate,
        /// so to produce `hidden` columns the widening layer has to make **2 x hidden** - which
        /// makes it a different network, not the same one with a different nonlinearity.
        ///
        ///     relu     widen (model -> hidden),     relu,   narrow (hidden -> model)
        ///     swiglu   widen (model -> 2 x hidden), swiglu, narrow (hidden -> model)
        ///
        /// At `model_dim = 4, hidden = 16` that is 148 parameters against 228. A caller comparing
        /// the two is comparing capacities as well as gates, and the doc says so rather than
        /// letting them conclude the gate alone did it.
        pub const FeedForward = enum { relu, swiglu };

        /// `hidden` is the width of the feed-forward middle. Four times `model_dim` is the usual
        /// choice and is the caller's to make rather than a constant hidden here.
        pub fn init(
            gpa: Allocator,
            rng: Rng,
            model_dim: usize,
            hidden: usize,
            heads: usize,
            epsilon: T,
            feed_forward: FeedForward,
        ) Error!Self {
            // SwiGLU splits the widened columns in half, so it needs twice as many to hand the
            // same width to the narrowing layer.
            const widened: usize = switch (feed_forward) {
                .relu => hidden,
                .swiglu => hidden * 2,
            };
            return .{
                .attention = try Attention(T).init(gpa, rng.split(0), model_dim, model_dim, heads),
                .widen = try Dense(T).init(gpa, rng.split(1), model_dim, widened, .xavier),
                .narrow = try Dense(T).init(gpa, rng.split(2), hidden, model_dim, .xavier),
                .epsilon = epsilon,
                .feed_forward = feed_forward,
            };
        }

        pub fn attach(
            self: Self,
            graph: *Graph(T),
            input: Var,
            look: Attention(T).Look,
        ) Error!Attached {
            // Attention sublayer. `input` goes into the add untouched - that is the residual.
            const before_attention: Var = try graph.layerNormRows(input, self.epsilon);
            const attended: Attention(T).Attached = try self.attention.attach(graph, before_attention, look);
            const mixed: Var = try graph.add(input, attended.out);

            // Feed-forward sublayer, position by position, with its own residual.
            const before_feedforward: Var = try graph.layerNormRows(mixed, self.epsilon);
            const wide: Dense(T).Attached = try self.widen.attach(graph, before_feedforward);
            const activated: Var = switch (self.feed_forward) {
                .relu => try graph.relu(wide.out),
                // Halves the width, which is why `init` doubled it.
                .swiglu => try graph.swiglu(wide.out),
            };
            const narrowed: Dense(T).Attached = try self.narrow.attach(graph, activated);

            return .{
                .out = try graph.add(mixed, narrowed.out),
                .parameters = .{
                    attended.query, attended.key, attended.value,
                    wide.weight,    wide.bias,    narrowed.weight,
                    narrowed.bias,
                },
            };
        }
    };
}

It looks like an activation swap and is not. SwiGLU consumes half its input as a gate, so to hand hidden columns to the narrowing layer, the widening layer has to produce 2 x hidden:

relu     widen (model -> hidden),     relu,   narrow (hidden -> model)
swiglu   widen (model -> 2 x hidden), swiglu, narrow (hidden -> model)

At model_dim = 4, hidden = 16 that is 148 parameters against 228. A caller comparing the two is comparing capacities as well as gates, which is worth knowing before concluding the gate alone moved a training curve. The test asserts both widths and that the narrowing layer is unchanged.

What does not change: the output shape, so a block is still a block and still stacks; and the parameter count, still seven — the gate changed a shape, not the number of things to train.

Causality is re-checked for the gated block too. The mask is in the attention, but a residual carries the input around it either way, so the perturbation test runs again rather than being assumed to transfer.

10.22 Gated units, and a backward nobody wrote#

const h = try graph.glu(x);      // slice * sigmoid(slice)
const h = try graph.swiglu(x);   // slice * silu(slice)

Half the columns carry the value and half the gate, so the output is half as wide. SwiGLU is the gate in every recent transformer feed-forward.

Neither has a backward. A hand-derived backward would walk coordinates and apply the product rule by hand. Here a GLU is

slice(x, 0, half) * sigmoid(slice(x, half, half))

and every one of those is already a tape node, so the gradient is the tape's. There is no second derivation to keep in step with the first, and no chance of the pair disagreeing under maintenance.

This is the third thing graph.slice and graph.concat paid for, after multi-head attention and the batched cartpole twin. They were built because their absence had shaped two designs; they keep shaping the ones that come after.

The test still checks the gradient against central differences at every element — over the value half and the gate half, since a product rule applied by hand is exactly the kind of thing that is right on one branch and wrong on the other. And it asserts SwiGLU differs numerically from GLU, because a version ignoring the gate kind would pass the shape check and every gradient check above it.

10.23 Keeping a trained network#

try zn.saveParameters(f64, gpa, &bytes, &graph, run.parameters);
// ... later, in a fresh process ...
try zn.loadParameters(f64, gpa, bytes, &graph, run.parameters);
saveParameters
/// Write a network's parameters, named by position.
///
/// THE GAP THIS CLOSES: A TRAINED MODEL YOU CANNOT SAVE IS A DEMO
///
/// `saveTensors` and `loadTensors` have been here all along, and they take names and tensors.
/// What was missing is the bridge from a network to those two lists - so a library that could
/// train a cartpole agent could not keep it, and every run started from noise.
///
/// NAMED BY POSITION, AND THAT IS A REAL CONSTRAINT
///
/// The names are `p0`, `p1`, ... in `attach` order. A `Var` carries no name, so there is nothing
/// better available - and the consequence has to be stated rather than discovered: **the loading
/// network must have the same architecture in the same order.** `loadTensors` checks the SHAPES,
/// so a mismatched layer is caught; a same-shaped layer in a different role is not.
///
/// Owned names would suit a network assembled dynamically. Positional names are enough for a
/// `Chain`, whose layers are a comptime tuple and therefore always in the same order.
pub fn saveParameters(
    comptime T: type,
    gpa: Allocator,
    out: *ArrayList(u8),
    graph: *const Graph(T),
    parameters: []const Var,
) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const names: [][]const u8 = gpa.alloc([]const u8, parameters.len) catch
        return Error.OutOfMemory;
    defer {
        for (names) |name| {
            gpa.free(name);
        }
        gpa.free(names);
    }
    const tensors: []Tensor(T) = gpa.alloc(Tensor(T), parameters.len) catch
        return Error.OutOfMemory;
    defer gpa.free(tensors);
    for (parameters, 0..) |parameter, i| {
        names[i] = allocPrint(gpa, "p{d}", .{i}) catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
        tensors[i] = graph.valueOf(parameter);
    }
    return saveTensors(T, gpa, out, names, tensors);
}
loadParameters
/// Read a network's parameters back into it, in place.
///
/// The tensors are written THROUGH the graph's parameter values, so a network built with the
/// same architecture picks up the saved weights and is ready to run. `loadTensors` refuses a
/// shape that disagrees, which catches the common mistake of loading into a different
/// architecture.
pub fn loadParameters(
    comptime T: type,
    gpa: Allocator,
    bytes: []const u8,
    graph: *const Graph(T),
    parameters: []const Var,
) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const names: [][]const u8 = gpa.alloc([]const u8, parameters.len) catch
        return Error.OutOfMemory;
    defer {
        for (names) |name| {
            gpa.free(name);
        }
        gpa.free(names);
    }
    const tensors: []Tensor(T) = gpa.alloc(Tensor(T), parameters.len) catch
        return Error.OutOfMemory;
    defer gpa.free(tensors);
    for (parameters, 0..) |parameter, i| {
        names[i] = allocPrint(gpa, "p{d}", .{i}) catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
        tensors[i] = graph.valueOf(parameter);
    }
    return loadTensors(T, bytes, names, tensors);
}

saveTensors and loadTensors were always here, and they take a list of names and a list of tensors. What was missing is the bridge from a network to those two lists — so this library could train a cartpole agent and not keep it, and every run started from noise.

What this guarantees

Not that the bytes round-trip — the tensor tests already make that claim. The claim is that a network rebuilt from a different seed and then loaded produces the same output as the one that trained.

Three things make that meaningful rather than decorative:

  • The network is trained first, so the weights are no longer the initialisation. A round trip that silently restored the seed rather than the weights would otherwise pass.
  • The fresh network uses a different seed, so if the load does nothing the answers differ. The test asserts they differ before loading — a control, so the comparison after means something.
  • It compares every output, not just the loss. A loss is one number, and two different networks can share it by coincidence.

Named by position, which is a real constraint

The parameters are saved as p0, p1, ... in attach order, because a Var carries no name. The loading network must have the same architecture in the same order.

loadTensors checks the shapes, so a changed layer is caught — loading a checkpoint into a network whose hidden width grew and gets a ShapeMismatch. A same-shaped layer in a different role is not caught, and that is worth knowing rather than discovering.

10.26 numericalGrad: checking a gradient you cannot put on the tape#

const Eval = struct {
    fn loss(self: @This(), t: zn.Tensor(f64)) zn.Error!f64 {
        _ = self;
        return zn.crossEntropyRows(f64, t, &.{ 2, 0 });
    }
};
try zn.numericalGrad(f64, out, x, 1.0e-6, Eval{});
Tensor
/// A view of `T`-typed storage as a multidimensional array.
///
/// A TENSOR NEVER OWNS ITS STORAGE, AND THAT IS THE DESIGN
///
/// There is no ownership flag and no `deinit`. `data` is a slice the tensor addresses; whoever
/// allocated it frees it, with the allocator that allocated it. Usually that is an arena, in
/// which case nobody frees anything and `arena.deinit()` ends the matter.
///
/// The alternative - an `owns: bool` and a `deinit` that is a no-op for views - is the shape
/// this library was warned about before it had a tensor: both of its failure modes are SILENT.
/// `deinit` on a view does nothing and reads as if it did something; a missing `deinit` on an
/// owner just grows memory. Having no `deinit` at all means a free appears exactly where an
/// allocation appears, and a view has neither.
///
/// Strides are in ELEMENTS and signed, so a reversed or negatively-strided view is expressible
/// without changing this type. `at` computes a signed offset and casts once.
pub fn Tensor(comptime T: type) type {
    return struct {
        const Self = @This();

        /// The storage this tensor addresses. Not owned - see the type's doc comment.
        data: []T,
        /// Extent of each axis. Only the first `rank` entries are meaningful.
        shape: [max_rank]usize,
        /// Step in ELEMENTS between consecutive positions along each axis.
        strides: [max_rank]isize,
        rank: u8,
        /// WHERE THIS VIEW STARTS INSIDE `data`
        ///
        /// Every view until now began at element 0, which is why `slice` could not exist: a
        /// window into the middle of a tensor IS an offset. With this, `slice` and the other
        /// indexing operations become views rather than copies.
        ///
        /// IT ALSO WEAKENS WHAT `data.len` MEANS. `data` is the whole backing store; `base`
        /// and the strides say which of it this view addresses. Everything that walked
        /// `data[0..size()]` assuming those coincide had to be corrected - five sites, all of
        /// them fast paths that skip the index walk, which is exactly where such an assumption
        /// hides.
        base: usize = 0,

        /// A dense row-major tensor over `shape`, allocated from `gpa`.
        ///
        /// The caller frees `result.data` with the same allocator - or allocates from an arena
        /// and frees nothing.
        pub fn alloc(gpa: Allocator, shape: []const usize) Error!Self {
            if (shape.len > max_rank) {
                return Error.UnsupportedShape;
            }
            var count: usize = 1;
            for (shape) |extent| {
                count *= extent;
            }
            const storage: []T = gpa.alloc(T, count) catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
            return fromSlice(storage, shape);
        }

        /// A dense row-major view of `data` as `shape`. `data.len` must be exactly the product of
        /// the extents - a slice that is merely LARGE ENOUGH is rejected, because the usual reason
        /// for the mismatch is a shape that is wrong rather than storage that is generous.
        pub fn fromSlice(data: []T, shape: []const usize) Error!Self {
            if (shape.len > max_rank) {
                return Error.UnsupportedShape;
            }
            var count: usize = 1;
            for (shape) |extent| {
                count *= extent;
            }
            if (count != data.len) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }

            var self: Self = .{
                .data = data,
                .shape = @splat(1),
                .strides = @splat(0),
                .rank = @intCast(shape.len),
                .base = 0,
            };
            // Row-major: the last axis is contiguous, and each earlier stride is the product of
            // the extents to its right.
            var stride: isize = 1;
            var axis: usize = shape.len;
            while (axis > 0) {
                axis -= 1;
                self.shape[axis] = shape[axis];
                self.strides[axis] = stride;
                stride *= @intCast(shape[axis]);
            }
            return self;
        }

        /// The number of elements this tensor addresses.
        pub fn size(self: Self) usize {
            var count: usize = 1;
            var axis: usize = 0;
            while (axis < self.rank) : (axis += 1) {
                count *= self.shape[axis];
            }
            return count;
        }

        /// Whether the strides are dense row-major, so `data[0..size()]` is the tensor in order.
        ///
        /// An operation that walks memory linearly must ask this rather than assume it: a view
        /// produced by `transpose` addresses the same storage in a different order, and a linear
        /// walk over it silently reads the wrong elements rather than failing.
        pub fn isContiguous(self: Self) bool {
            var expected: isize = 1;
            var axis: usize = self.rank;
            while (axis > 0) {
                axis -= 1;
                if (self.shape[axis] != 1 and self.strides[axis] != expected) {
                    return false;
                }
                expected *= @intCast(self.shape[axis]);
            }
            return true;
        }

        /// The offset into `data` of the element at `indices`.
        pub fn flatIndex(self: Self, indices: []const usize) Error!usize {
            if (indices.len != self.rank) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }
            var offset: isize = @intCast(self.base);
            for (indices, 0..) |i, axis| {
                if (i >= self.shape[axis]) {
                    return Error.OutOfRange;
                }
                offset += self.strides[axis] * @as(isize, @intCast(i));
            }
            return @intCast(offset);
        }

        /// The element at `indices`.
        pub fn at(self: Self, indices: []const usize) Error!T {
            return self.data[try self.flatIndex(indices)];
        }

        /// The flat offset for a coordinate, with no error.
        ///
        /// THE 45 `flatIndex(...) catch unreachable` SITES ARE ALL THIS SHAPE
        ///
        ///     const at: []const usize = walker[0..out.rank];
        ///     out.data[out.offsetOf(at)] = ...
        ///
        /// The slice is `walker[0..rank]`, so `indices.len != rank` **cannot** happen - the
        /// caller built it from the rank. And the coordinate came from a `Walk` over this very
        /// shape, so the bounds cannot fail either. Two impossible checks, one `catch
        /// unreachable`, on the hottest line in the library.
        ///
        /// This computes the offset and returns it. The remaining safety is `data[offset]`,
        /// which is where Zig puts it: a panic with a message in Debug and ReleaseSafe.
        ///
        /// **Use it where the rank is an invariant you have already established** - after a
        /// shape check, or inside a walk over the tensor's own shape. Use `flatIndex` where the
        /// coordinate came from outside and might be wrong.
        pub fn offsetOf(self: Self, indices: []const usize) usize {
            var offset: isize = @intCast(self.base);
            for (indices, 0..) |i, axis| {
                offset += self.strides[axis] * @as(isize, @intCast(i));
            }
            return @intCast(offset);
        }

        /// Read from a rank-2 tensor. **Does not return an error.**
        ///
        /// WHY `at` HAS TO AND THIS DOES NOT
        ///
        /// `at(indices: []const usize)` can fail for two reasons. One is a real bounds check.
        /// The other is `indices.len != rank` - and that check exists ONLY because a slice hides
        /// its arity from the type system. Every call site writes a literal `&.{ i, j }`; the
        /// compiler could know it is two, and does not.
        ///
        /// Naming the arity in the function removes that half entirely. What remains is the
        /// bounds check, and **Zig already has a name for that**: it is what `data[idx]` does -
        /// a panic with a message and a stack trace in Debug and ReleaseSafe, the same UB as any
        /// other slice index in ReleaseFast.
        ///
        /// Nobody writes `arr[i] catch unreachable`. This file had **105 `catch unreachable`**,
        /// most of them on an `at` whose rank the author had checked three lines earlier, and
        /// that noise is the single biggest thing that makes numeric Zig look worse than it is.
        ///
        /// The safety is not weaker - it is Zig's, in the place Zig puts it.
        pub fn at2(self: Self, i: usize, j: usize) T {
            const offset: isize = @as(isize, @intCast(self.base)) +
                self.strides[0] * @as(isize, @intCast(i)) +
                self.strides[1] * @as(isize, @intCast(j));
            return self.data[@intCast(offset)];
        }

        /// Write to a rank-2 tensor. The mirror of `at2`, and error-free for the same reason.
        pub fn setAt2(self: Self, i: usize, j: usize, value: T) void {
            const offset: isize = @as(isize, @intCast(self.base)) +
                self.strides[0] * @as(isize, @intCast(i)) +
                self.strides[1] * @as(isize, @intCast(j));
            self.data[@intCast(offset)] = value;
        }

        /// Read from a rank-1 tensor, error-free.
        pub fn at1(self: Self, i: usize) T {
            const offset: isize = @as(isize, @intCast(self.base)) +
                self.strides[0] * @as(isize, @intCast(i));
            return self.data[@intCast(offset)];
        }

        /// Write to a rank-1 tensor, error-free.
        pub fn setAt1(self: Self, i: usize, value: T) void {
            const offset: isize = @as(isize, @intCast(self.base)) +
                self.strides[0] * @as(isize, @intCast(i));
            self.data[@intCast(offset)] = value;
        }

        /// Write `value` at `indices`.
        pub fn setAt(self: Self, indices: []const usize, value: T) Error!void {
            self.data[try self.flatIndex(indices)] = value;
        }

        /// Set every element to `value`.
        pub fn fill(self: Self, value: T) void {
            if (self.isContiguous()) {
                @memset(self.data[self.base..][0..self.size()], value);
                return;
            }
            var walker: [max_rank]usize = @splat(0);
            var remaining: usize = self.size();
            while (remaining > 0) : (remaining -= 1) {
                self.data[self.offsetOf(walker[0..self.rank])] = value;
                advance(self.shape[0..self.rank], walker[0..self.rank]);
            }
        }

        /// The same storage seen as `shape`. Requires a contiguous tensor and an equal element
        /// count; both are checked rather than assumed.
        pub fn reshape(self: Self, shape: []const usize) Error!Self {
            if (!self.isContiguous()) {
                return Error.UnsupportedShape;
            }
            var count: usize = 1;
            for (shape) |extent| {
                count *= extent;
            }
            if (count != self.size()) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }
            // From `base`, not 0: reshaping a slice must keep addressing that slice.
            return fromSlice(self.data[self.base..][0..self.size()], shape);
        }

        /// Whether two distinct index positions address the same element, which happens exactly
        /// when a stretched axis (stride 0) has extent above 1.
        ///
        /// An operation that WRITES must refuse an aliased destination. Many indices landing on
        /// one element means the last write wins and every earlier one vanishes - a result that is
        /// wrong in a way no bounds check catches. `map` and `zip` check this so a caller who
        /// passes a broadcast view as an output gets an error rather than a plausible answer.
        pub fn isAliased(self: Self) bool {
            var axis: usize = 0;
            while (axis < self.rank) : (axis += 1) {
                if (self.shape[axis] > 1 and self.strides[axis] == 0) {
                    return true;
                }
            }
            return false;
        }

        /// A read-only view of this tensor stretched to `shape` by the broadcasting rule.
        ///
        /// BROADCASTING IS A STRIDE OF ZERO, NOT A COPY
        ///
        /// An axis whose extent is 1 is stretched by setting its stride to 0, so every position
        /// along it addresses the same element. No storage is allocated and no data moves; a
        /// `(3, 1, 5)` tensor viewed as `(3, 4, 5)` is the same 15 values read four times.
        ///
        /// **WRITING THROUGH A STRETCHED VIEW IS ALMOST CERTAINLY A MISTAKE.** Many indices
        /// alias one element, so the last write wins and the others vanish. This returns a view
        /// because that is what the type system has; treat it as an input.
        ///
        /// `isContiguous` reports false for any stretched axis with extent > 1, which is what
        /// stops a linear walk from reading the underlying 15 values as if they were 60.
        pub fn broadcastTo(self: Self, shape: []const usize) Error!Self {
            if (shape.len > max_rank or shape.len < self.rank) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }
            var view: Self = .{
                .data = self.data,
                .shape = @splat(1),
                .strides = @splat(0),
                .rank = @intCast(shape.len),
                // Stretching does not move where the view starts.
                .base = self.base,
            };
            // Align at the TRAILING axis, as the broadcast rule does: an axis this tensor does not
            // have behaves as extent 1, and so does an axis it has with extent 1. Both get a
            // stride of 0.
            for (shape, 0..) |extent, axis| {
                const from_end: usize = shape.len - axis;
                view.shape[axis] = extent;
                if (self.rank < from_end) {
                    continue;
                }
                const own_axis: usize = self.rank - from_end;
                const own_extent: usize = self.shape[own_axis];
                if (own_extent == extent) {
                    view.strides[axis] = self.strides[own_axis];
                } else if (own_extent != 1) {
                    return Error.ShapeMismatch;
                }
            }
            return view;
        }

        /// A window into this tensor: `len` positions along `axis`, starting at `start`.
        ///
        /// A SLICE IS AN OFFSET, WHICH IS WHY `base` EXISTS
        ///
        /// Nothing is copied: the view keeps every stride and simply starts `start` steps further
        /// into the data along one axis. A batch of 32 rows out of 4096 is a `Tensor` the same
        /// size as any other, addressing 32 rows of the same buffer.
        ///
        /// `start + len` must fit. Clamping instead would hand back a view SMALLER than asked
        /// for, and the caller's next loop would read the shape it requested rather than the one
        /// it got.
        pub fn slice(self: Self, axis: usize, start: usize, len: usize) Error!Self {
            if (axis >= self.rank) {
                return Error.OutOfRange;
            }
            if (start + len > self.shape[axis]) {
                return Error.OutOfRange;
            }
            var view: Self = self;
            const step: isize = self.strides[axis] * @as(isize, @intCast(start));
            const moved: isize = @as(isize, @intCast(self.base)) + step;
            if (moved < 0) {
                return Error.OutOfRange;
            }
            view.base = @intCast(moved);
            view.shape[axis] = len;
            return view;
        }

        /// A view with the axes reordered: `out` axis `i` is this tensor's axis `order[i]`.
        ///
        /// EVERY `manip` OPERATION HERE IS METADATA
        ///
        /// `permute`, `squeeze`, `unsqueeze`, `flatten` and `moveAxis` all return a view: they
        /// permute or insert entries in two fixed-size arrays and copy nothing. That is why they
        /// need no GPU kernel and no sweep row - **there is no arithmetic to disagree about.**
        /// The cost appears later, when a permuted view has to be BOUND to a kernel and must be
        /// densified first, which is the constraint recorded in section 10.3.
        ///
        /// `order` must be a permutation of `0..rank`. A repeated axis would produce a view
        /// where two indices alias, which is `isAliased`'s job to reject at write time - but
        /// catching it here names the actual mistake.
        pub fn permute(self: Self, order: []const usize) Error!Self {
            if (order.len != self.rank) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }
            var seen: [max_rank]bool = @splat(false);
            for (order) |axis| {
                if (axis >= self.rank or seen[axis]) {
                    return Error.OutOfRange;
                }
                seen[axis] = true;
            }
            var view: Self = self;
            for (order, 0..) |axis, i| {
                view.shape[i] = self.shape[axis];
                view.strides[i] = self.strides[axis];
            }
            return view;
        }

        /// A view with a size-1 axis removed.
        ///
        /// Removing an axis whose extent is NOT 1 would change how many elements the view
        /// addresses, so it is `ShapeMismatch` rather than a silent reshape.
        pub fn squeeze(self: Self, axis: usize) Error!Self {
            if (axis >= self.rank) {
                return Error.OutOfRange;
            }
            if (self.shape[axis] != 1) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }
            var view: Self = self;
            var i: usize = axis;
            while (i + 1 < self.rank) : (i += 1) {
                view.shape[i] = self.shape[i + 1];
                view.strides[i] = self.strides[i + 1];
            }
            view.shape[self.rank - 1] = 1;
            view.strides[self.rank - 1] = 0;
            view.rank = @intCast(self.rank - 1);
            return view;
        }

        /// A view with a size-1 axis inserted at `axis`. `axis == rank` appends.
        ///
        /// The new axis gets a stride of 0, which is harmless because its extent is 1 - a
        /// single position cannot step anywhere. `isAliased` only objects when extent exceeds 1.
        pub fn unsqueeze(self: Self, axis: usize) Error!Self {
            if (axis > self.rank or self.rank + 1 > max_rank) {
                return Error.OutOfRange;
            }
            var view: Self = self;
            var i: usize = self.rank;
            while (i > axis) : (i -= 1) {
                view.shape[i] = self.shape[i - 1];
                view.strides[i] = self.strides[i - 1];
            }
            view.shape[axis] = 1;
            view.strides[axis] = 0;
            view.rank = @intCast(self.rank + 1);
            return view;
        }

        /// A rank-1 view of the whole tensor. Contiguous only, for `reshape`'s reason.
        pub fn flatten(self: Self) Error!Self {
            return self.reshape(&.{self.size()});
        }

        /// A view with one axis moved from `from` to `to`, the others keeping their order.
        pub fn moveAxis(self: Self, from: usize, to: usize) Error!Self {
            if (from >= self.rank or to >= self.rank) {
                return Error.OutOfRange;
            }
            var order: [max_rank]usize = @splat(0);
            var k: usize = 0;
            var i: usize = 0;
            while (i < self.rank) : (i += 1) {
                if (i == from) {
                    continue;
                }
                order[k] = i;
                k += 1;
            }
            // Open a slot at `to` and drop the moved axis into it.
            var j: usize = self.rank - 1;
            while (j > to) : (j -= 1) {
                order[j] = order[j - 1];
            }
            order[to] = from;
            return self.permute(order[0..self.rank]);
        }

        /// A view with axes `a` and `b` exchanged. Shares storage; changes through one are visible
        /// through the other.
        pub fn transpose(self: Self, a: usize, b: usize) Error!Self {
            if (a >= self.rank or b >= self.rank) {
                return Error.OutOfRange;
            }
            var view: Self = self;
            view.shape[a] = self.shape[b];
            view.shape[b] = self.shape[a];
            view.strides[a] = self.strides[b];
            view.strides[b] = self.strides[a];
            return view;
        }
    };
}
Error
/// Every error zimrnum can return. One set for the whole library, because a caller that wants to
/// handle "the shapes did not match" should not have to know which layer noticed.
pub const Error = error{
    /// An allocation failed. Distinct from every other error so a caller can retry or degrade.
    OutOfMemory,
    /// Two operands disagree about shape, and no broadcasting rule makes them agree.
    ShapeMismatch,
    /// An axis, index or dimension is outside the tensor it addresses.
    OutOfRange,
    /// The operation is defined but not for these values - a singular matrix, an empty sample,
    /// a quantile outside [0, 1].
    DomainError,
    /// The input has a shape the algorithm cannot accept (a non-square matrix to `cholesky`,
    /// a non-power-of-two length to a radix-2 transform).
    UnsupportedShape,
};
crossEntropyRows
/// Softmax cross-entropy of rank-2 `logits` against integer class `targets`, averaged over rows.
///
/// THE SOFTMAX IS NOT COMPUTED, AND THAT IS THE POINT
///
/// The definition is `-log(softmax(logits)[target])`, and computing it that way exponentiates,
/// normalises, then takes a logarithm - three chances to lose the answer. A logit of 800 gives an
/// infinite exponential and a loss of NaN; a correct probability of 1e-40 underflows to zero and
/// the logarithm is `-inf`.
///
/// The identity `-log(softmax(x)[t]) = logsumexp(x) - x[t]` avoids both: `logsumexp` is evaluated
/// by subtracting the row maximum, so the largest exponent is `e^0`, and the subtraction happens
/// in log space where the numbers are small. This form is finite for every finite input.
///
/// Takes LOGITS, not probabilities. A version taking probabilities would have to undo a softmax
/// the caller had already applied, which is where the precision is lost.
pub fn crossEntropyRows(
    comptime T: type,
    logits: Tensor(T),
    targets: []const usize,
) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    if (logits.rank != 2) {
        return Error.UnsupportedShape;
    }
    const rows: usize = logits.shape[0];
    const cols: usize = logits.shape[1];
    if (targets.len != rows) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }
    if (rows == 0 or cols == 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    for (targets) |t| {
        if (t >= cols) {
            return Error.OutOfRange;
        }
    }

    var total: CompensatedSum(T) = .{};
    var row: usize = 0;
    while (row < rows) : (row += 1) {
        var largest: T = logits.at2(row, 0);
        var col: usize = 1;
        while (col < cols) : (col += 1) {
            largest = @max(largest, logits.at2(row, col));
        }
        var sum_exp: T = 0;
        col = 0;
        while (col < cols) : (col += 1) {
            sum_exp += @exp(logits.at2(row, col) - largest);
        }
        const log_sum_exp: T = largest + @log(sum_exp);
        total.add(log_sum_exp - logits.at2(row, targets[row]));
    }
    return total.value() / @as(T, @floatFromInt(rows));
}
numericalGrad
/// Central-difference gradient of a scalar loss with respect to every element of `x`.
///
/// WHY THIS IS A FUNCTION AND NOT A PATTERN
///
/// Ten tests in this file had written their own: perturb one element by `+step`, evaluate,
/// perturb by `-step`, evaluate, divide the difference by `2 * step`, restore the element.
/// Ten chances to forget the restore, to divide by `step` instead of `2 * step`, or to leave
/// `x` mutated for whatever the test does next. The arithmetic is four lines and the bookkeeping
/// around it is where the mistakes live, which is exactly the shape that wants one
/// implementation.
///
/// `Graph.checkGradient` is the same idea one level up: it differentiates a loss ON THE TAPE
/// and compares against `backward`. This one takes any callable, so it reaches the losses that
/// are plain functions - `crossEntropyRows`, a GLU forward, a hand-built reduction - which the
/// tape version cannot see.
///
/// `x` IS RESTORED EXACTLY. Each element is written back from a saved copy rather than by
/// adding `step` back, because `(v + h) - h` is not `v` in floating point and a test that ran
/// this twice would drift.
///
/// `evaluator` is anything with `fn loss(self, Tensor(T)) Error!T` - a struct holding whatever
/// context the loss needs. Passing the function alone would not reach the targets, allocators
/// and shapes these losses close over.
pub fn numericalGrad(
    comptime T: type,
    out: Tensor(T),
    x: Tensor(T),
    step: T,
    evaluator: anytype,
) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    if (step <= 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    if (out.rank != x.rank) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }
    for (0..x.rank) |axis| {
        if (out.shape[axis] != x.shape[axis]) {
            return Error.ShapeMismatch;
        }
    }
    const count: usize = x.size();
    var index: usize = 0;
    while (index < count) : (index += 1) {
        const at: usize = x.base + index;
        const original: T = x.data[at];
        x.data[at] = original + step;
        const up: T = try evaluator.loss(x);
        x.data[at] = original - step;
        const down: T = try evaluator.loss(x);
        x.data[at] = original;
        out.data[out.base + index] = (up - down) / (2 * step);
    }
}

Graph.checkGradient differentiates a loss on the tape and compares against backward. That only reaches losses the tape can see. crossEntropyRows, a GLU forward, ppoClipObjective over a raw slice — these are plain functions, and the tape has never heard of them.

The arithmetic of a central difference is four lines. The bookkeeping around it is where the mistakes live: restore the element you perturbed, divide by 2h and not h, leave x unmutated for whatever runs next, and get the output shape right. Four chances to be wrong, once per call site.

One detail worth its own sentence: the element is restored from a saved copy, not by adding h back. (v + h) - h is not v in floating point, and a test that ran the sweep twice would drift a little each time.

The evaluator is a struct with a fn loss rather than a bare function pointer, because these losses close over things — targets, an allocator, shapes, a clip parameter — that a function alone cannot carry. numericalGradWorst is the same thing reporting a single worst-case ratio when you want one number instead of a tensor.

Two central differences in this file deliberately stay hand-written. They differentiate a scalar: (zm.sigmoid(x+h) - zm.sigmoid(x-h)) / 2h. A scalar overload for two call sites would be machinery rather than reuse, so they are left as-is and recorded rather than converted for tidiness.

10.27 Gradient clipping, and the direction it must keep#

const norm = try zn.clipGradNorm(f64, &graph, run.parameters, 1.0);
// `norm` is the value BEFORE clipping - log it
clipGradNorm
/// Scale every gradient down together if their combined norm exceeds `max_norm`.
///
/// Returns the norm BEFORE clipping, which is the number worth logging: a spike in it is how you
/// find out a batch was bad, and clipping silently would hide exactly that.
///
/// ONE NORM ACROSS ALL PARAMETERS, NOT ONE PER TENSOR
///
/// This is the part that is easy to get wrong and hard to notice. Clipping each tensor to its own
/// limit **changes the direction of the update**: a layer whose gradient was twice its neighbour's
/// comes out the same size, so the step now points somewhere the loss surface never suggested.
///
/// Scaling everything by one factor keeps the direction exactly and shortens the step, which is
/// what "clip the gradient" is supposed to mean. The test asserts the direction survives, because
/// a per-tensor version passes every test about magnitude.
///
/// WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN THE OPTIMISER YOU PICK
///
/// A transformer meets a bad batch, the loss spikes, and one enormous update moves the weights
/// somewhere the model never recovers from. Adam does not save you - it normalises by a RUNNING
/// average, so a single outlier is still an outlier. Clipping is the thing that does.
pub fn clipGradNorm(
    comptime T: type,
    graph: *const Graph(T),
    parameters: []const Var,
    max_norm: T,
) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    if (max_norm <= 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    var squares: CompensatedSum(T) = .{};
    for (parameters) |parameter| {
        const slopes: Tensor(T) = try graph.gradOf(parameter);
        for (0..slopes.size()) |i| {
            const g: T = slopes.data[i];
            squares.add(g * g);
        }
    }
    const total: T = @sqrt(squares.value());
    if (total <= max_norm) {
        return total;
    }
    // A SINGLE FACTOR, APPLIED TO EVERYTHING - that is what keeps the direction.
    const factor: T = max_norm / total;
    for (parameters) |parameter| {
        const slopes: Tensor(T) = try graph.gradOf(parameter);
        for (0..slopes.size()) |i| {
            slopes.data[i] *= factor;
        }
    }
    return total;
}

A transformer meets a bad batch, the loss spikes, and one enormous update moves the weights somewhere the model never recovers from. Adam does not save you — it normalises by a running average, so a single outlier is still an outlier. Clipping is the thing that does.

The return value is the norm before clipping, which is the number worth logging: a spike in it is how you learn a batch was bad, and clipping silently would hide exactly that.

One norm across all parameters, not one per tensor

This is the part that is easy to get wrong and hard to notice. Say two parameters whose gradients have norms 5 and 1:

global   both scaled by 1/sqrt(26)   ->  norms 0.98 and 0.196, ratio still 5
per-tensor  each scaled to 1         ->  norms 1 and 1,        ratio now 1

Clipping each tensor to its own limit changes the direction of the update. The layer whose gradient was five times its neighbour's comes out the same size, and the step now points somewhere the loss surface never suggested.

Scaling everything by one factor keeps the direction exactly and shortens the step, which is what "clip the gradient" is supposed to mean.

The test asserts the ratio survives, not just the final magnitude — a per-tensor version passes every check about size. Verified by writing the per-tensor version and watching the test fail.

One asymmetry worth noting: a gradient already under the limit is left alone, not scaled up to meet it. That would be a different operation entirely, and a tempting symmetry to add.

11. Statistics#

const v  = try zn.variance(f64, t, .sample);
const sd = try zn.stdDev(f64, t, .population);
const r  = try zn.rootMeanSquare(f64, t);
const d  = try zn.meanAbsDev(f64, t);
const se = try zn.stdErr(f64, t);

try zn.zscore(f64, out, t);        // mean 0, sample deviation 1
try zn.minMaxScale(f64, out, t);   // into [0, 1]

const c    = try zn.covariance(f64, a, b, .sample);
const corr = try zn.correlation(f64, a, b);
variance
/// The variance of every element, with the divisor chosen by `ddof`.
///
/// TWO PASSES, FOR THE REASON `layerNormRows` GIVES
///
/// `E[x^2] - E[x]^2` is one pass and subtracts two large nearly-equal numbers, losing most of its
/// significant digits when the mean is large relative to the spread. Two passes cost one more
/// read of memory that is already in cache and are correct for every input.
///
/// Returns `DomainError` when the divisor is undefined - `n = 0`, or `n = 1` with
/// `.sample` - rather than a NaN that propagates into a result nobody examines. That is what
/// `Ddof.divisor` returning an optional is for.
pub fn variance(comptime T: type, a: Tensor(T), ddof: Ddof) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const n: usize = a.size();
    const divisor: f64 = ddof.divisor(n) orelse return Error.DomainError;
    const mean: T = try meanAll(T, a);

    var total: CompensatedSum(T) = .{};
    var walk: Walk = .over(a.shape[0..a.rank]);
    while (walk.next()) |at| {
        const d: T = (try a.at(at)) - mean;
        const term: T = d * d;
        total.add(term);
    }
    const divide_by: T = @floatCast(divisor);
    return total.value() / divide_by;
}
stdDev
/// The standard deviation: the square root of `variance`.
pub fn stdDev(comptime T: type, a: Tensor(T), ddof: Ddof) Error!T {
    return @sqrt(try variance(T, a, ddof));
}
rootMeanSquare
/// The root mean square of every element.
pub fn rootMeanSquare(comptime T: type, a: Tensor(T)) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const n: usize = a.size();
    if (n == 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    var total: CompensatedSum(T) = .{};
    var walk: Walk = .over(a.shape[0..a.rank]);
    while (walk.next()) |at| {
        const x: T = try a.at(at);
        const term: T = x * x;
        total.add(term);
    }
    return @sqrt(total.value() / @as(T, @floatFromInt(n)));
}
meanAbsDev
/// The mean absolute deviation from the mean.
pub fn meanAbsDev(comptime T: type, a: Tensor(T)) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const n: usize = a.size();
    if (n == 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    const mean: T = try meanAll(T, a);
    var total: T = 0;
    var walk: Walk = .over(a.shape[0..a.rank]);
    while (walk.next()) |at| {
        total += @abs((try a.at(at)) - mean);
    }
    return total / @as(T, @floatFromInt(n));
}
stdErr
/// The standard error of the mean: `stdDev(.sample) / sqrt(n)`.
pub fn stdErr(comptime T: type, a: Tensor(T)) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const n: usize = a.size();
    if (n < 2) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    return (try stdDev(T, a, .sample)) / @sqrt(@as(T, @floatFromInt(n)));
}
zscore
/// `out = (a - mean) / stdDev`, elementwise - the z-score of every element.
///
/// Uses the SAMPLE deviation, matching what a reader gets from R or scipy by default. The
/// population form is a different number and the difference is visible at small n, so the choice
/// is stated rather than left to whichever the implementer reached for.
pub fn zscore(comptime T: type, out: Tensor(T), a: Tensor(T)) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const mean: T = try meanAll(T, a);
    const sd: T = try stdDev(T, a, .sample);
    if (sd == 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    if (out.isAliased()) {
        return Error.UnsupportedShape;
    }
    const shape: []const usize = out.shape[0..out.rank];
    const va: Tensor(T) = try a.broadcastTo(shape);
    var walk: Walk = .over(shape);
    while (walk.next()) |at| {
        const x: T = va.data[va.offsetOf(at)];
        out.data[out.offsetOf(at)] = (x - mean) / sd;
    }
}
minMaxScale
/// Normalise every element into `[0, 1]` by the tensor's own range.
pub fn minMaxScale(comptime T: type, out: Tensor(T), a: Tensor(T)) Error!void {
    comptime requireNumeric(T);
    const lo: T = try minAll(T, a);
    const hi: T = try maxAll(T, a);
    if (hi == lo) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    if (out.isAliased()) {
        return Error.UnsupportedShape;
    }
    const shape: []const usize = out.shape[0..out.rank];
    const va: Tensor(T) = try a.broadcastTo(shape);
    var walk: Walk = .over(shape);
    while (walk.next()) |at| {
        const x: T = va.data[va.offsetOf(at)];
        out.data[out.offsetOf(at)] = (x - lo) / (hi - lo);
    }
}
covariance
/// The covariance of two tensors of equal size, with the divisor chosen by `ddof`.
pub fn covariance(comptime T: type, a: Tensor(T), b: Tensor(T), ddof: Ddof) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const n: usize = a.size();
    if (n != b.size()) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }
    const divisor: f64 = ddof.divisor(n) orelse return Error.DomainError;
    const mean_a: T = try meanAll(T, a);
    const mean_b: T = try meanAll(T, b);

    var total: CompensatedSum(T) = .{};
    var pair: Walk2 = .over(a.shape[0..a.rank], b.shape[0..b.rank]);
    while (pair.next()) |at| {
        const x: T = (try a.at(at.first)) - mean_a;
        const y: T = (try b.at(at.second)) - mean_b;
        const term: T = x * y;
        total.add(term);
    }
    const divide_by: T = @floatCast(divisor);
    return total.value() / divide_by;
}
correlation
/// Pearson's correlation coefficient of two tensors of equal size.
///
/// NOT clamped to [-1, 1]. Rounding can put it a few ULP outside, and clamping would hide the
/// only signal that something upstream is wrong - a correlation of 1.0000003 says the inputs are
/// collinear AND that the arithmetic is at its limit; a clamped 1.0 says only the first.
pub fn correlation(comptime T: type, a: Tensor(T), b: Tensor(T)) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const sa: T = try stdDev(T, a, .sample);
    const sb: T = try stdDev(T, b, .sample);
    if (sa == 0 or sb == 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    return (try covariance(T, a, b, .sample)) / (sa * sb);
}

variance is two-pass, for layerNormRows's reason. Both it and covariance take a Ddof and return DomainError where the divisor is undefined. zscore and stdErr use the sample deviation, matching R and scipy.

correlation is not clamped to [−1, 1]. Rounding can put it a few ULP outside, and a value slightly beyond the range is a signal about the inputs' conditioning that clamping would erase.

minMaxScale and zscore return DomainError for a constant tensor, which has no range and no deviation to divide by.

11.1 Quantiles, shape and the mean family#

const q = try zn.quantile(f64, a, 0.9, scratch);   // scratch is sorted in place
const mid = try zn.median(f64, a, scratch);
const lean = try zn.skew(f64, a);
const tails = try zn.kurtosis(f64, a);             // excess: normal reads as zero
const g = try zn.geoMean(f64, a);
const hm = try zn.harmMean(f64, a);
try zn.histogram(f64, &counts, a, low, high);
quantile
/// The value below which a fraction `q` of the data lies, by linear interpolation between the
/// two neighbouring order statistics.
///
/// `scratch` must be at least `a.size()` long and is overwritten with the sorted values, so a
/// caller wanting several quantiles sorts once and calls `quantileSorted` for each.
///
/// THE INTERPOLATION RULE IS A CHOICE, AND THIS IS THE COMMON ONE
///
/// `q` maps to position `q * (n - 1)` in the sorted array: q=0 is the first element, q=1 the
/// last, and anything between is a weighted blend of its two neighbours. Nine such rules are in
/// common use and they disagree on small samples; this is the one numpy calls "linear", so a reader
/// comparing against numpy gets the same number.
pub fn quantile(comptime T: type, a: Tensor(T), q: T, scratch: []T) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const n: usize = a.size();
    if (n == 0 or scratch.len < n) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }
    if (q < 0 or q > 1) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    var walker: [max_rank]usize = @splat(0);
    const shape: []const usize = a.shape[0..a.rank];
    for (0..n) |i| {
        scratch[i] = a.data[a.offsetOf(walker[0..a.rank])];
        advance(shape, walker[0..a.rank]);
    }
    sortSlice(T, scratch[0..n], {}, std.sort.asc(T));
    return quantileSorted(T, scratch[0..n], q);
}
median
/// The middle value: `quantile(0.5)`.
pub fn median(comptime T: type, a: Tensor(T), scratch: []T) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    return quantile(T, a, 0.5, scratch);
}
skew
/// The third standardised moment: how far the distribution leans.
///
/// Zero for anything symmetric, positive when the long tail is to the right. This is the
/// POPULATION form, dividing by `n` and by the population deviation cubed - what most plotting
/// libraries show. The sample-corrected form multiplies by
/// `sqrt(n(n-1))/(n-2)` and matters below about twenty points.
pub fn skew(comptime T: type, a: Tensor(T)) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    return standardisedMoment(T, a, 3);
}
kurtosis
/// The fourth standardised moment, minus three: how heavy the tails are.
///
/// Three is subtracted so that a normal distribution reads as ZERO rather than as three, which
/// is what "excess kurtosis" means and what every reader expects when a number is called
/// kurtosis. Positive is heavier-tailed than normal.
pub fn kurtosis(comptime T: type, a: Tensor(T)) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    return (try standardisedMoment(T, a, 4)) - 3;
}
geoMean
/// The geometric mean: `exp(mean(log x))`. Every value must be positive.
///
/// Written through logarithms rather than as the n-th root of the product, because the product
/// of a few hundred values well inside the float range still overflows it. The logarithm turns
/// the multiplication into an addition that cannot.
pub fn geoMean(comptime T: type, a: Tensor(T)) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const n: usize = a.size();
    if (n == 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    var total: CompensatedSum(T) = .{};
    var walk: Walk = .over(a.shape[0..a.rank]);
    while (walk.next()) |at| {
        const x: T = try a.at(at);
        if (x <= 0) {
            return Error.DomainError;
        }
        total.add(@log(x));
    }
    return @exp(total.value() / @as(T, @floatFromInt(n)));
}
harmMean
/// The harmonic mean: `n / sum(1/x)`. Every value must be positive.
///
/// The right average for rates: two legs of a journey at 30 and 60 give a harmonic mean of 40,
/// which is the speed that covers the same distance in the same time. The arithmetic mean of 45
/// answers a question nobody asked.
pub fn harmMean(comptime T: type, a: Tensor(T)) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const n: usize = a.size();
    if (n == 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    var total: CompensatedSum(T) = .{};
    var walk: Walk = .over(a.shape[0..a.rank]);
    while (walk.next()) |at| {
        const x: T = try a.at(at);
        if (x <= 0) {
            return Error.DomainError;
        }
        total.add(1 / x);
    }
    return @as(T, @floatFromInt(n)) / total.value();
}
histogram
/// Count values into `counts.len` equal-width bins spanning `[low, high)`, with the top edge
/// closed so the largest value lands in the last bin rather than outside every bin.
///
/// Values outside the range are not counted, and `Error.DomainError` if the range is empty.
pub fn histogram(
    comptime T: type,
    counts: []usize,
    a: Tensor(T),
    low: T,
    high: T,
) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    if (counts.len == 0 or !(high > low)) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    @memset(counts, 0);
    const bins: T = @floatFromInt(counts.len);
    const width: T = (high - low) / bins;
    var walker: [max_rank]usize = @splat(0);
    const shape: []const usize = a.shape[0..a.rank];
    var remaining: usize = a.size();
    while (remaining > 0) : (remaining -= 1) {
        const x: T = a.data[a.offsetOf(walker[0..a.rank])];
        advance(shape, walker[0..a.rank]);
        if (x < low or x > high) {
            continue;
        }
        // The top edge is closed: without this, `high` itself falls one past the last bin.
        const slot: usize = if (x == high)
            counts.len - 1
        else
            @floor((x - low) / width);
        counts[@min(slot, counts.len - 1)] += 1;
    }
}

Nine interpolation rules for quantiles are in common use and they disagree on small samples. This is the one numpy calls "linear": q maps to position q·(n−1), so q=0 is the first element, q=1 the last, and anything between is a weighted blend of its two neighbours. The test asserts a case that does not land on an element, because an all-integer sample would hide the rule entirely.

kurtosis subtracts three so a normal distribution reads as zero rather than as three — that is what "excess kurtosis" means and what a reader expects from a number with that name. The test pins it against a uniform distribution, whose excess kurtosis is exactly −6/5: a number that merely looked small would not distinguish a correct fourth moment from a slightly wrong one.

geoMean goes through logarithms rather than taking the n-th root of a product, because the product of a few hundred values well inside the float range still overflows it. Three hundred values of 1e5 have a product near 1e1500; the answer is still exactly 1e5.

The three means are tested against each other: harmonic ≤ geometric ≤ arithmetic holds for any positive sample, with equality only when every value is the same. That one inequality checks all three at once, where three separate expected numbers would check none of them against the others.

11.2 Robust statistics, ties, and scales that have no answer#

const spread   = try zn.medianAbsDev(f64, scratch, a);
const relative = try zn.coefficientOfVariation(f64, a, .sample);
const err      = try zn.standardError(f64, a, .sample);
const common   = try zn.mode(f64, scratch, a);
const n        = try zn.valueCounts(f64, &values, &counts, scratch, a);
try zn.correlationMatrix(f64, out, &.{ x, y, z });
medianAbsDev
/// The median of the absolute deviations from the median.
///
/// TWO FUNCTIONS, NOT ONE WITH A FLAG - BECAUSE "MAD" MEANS BOTH
///
/// `meanAbsDev` sits beside this one. A single `mad` with an enum selecting between them would make
/// every call site read `mad(x, .median)` and every reader know the enum; two names say it without
/// one.
///
/// The median version is the robust one: half the data can be arbitrarily wrong and this barely
/// budges, where a single outlier can dominate a standard deviation. That is the whole reason it
/// exists, so it is the one whose name should be unambiguous.
pub fn medianAbsDev(comptime T: type, scratch: []T, a: Tensor(T)) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    if (scratch.len < a.size()) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }
    const centre: T = try median(T, a, scratch[0..a.size()]);
    var index: usize = 0;
    var walk: Walk = .over(a.shape[0..a.rank]);
    while (walk.next()) |at| : (index += 1) {
        scratch[index] = @abs((try a.at(at)) - centre);
    }
    sortSlice(T, scratch[0..a.size()], {}, std.sort.asc(T));
    return quantileSorted(T, scratch[0..a.size()], 0.5);
}
coefficientOfVariation
/// The standard deviation as a fraction of the mean.
///
/// Spelled out rather than `cv`, because two letters that stand for three words are a lookup.
/// It answers "is this spread large FOR THIS SCALE" - a deviation of 3 means nothing until you
/// know whether the mean is 5 or 5000.
///
/// A mean of zero has no scale to be a fraction of, and that is a `DomainError` rather than an
/// infinity: the question does not apply, which is different from the answer being large.
pub fn coefficientOfVariation(comptime T: type, a: Tensor(T), ddof: Ddof) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const centre: T = try meanAll(T, a);
    if (centre == 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    return @sqrt(try variance(T, a, ddof)) / @abs(centre);
}
standardError
/// How far the MEAN of a sample is likely to be from the mean of the whole.
///
/// The standard deviation shrunk by the square root of the count: more data, steadier estimate.
/// Spelled out rather than `sem`, on the same grounds as `coefficientOfVariation`.
pub fn standardError(comptime T: type, a: Tensor(T), ddof: Ddof) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const n: usize = a.size();
    if (n == 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    return @sqrt(try variance(T, a, ddof)) / @sqrt(@as(T, @floatFromInt(n)));
}
mode
/// The most common value, ties going to the smallest.
///
/// TIES GO TO THE SMALLEST, AND THAT IS A CHOICE THE CALLER SHOULD NOT HAVE TO GUESS
///
/// Two values can be equally common, and "the mode" is then ambiguous. Returning whichever the
/// scan happened to see first makes the answer depend on element order, which is exactly the
/// kind of thing that is reproducible until the day it is not. The smallest is arbitrary too,
/// but it is arbitrary the SAME WAY every time.
pub fn mode(comptime T: type, scratch: []T, a: Tensor(T)) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const n: usize = a.size();
    if (n == 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    if (scratch.len < n) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }
    try sort(T, scratch[0..n], a);
    var best: T = scratch[0];
    var best_run: usize = 0;
    var run: usize = 0;
    for (0..n) |i| {
        run = if (i > 0 and scratch[i] == scratch[i - 1]) run + 1 else 1;
        // Strictly greater: the sorted order means the first run of a given length starts at the
        // smallest value, so ties resolve downward without a second comparison.
        if (run > best_run) {
            best_run = run;
            best = scratch[i];
        }
    }
    return best;
}
valueCounts
/// The distinct values of `a` and how often each occurs, most common first.
///
/// Writes into `out_values` and `out_counts` and returns how many distinct values there were, so
/// the caller sizes the buffers for the worst case and reads back the truth. Ties in frequency
/// are broken by value, ascending, for the same reason `mode` does it.
pub fn valueCounts(
    comptime T: type,
    out_values: []T,
    out_counts: []usize,
    scratch: []T,
    a: Tensor(T),
) Error!usize {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const n: usize = a.size();
    if (scratch.len < n or out_values.len < n or out_counts.len < n) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }
    try sort(T, scratch[0..n], a);
    var distinct: usize = 0;
    var i: usize = 0;
    while (i < n) {
        var run: usize = 1;
        while (i + run < n and scratch[i + run] == scratch[i]) {
            run += 1;
        }
        out_values[distinct] = scratch[i];
        out_counts[distinct] = run;
        distinct += 1;
        i += run;
    }
    // Insertion sort by descending count, ascending value - stable and short, and the list is
    // the number of DISTINCT values, which is usually far smaller than the input.
    var head: usize = 1;
    while (head < distinct) : (head += 1) {
        const value: T = out_values[head];
        const times: usize = out_counts[head];
        var slot: usize = head;
        while (slot > 0 and (out_counts[slot - 1] < times or
            (out_counts[slot - 1] == times and out_values[slot - 1] > value))) : (slot -= 1)
        {
            out_values[slot] = out_values[slot - 1];
            out_counts[slot] = out_counts[slot - 1];
        }
        out_values[slot] = value;
        out_counts[slot] = times;
    }
    return distinct;
}
correlationMatrix
/// Every pairwise correlation between `columns`, written into a square `out`.
///
/// The diagonal is exactly 1 - not computed, ASSIGNED, because a column's correlation with
/// itself is one by definition and letting the arithmetic produce 0.9999999 would invite a
/// reader to wonder. The matrix is symmetric, so only one triangle is computed and mirrored.
pub fn correlationMatrix(
    comptime T: type,
    out: Tensor(T),
    columns: []const Tensor(T),
) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    if (out.rank != 2 or out.shape[0] != columns.len or out.shape[1] != columns.len) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }
    for (0..columns.len) |i| {
        try out.setAt(&.{ i, i }, 1);
        for (i + 1..columns.len) |j| {
            const r: T = try correlation(T, columns[i], columns[j]);
            try out.setAt(&.{ i, j }, r);
            try out.setAt(&.{ j, i }, r);
        }
    }
}

medianAbsDev and meanAbsDev are two functions, not one with a flag. "MAD" means both, and an enum to disambiguate would make every call site read mad(x, .median) and every reader know the enum. Two names say it without one, and the median version is the robust one: replacing a single value with 1000 multiplies the standard deviation by 282× while the median deviation does not move at all. That gap is the whole reason the function exists.
