/// So: **turns for angles that are drawn, radians for angles that are differentiated**, and the
/// name carries the unit either way. `pole_rad` cannot be mistaken for `pole_turns`.
///
/// The limit is not a rounded constant: `radFromDeg(12)` is twelve degrees exactly as far as the
/// type can express it, where a literal `0.2095` would be 12.0035 degrees.
///
/// The dynamics are the standard ones - Barto, Sutton and Anderson 1983 - and the integration is
/// SEMI-IMPLICIT Euler: the position update uses the NEW velocity. Gym's default is explicit
/// Euler, which drifts over a long episode.
pub fn cartpoleStep(
    comptime T: type,
    state: CartpoleState(T),
    push: Push,
) CartpoleStep(T) {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const push_force: T = 10.0;
    const force: T = switch (push) {
        .left => -push_force,
        .right => push_force,
    };
    return cartpoleContinuousStep(T, state, force);
}

That is the kernel. It imports zimrnum and calls the same function the CPU calls, because zimrnum compiles to SPIR-V. The sweep row now compares a function against itself.

The opt-in is .wants_zimrnum on the kernel's build entry. It is per-kernel because Zig rejects a --dep for a module the file does not import, so handing zn to every kernel fails on the ones with no use for it.

One detail worth knowing if you touch the build: --dep attaches to the next -M. Declaring -Mzn= without a matching --dep zn before -Mroot= names the module without making it visible to the kernel, and the error — module "zn" declared but not used — reads like the file failed to import it when the root module's dependency list was the short one.

13. Calculus and Fourier#

try zn.gradient(f64, out, values, h);      // central inside, one-sided at the ends
const area = try zn.trapezoid(f64, values, h);
try zn.interp(f64, out, at, xs, ys);        // clamps outside the range
gradient
/// The central-difference derivative of a sampled function, with one-sided differences at the
/// ends. `spacing` is the distance between samples.
///
/// CENTRAL IN THE INTERIOR, ONE-SIDED AT THE ENDS, which is the only choice that gives a
/// result the same length as the input. The interior error is O(h^2) and the two end points are
/// O(h) - stated here because a caller differentiating twice will see the ends degrade first.
pub fn gradient(
    comptime T: type,
    out: []T,
    values: []const T,
    spacing: T,
) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    if (out.len != values.len) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }
    if (values.len < 2 or spacing == 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    const n: usize = values.len;
    out[0] = (values[1] - values[0]) / spacing;
    out[n - 1] = (values[n - 1] - values[n - 2]) / spacing;
    var i: usize = 1;
    while (i + 1 < n) : (i += 1) {
        out[i] = (values[i + 1] - values[i - 1]) / (2 * spacing);
    }
}
trapezoid
/// The trapezoidal integral of evenly spaced samples.
///
/// Exact for any straight line, by construction, and that is what the test asserts - a rule
/// that is not exact on its own basis functions is not the rule it claims to be.
pub fn trapezoid(comptime T: type, values: []const T, spacing: T) Error!T {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    if (values.len < 2) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    var total: CompensatedSum(T) = .{};
    var i: usize = 1;
    while (i < values.len) : (i += 1) {
        total.add((values[i - 1] + values[i]) * 0.5 * spacing);
    }
    return total.value();
}
interp
/// Linear interpolation of `(xs, ys)` at each point of `at`, into `out`. `xs` must be strictly
/// increasing; points outside the range are clamped to the nearest endpoint.
///
/// Clamping rather than extrapolating: a linear extrapolation far outside the data is a number
/// with no support, and returning the endpoint is at least a value the data contains. A caller
/// who wants extrapolation can detect the clamp by comparing `at` with `xs`.
pub fn interp(
    comptime T: type,
    out: []T,
    at: []const T,
    xs: []const T,
    ys: []const T,
) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    if (xs.len != ys.len or out.len != at.len) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }
    if (xs.len < 2) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    var k: usize = 1;
    while (k < xs.len) : (k += 1) {
        if (xs[k] <= xs[k - 1]) {
            return Error.DomainError;
        }
    }
    for (out, at) |*slot, q| {
        if (q <= xs[0]) {
            slot.* = ys[0];
            continue;
        }
        if (q >= xs[xs.len - 1]) {
            slot.* = ys[ys.len - 1];
            continue;
        }
        // Linear scan: `at` is usually short and usually sorted, and a binary search here would
        // be the same speed on the sizes this is used at.
        var i: usize = 1;
        while (xs[i] < q) : (i += 1) {}
        const t: T = (q - xs[i - 1]) / (xs[i] - xs[i - 1]);
        slot.* = ys[i - 1] + t * (ys[i] - ys[i - 1]);
    }
}

Each rule is exact on the basis it is built from, and that basis is what fixes each one: the trapezoidal rule on any straight line, the central difference on any quadratic, linear interpolation on any straight line. A rule that is not exact on its own basis is not the rule it claims to be, and a test against a general function could not tell. The two end points of gradient are one-sided and therefore O(h) where the interior is O(h²); the test asserts they are close but not exact, so a reader knows which points to trust.

13.1 The transform#

const C = zn.ComplexNumber(f64);
try zn.fft(f64, data, -1);     // forward, in place, power-of-two length
try zn.ifft(f64, data);        // inverse, including the 1/n
try zn.dft(f64, out, in, -1);  // the definition, any length
try zn.fftFreq(f64, freqs, spacing);
ComplexNumber
/// A complex number, as a pair.
///
/// `ComplexNumber` rather than `Complex`, which is a reserved name - `zm` has its own, of a different
/// shape. `extern` so an array of them is exactly interleaved re/im, which
/// is the layout every FFT library and every GPU buffer expects.
pub fn ComplexNumber(comptime T: type) type {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    return extern struct {
        const Self = @This();

        re: T = 0,
        im: T = 0,

        pub fn add(a: Self, b: Self) Self {
            return .{ .re = a.re + b.re, .im = a.im + b.im };
        }

        pub fn sub(a: Self, b: Self) Self {
            return .{ .re = a.re - b.re, .im = a.im - b.im };
        }

        pub fn mul(a: Self, b: Self) Self {
            return .{
                .re = a.re * b.re - a.im * b.im,
                .im = a.re * b.im + a.im * b.re,
            };
        }

        pub fn magnitude(a: Self) T {
            return @sqrt(a.re * a.re + a.im * a.im);
        }
    };
}
fft
/// The radix-2 Cooley-Tukey transform, in place. `data.len` must be a power of two.
///
/// O(n log n), WHICH IS THE WHOLE REASON THE NAME EXISTS
///
/// A DFT of 4096 points is 16.8 million complex multiplies; this is 49 152 - 341 times fewer by
/// operation count, and **630 times faster measured**: 10 transforms of 4096 points take
/// **2 520 ms** through `dft` and **4 ms** through `fft`. The measured ratio beats the operation
/// count because the DFT calls `sin` and `cos` per element pair while the butterflies compute one
/// twiddle per pair of blocks.
///
/// The O(n^2) definition remains available as `dft`, for anyone who wants the reference.
///
/// THE FAST TRANSFORM IS CHECKED AGAINST THE SLOW ONE, element by element, at every power of
/// two the test can afford. That is the only check that does not compare an FFT against another
/// FFT written by the same hand.
///
/// Decimation in time: the input is first permuted into bit-reversed order, after which the
/// butterflies combine adjacent pairs, then pairs of pairs, and so on. The permutation is what
/// lets every stage read and write the same array.
pub fn fft(comptime T: type, data: []ComplexNumber(T), exponent_sign: T) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const n: usize = data.len;
    if (n == 0 or (n & (n - 1)) != 0) {
        return Error.UnsupportedShape;
    }
    if (n == 1) {
        return;
    }

    // Bit-reversal permutation.
    var i: usize = 1;
    var j: usize = 0;
    while (i < n) : (i += 1) {
        var bit: usize = n >> 1;
        while (j & bit != 0) : (bit >>= 1) {
            j ^= bit;
        }
        j |= bit;
        if (i < j) {
            const tmp: ComplexNumber(T) = data[i];
            data[i] = data[j];
            data[j] = tmp;
        }
    }

    // Butterflies, stage by stage. A stage of blocks `width` long uses `width / 2` twiddles, the same in
    // every block: each is computed once, and applied to its place in every block.
    var width: usize = 2;
    while (width <= n) : (width <<= 1) {
        const step: T = exponent_sign * @as(T, tau) / @as(T, @floatFromInt(width));
        var k: usize = 0;
        while (k < width / 2) : (k += 1) {
            const angle: T = step * @as(T, @floatFromInt(k));
            const twiddle: ComplexNumber(T) = .{ .re = scalarCos(angle), .im = scalarSin(angle) };
            var block: usize = 0;
            while (block < n) : (block += width) {
                const even: ComplexNumber(T) = data[block + k];
                const odd: ComplexNumber(T) = twiddle.mul(data[block + k + width / 2]);
                data[block + k] = even.add(odd);
                data[block + k + width / 2] = even.sub(odd);
            }
        }
    }
}
ifft
/// The inverse transform: `fft` with the opposite sign, divided by `n`.
///
/// The 1/n lives here rather than being split as 1/sqrtn between the two directions. Splitting
/// makes the pair unitary, which matters for a spectrogram and not for a round trip; putting it
/// all on the inverse means the forward transform's bin 0 is the plain sum of the input, which is
/// the convention every reader expects.
pub fn ifft(comptime T: type, data: []ComplexNumber(T)) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    try fft(T, data, 1);
    const scale_by: T = 1 / @as(T, @floatFromInt(data.len));
    for (data) |*z| {
        z.re *= scale_by;
        z.im *= scale_by;
    }
}
dft
/// The discrete Fourier transform by its definition, in place. `sign` is -1 forward, +1 inverse.
///
/// O(n^2), AND IT EXISTS TO CHECK THE FAST ONE
///
/// This is the definition written out: every output bin is a sum over every input sample. It is
/// unusably slow past a few thousand points and it is the only thing `fft` can be checked
/// against that is not another FFT, so it keeps its own name and the fast one sits beside it.
pub fn dft(
    comptime T: type,
    out: []ComplexNumber(T),
    input: []const ComplexNumber(T),
    exponent_sign: T,
) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    if (out.len != input.len) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }
    const n: usize = input.len;
    if (n == 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    for (out, 0..) |*slot, bin| {
        var re: CompensatedSum(T) = .{};
        var im: CompensatedSum(T) = .{};
        for (input, 0..) |x, sample| {
            const angle: T = exponent_sign * @as(T, tau) * @as(T, @floatFromInt(bin * sample % n)) /
                @as(T, @floatFromInt(n));
            const c: T = scalarCos(angle);
            const s: T = scalarSin(angle);
            re.add(x.re * c - x.im * s);
            im.add(x.re * s + x.im * c);
        }
        slot.* = .{ .re = re.value(), .im = im.value() };
    }
}
fftFreq
/// The frequency, in cycles per sample-spacing, of each bin of an `n`-point transform. Bins past
/// the halfway point are negative frequencies, as they are everywhere else.
pub fn fftFreq(comptime T: type, out: []T, spacing: T) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const n: usize = out.len;
    if (n == 0 or spacing == 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    const denom: T = @as(T, @floatFromInt(n)) * spacing;
    for (out, 0..) |*slot, bin| {
        const signed: isize = if (bin * 2 < n)
            @intCast(bin)
        else
            @as(isize, @intCast(bin)) - @as(isize, @intCast(n));
        slot.* = @as(T, @floatFromInt(signed)) / denom;
    }
}
dft is the definition and fft is the fast transform, and both exist on purpose. dft is the formula transcribed — every output bin a sum over every input sample — unusable past a few thousand points and the only thing fft can be checked against that is not another FFT. The test compares them element by element at every power of two up to 256.

Measured at 4096 points, ten transforms: 2 520 ms through dft, 4 ms through fft — 630×. The operation counts predict 341×; the rest is the DFT calling sin and cos per element pair where the butterflies compute one twiddle per pair of blocks.

ComplexNumber(T) is extern, so an array of them is exactly interleaved re/im — the layout every FFT library and every GPU buffer expects. The whole 1/n lives on the inverse rather than being split as 1/√n between the two directions: splitting makes the pair unitary, which matters for a spectrogram and not for a round trip, and putting it all on the inverse means a forward transform's bin 0 is the plain sum of the input.

Beyond the round trip, this is exact for that a pure tone puts all its energy in bins k and n − k and nowhere else. A transform with a sign error, a wrong twiddle or a botched permutation still returns numbers; it does not return a spectrum with two spikes in the right places.

13.2 Real input#

try zn.rfft(f64, out, signal, scratch);   // out is n/2 + 1, scratch is n/2
rfft
/// The transform of a real signal, into `out`, which must hold `n/2 + 1` bins.
///
/// HALF THE WORK, BECAUSE A REAL SIGNAL'S SPECTRUM IS SYMMETRIC
///
/// `X[n - k]` is the conjugate of `X[k]` when the input is real, so bins past the halfway point
/// carry no information and computing them is waste. The saving is not the discarded half of the
/// output - it is the transform itself: the `n` real samples are packed into `n/2` complex values
/// (`z[k] = x[2k] + i*x[2k+1]`), ONE transform of half the length is run, and the result is
/// untangled into the spectrum. **Half the transform, not a full transform with half thrown
/// away.**
///
/// THE UNTANGLING IS THE PART THAT CAN BE WRONG, so it is checked against a full `fft` of the
/// same signal, bin for bin, at every power of two the test can afford. A packed transform that
/// got the twiddle or the conjugate wrong still returns a plausible spectrum.
///
/// `input.len` must be even and `n/2` a power of two.
pub fn rfft(
    comptime T: type,
    out: []ComplexNumber(T),
    input: []const T,
    scratch: []ComplexNumber(T),
) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const n: usize = input.len;
    const half: usize = n / 2;
    if (n < 2 or n % 2 != 0 or (half & (half - 1)) != 0) {
        return Error.UnsupportedShape;
    }
    if (out.len != half + 1 or scratch.len != half) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }

    // Pack: even samples into the real parts, odd into the imaginary.
    for (scratch, 0..) |*z, k| {
        z.* = .{ .re = input[2 * k], .im = input[2 * k + 1] };
    }
    try fft(T, scratch, -1);

    // Untangle. `Z[k]` and the conjugate of `Z[half - k]` separate the transforms of the even and
    // odd sub-sequences; one twiddle recombines them into `X[k]`.
    const step: T = -@as(T, tau) / @as(T, @floatFromInt(n));
    for (out, 0..) |*slot, k| {
        const a: ComplexNumber(T) = scratch[k % half];
        const b: ComplexNumber(T) = scratch[(half - k) % half];
        // Even part: (Z[k] + conj(Z[half-k])) / 2. Odd part: (Z[k] - conj(Z[half-k])) / 2i,
        // written as a multiply by -i/2 to avoid a complex division.
        const even: ComplexNumber(T) = .{ .re = (a.re + b.re) * 0.5, .im = (a.im - b.im) * 0.5 };
        const gap: ComplexNumber(T) = .{ .re = (a.re - b.re) * 0.5, .im = (a.im + b.im) * 0.5 };
        const odd: ComplexNumber(T) = .{ .re = gap.im, .im = -gap.re };
        const angle: T = step * @as(T, @floatFromInt(k));
        const twiddle: ComplexNumber(T) = .{ .re = scalarCos(angle), .im = scalarSin(angle) };
        slot.* = even.add(twiddle.mul(odd));
    }
}

X[n − k] is the conjugate of X[k] when the input is real, so bins past the halfway point carry no information. The saving is not the discarded half of the output — it is the transform itself: the n real samples are packed into n/2 complex values, one transform of half the length is run, and the result is untangled. Half the transform, not a full transform with half thrown away, which is the obvious implementation.

The untangling is the part that can be wrong — a wrong twiddle or conjugate still returns a plausible spectrum — so it is checked against a full fft of the same signal, bin for bin, at every power of two to 256. Bin 0 and the Nyquist bin of a real signal are themselves real.

13.3 Convolution#

try zn.convolve(f64, out, a, v, .full);    // a.len + v.len - 1
try zn.convolve(f64, out, a, v, .same);    // a.len
try zn.convolve(f64, out, a, v, .valid);   // a.len - v.len + 1
try zn.correlate(f64, out, a, v, .full);
convolve
/// Discrete convolution of `a` with `v`, into `out`.
///
/// CONVOLUTION FLIPS THE KERNEL AND CORRELATION DOES NOT - which is the whole difference
/// between this and `correlate`, and the reason both exist. `conv2d` is named for the
/// framework convention and does not flip; this one is named for the mathematics and does.
pub fn convolve(
    comptime T: type,
    out: []T,
    a: []const T,
    v: []const T,
    extent: ConvMode,
) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    return overlap(T, out, a, v, extent, true);
}
correlate
/// Discrete cross-correlation of `a` with `v`, into `out`. The kernel is not flipped.
pub fn correlate(
    comptime T: type,
    out: []T,
    a: []const T,
    v: []const T,
    extent: ConvMode,
) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    return overlap(T, out, a, v, extent, false);
}

Convolution flips the kernel and correlation does not — the whole difference between the two, and the reason both exist. The test asserts correlate(a, v) == convolve(a, reverse(v)) on an asymmetric kernel, and separately that the two differ on it, so the identity has content. Note that conv2d is named for the framework convention and does not flip; this one is named for the mathematics and does.

Every mode is a window onto full and exactly that rather than checking each mode's numbers independently — an off-by-one in same or valid is the classic error, and a standalone test of either would not see it.

13.4 The inverse MDCT#

try zn.imdct(f32, block, coefficients, scratch);   // block is 2N, scratch is N/2, N a power of two
try zn.imdctDirect(f64, block, coefficients);      // the definition, any N
imdct
/// The inverse modified discrete cosine transform of `coefficients` - `N` of them, a power of two, at least
/// 2 - into `out`, its `2N` samples, as `imdctDirect` defines it; `scratch` holds `N/2` complex values.
///
/// WHAT IT IS FOR
///
/// Transform codecs - Vorbis, AAC, Opus's CELT - cut sound into blocks of `2N` samples, each overlapping
/// half of the next, and describe each block by `N` coefficients: half as many numbers as samples, so the
/// blocks' overlap costs nothing. The `N` coefficients cannot hold `2N` samples, and the inverse does not
/// give them back: each half of its block comes out with a mirror image of itself added - time-domain
/// aliasing - the first half's mirror negated, the second's not. Windowed, and added to the halves of the
/// blocks either side, the mirrors cancel: time-domain aliasing cancellation (Princen and Bradley, 1986).
/// With a window `w` whose halves meet `w[t]^2 + w[t + N]^2 = 1`, the sum is the signal again, times
/// `N/2` for this unscaled pair.
///
/// HOW: A DCT-IV, UNFOLDED
///
/// The cosine at sample `t` is the DCT-IV's cosine at `m = t + N/2`:
///
///     Y[m] = sum over k of  coefficients[k] * cos(pi/N * (m + 1/2) * (k + 1/2)),   m = 0 .. N-1
///
/// and past `m = N` the cosine's symmetries fold `m` back - about `N` with its sign turned, about `2N`
/// with its sign turned again. So the `2N` samples are the `N` values of `Y`, each written twice:
///
///     t in [0, N/2):        out[t] =  Y[t + N/2]
///     t in [N/2, 3N/2):     out[t] = -Y[3N/2 - 1 - t]
///     t in [3N/2, 2N):      out[t] = -Y[t - 3N/2]
///
/// AND THE DCT-IV THROUGH ONE COMPLEX TRANSFORM OF N/2 POINTS
///
/// The even coefficients go into the real parts and the odd ones, from the top down, into the imaginary
/// parts: `z[j] = coefficients[2j] + i * coefficients[N - 1 - 2j]`. Turned by `e^(-i pi (4j + 1) / 4N)`,
/// transformed, and turned again by `e^(-i pi j / N)`, the results hold the DCT-IV's outputs in pairs:
/// `Y[2j]` is the real part, and `Y[N - 1 - 2j]` the imaginary part negated. The work is the `N/2`-point
/// `fft` and two passes of `N/2` turns - against the definition's `2N^2` products.
///
/// `imdctDirect` checks it at every power of two from 2 to 1024, sample for sample.
pub fn imdct(
    comptime T: type,
    out: []T,
    coefficients: []const T,
    scratch: []ComplexNumber(T),
) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const n: usize = coefficients.len;
    if (n < 2 or (n & (n - 1)) != 0) {
        return Error.UnsupportedShape;
    }
    if (out.len != 2 * n or scratch.len != n / 2) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }
    const n_float: T = @floatFromInt(n);
    // Packed, the odd coefficients reversed, and turned by e^(-i pi (4j + 1) / 4N): -(4j + 1) / 8N of a turn.
    for (scratch, 0..) |*point, j| {
        const packed_point: ComplexNumber(T) = .{ .re = coefficients[2 * j], .im = coefficients[n - 1 - 2 * j] };
        const turns: T = -@as(T, @floatFromInt(4 * j + 1)) / (8 * n_float);
        const turn: ComplexNumber(T) = .{ .re = scalarCosTurns(turns), .im = scalarSinTurns(turns) };
        point.* = packed_point.mul(turn);
    }
    try fft(T, scratch, -1);
    // Turned by e^(-i pi j / N) - -j / 2N of a turn - into the DCT-IV's outputs in pairs, each written to its
    // two places in the block.
    for (scratch, 0..) |point, j| {
        const turns: T = -@as(T, @floatFromInt(j)) / (2 * n_float);
        const turn: ComplexNumber(T) = .{ .re = scalarCosTurns(turns), .im = scalarSinTurns(turns) };
        const turned: ComplexNumber(T) = point.mul(turn);
        writeImdctOutput(T, out, n, 2 * j, turned.re);
        writeImdctOutput(T, out, n, n - 1 - 2 * j, -turned.im);
    }
}
imdctDirect
/// The inverse modified discrete cosine transform, written out: of `N` coefficients, the `2N` samples
///
///     out[t] = sum over k of  coefficients[k] * cos(pi/N * (t + 1/2 + N/2) * (k + 1/2)),   t = 0 .. 2N-1
///
/// unscaled, as `dft` is. O(N^2), and the one thing `imdct` can be checked against that is not another
/// fast transform. The phase is kept exact: the cosine's angle is pi * (2t + 1 + N) * (2k + 1) / (4N),
/// so its turns are the integer (2t + 1 + N) * (2k + 1), taken modulo 8N, over 8N - where the product
/// itself, near 2N^2 for the last sample and coefficient, would have lost its fraction in a float.
pub fn imdctDirect(comptime T: type, out: []T, coefficients: []const T) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const n: usize = coefficients.len;
    if (n == 0) {
        return Error.UnsupportedShape;
    }
    if (out.len != 2 * n) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }
    const turn_denominator: usize = 8 * n;
    for (out, 0..) |*sample, t| {
        var sum: T = 0;
        for (coefficients, 0..) |coefficient, k| {
            const phase_numerator: usize = ((2 * t + 1 + n) * (2 * k + 1)) % turn_denominator;
            const phase_turns: T = @as(T, @floatFromInt(phase_numerator)) / @as(T, @floatFromInt(turn_denominator));
            sum += coefficient * scalarCosTurns(phase_turns);
        }
        sample.* = sum;
    }
}

Transform codecs - Vorbis, AAC, the CELT half of Opus - describe sound as a run of blocks of 2N samples, each overlapping half of the next, and each block by N coefficients: how much of each of N cosines it holds. Half as many numbers as samples, so the overlap costs nothing; the price is that one block's coefficients cannot give back its samples. The inverse transform, the IMDCT, gives each half of the block back with a mirror image of itself added - the first half's mirror negated, the second's not. This is time-domain aliasing, and it is meant: windowed, and added to the halves of the blocks either side, the mirrors cancel, and the sound between is exact.

   the sound   . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
   block 0     [  a0           |  b0          ]
   block 1                     [  a1           |  b1          ]
   block 2                                     [  a2           |  b2          ]

   each block, back from its coefficients:   [ a - mirror(a) | b + mirror(b) ]

   b0 + mirror(b0)  overlaps  a1 - mirror(a1): the same stretch of sound, windowed
   twice; added, the mirrors cancel and the stretch is whole again

The definition is a sum of cosines, one for each coefficient k, read at each sample t of the block, 2N of them:

   out[t] = sum over k of  X[k] * cos(pi/N * (t + 1/2 + N/2) * (k + 1/2))      t = 0 .. 2N-1

With N = 2 the whole of it fits on a line. A block of four samples from two coefficients; each coefficient alone:

   X = [1, 0]    out = [ +0.383  -0.383 | -0.924  -0.924 ]
   X = [0, 1]    out = [ -0.924  +0.924 | -0.383  -0.383 ]
                         first half:       second half:
                         odd - its mirror  even - its mirror
                         negated           added

That shape - every block's first half odd about its middle, its second half even - is the aliasing, there before any window: the block's own halves are folded onto themselves. The window that cancels it needs its two halves to meet w[t]^2 + w[t + N]^2 = 1 (Princen and Bradley); the sine window, w[t] = sin(pi * (t + 1/2) / 2N), does, and Vorbis's window is a smoother one that also does. With both transforms unscaled, as these are, overlapped blocks give the sound back times N/2.

imdct computes the same 2N samples in two moves. The cosine at sample t is that of a smaller transform, the DCT-IV, at m = t + N/2; past m = N the cosine's symmetries fold m back, with a sign. So the block is the DCT-IV's N outputs Y, each written twice:

   samples t           0 .. N/2         N/2 .. 3N/2               3N/2 .. 2N
   out[t]              Y[t + N/2]       -Y[3N/2 - 1 - t]          -Y[t - 3N/2]

   N = 4:  out = [ Y2  Y3 | -Y3 -Y2 -Y1 -Y0 | -Y0 -Y1 ]

And the DCT-IV of N real values goes through one complex transform of N/2 points (13.1): the even coefficients as real parts and the odd ones, from the top down, as imaginary parts; turned by e^(-i pi (4j + 1) / 4N), transformed, and turned by e^(-i pi j / N), each result holds two outputs - the real part Y[2j], the imaginary part negated Y[N - 1 - 2j]. For a Vorbis long block, N = 1024: a 512-point FFT and two passes of 512 turns, where the definition takes two million products.

The fast transform is checked against the definition at every power of two from 2 to 1024, sample for sample; and four overlapping blocks of a random signal, windowed, transformed forward by the definition and back by imdct, give the signal back times N/2 wherever two blocks meet.

14. Saving and loading#

var file: std.ArrayList(u8) = .empty;
defer file.deinit(gpa);
const names = [_][]const u8{ "l1.w", "l1.b", "l2.w", "l2.b" };
try zn.saveTensors(f64, gpa, &file, &names, &.{ l1.weight, l1.bias, l2.weight, l2.bias });

try zn.loadTensors(f64, file.items, &names, &.{ r1.weight, r1.bias, r2.weight, r2.bias });
saveTensors
pub fn saveTensors(
    comptime T: type,
    gpa: Allocator,
    out: *ArrayList(u8),
    names: []const []const u8,
    tensors: []const Tensor(T),
) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    if (names.len != tensors.len) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }
    for (tensors) |t| {
        if (!t.isContiguous()) {
            return Error.UnsupportedShape;
        }
        if (t.rank > max_rank) {
            return Error.UnsupportedShape;
        }
    }
    out.appendSlice(gpa, magic) catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
    out.append(gpa, format_version) catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
    try putInt(gpa, out, u32, @intCast(tensors.len));
    for (names, tensors) |name, t| {
        if (name.len > maxInt(u16)) {
            return Error.UnsupportedShape;
        }
        try putInt(gpa, out, u16, @intCast(name.len));
        out.appendSlice(gpa, name) catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
        out.append(gpa, @backingInt(DType.of(T))) catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
        out.append(gpa, t.rank) catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
        var axis: usize = 0;
        while (axis < t.rank) : (axis += 1) {
            try putInt(gpa, out, u64, @intCast(t.shape[axis]));
        }
        const elements: []const T = t.data[t.base..][0..t.size()];
        out.appendSlice(gpa, sliceAsBytes(elements)) catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
    }
}
loadTensors
/// Read a file written by `saveTensors` into tensors the caller has already allocated, matched by
/// name. Every requested name must be present with the right dtype and shape.
///
/// INTO EXISTING TENSORS, NOT NEW ONES. Loading a checkpoint means filling the weights a model
/// already holds; allocating fresh tensors would leave the caller to copy them across and to free
/// two sets. It also means the shape check is free: the destination states the expected shape,
/// and a file that disagrees is `ShapeMismatch` rather than a silent reshape.
pub fn loadTensors(
    comptime T: type,
    bytes: []const u8,
    names: []const []const u8,
    into: []const Tensor(T),
) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    if (names.len != into.len) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }
    var cursor: usize = 0;
    if (bytes.len < magic.len + 5 or !eql(u8, bytes[0..magic.len], magic)) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    cursor = magic.len;
    if (bytes[cursor] != format_version) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    cursor += 1;
    const count: u32 = try takeInt(bytes, &cursor, u32);

    var filled: usize = 0;
    var entry: u32 = 0;
    while (entry < count) : (entry += 1) {
        const name_len: u16 = try takeInt(bytes, &cursor, u16);
        if (cursor + name_len > bytes.len) {
            return Error.DomainError;
        }
        const name: []const u8 = bytes[cursor..][0..name_len];
        cursor += name_len;
        if (cursor + 2 > bytes.len) {
            return Error.DomainError;
        }
        const tag: u8 = bytes[cursor];
        const rank: u8 = bytes[cursor + 1];
        cursor += 2;
        if (rank > max_rank) {
            return Error.DomainError;
        }
        var shape: [max_rank]usize = @splat(1);
        var elements: usize = 1;
        var axis: usize = 0;
        while (axis < rank) : (axis += 1) {
            shape[axis] = @intCast(try takeInt(bytes, &cursor, u64));
            elements *= shape[axis];
        }
        const byte_len: usize = elements * @sizeOf(T);
        if (cursor + byte_len > bytes.len) {
            return Error.DomainError;
        }
        const payload: []const u8 = bytes[cursor..][0..byte_len];
        cursor += byte_len;

        // Is this entry one the caller asked for?
        for (names, into, 0..) |wanted, dest, i| {
            if (!eql(u8, wanted, name)) {
                continue;
            }
            if (tag != @backingInt(DType.of(T))) {
                return Error.DomainError;
            }
            if (dest.rank != rank or dest.size() != elements or !dest.isContiguous()) {
                return Error.ShapeMismatch;
            }
            var d: usize = 0;
            while (d < rank) : (d += 1) {
                if (dest.shape[d] != shape[d]) {
                    return Error.ShapeMismatch;
                }
            }
            @memcpy(sliceAsBytes(dest.data[dest.base..][0..elements]), payload);
            filled += 1;
            _ = i;
            break;
        }
    }
    if (filled != names.len) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
}

14.1 The layout#

magic            6 bytes  "ZIMR\0\0"
version          1 byte
entry count      4 bytes  little-endian
per entry:
  name length    2 bytes
  name           n bytes
  dtype tag      1 byte
  rank           1 byte
  shape          8 bytes per axis
  element data   sizeOf(T) per element, row-major, little-endian

The dtype tag encodes the type rather than counting it. The high nibble is the kind (1 float, 2 signed, 3 unsigned) and the low nibble is log₂ of the byte width, so f32 is 0x12 and f64 is 0x13. A reader computes the element size straight from the tag — 1 << (tag & 0xf), which is what byteWidth does — instead of consulting a table that has to be kept in step with the enum, and an unknown tag still says how many bytes to skip. A dense counter would be shorter to write and would make every future type a decision about where in the sequence it goes; this way i32 is 0x22 by construction.

The test pins the header's actual bytes and asserts byteWidth against @sizeOf for all three types, because a round trip agrees with itself whatever the tags are — both sides of it share any mistake. Everything is little-endian at a stated width: @bitCasting a struct into a file would be shorter and would break the first time the padding, the field order or the host's endianness changed, none of which the file records. A reader in another language needs only the table above.

14.2 Loading into a model that exists#

loadTensors fills tensors the caller already holds, matched by name, rather than allocating new ones. Loading a checkpoint means filling the weights a model already has; allocating fresh ones would leave the caller to copy them across and free two sets. It also makes the shape check free — the destination states the expected shape, and a file that disagrees is ShapeMismatch rather than a silent reshape.

Every way the file can be wrong is refused rather than read as something plausible: a bad magic, an unknown version, a truncated file, a requested name the file does not hold, a shape that disagrees, and a dtype that does not match. The test asserts all seven, and asserts the round trip by the model's predictions rather than its weights — comparing weights would pass on a loader that read them in the wrong order into same-shaped tensors.

The source must be contiguous: the file stores elements in order, and a strided view's data is not that order. materialise first.

14.3 numpy's format#

try zn.saveNpy(f64, gpa, &bytes, a);
try zn.loadNpy(f64, out, bytes);
const header = try zn.readNpyHeader(bytes);   // shape, width, where the data starts
saveNpy
/// Write one tensor in numpy's `.npy` format, version 1.0.
///
/// THE ONE FORMAT THAT LETS THIS LIBRARY TALK TO ANYTHING ELSE
///
/// `saveTensors` above is zimrnum's own container and is better at what it does - several named
/// tensors, a version byte, a self-describing dtype tag. But nothing else in the world reads it.
/// `.npy` is what numpy, scipy, PyTorch and every notebook already understand, and it costs
/// eighty lines.
///
/// The header is a Python dict literal in ASCII, padded with spaces so the DATA begins at a
/// 64-byte boundary. That padding is not decoration: it exists so a reader can memory-map the
/// array without copying, and writing it wrong produces a file every other tool rejects.
pub fn saveNpy(
    comptime T: type,
    gpa: Allocator,
    out: *ArrayList(u8),
    a: Tensor(T),
) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    var header: ArrayList(u8) = .empty;
    defer header.deinit(gpa);
    header.appendSlice(gpa, "{'descr': '") catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
    header.appendSlice(gpa, comptime npyDescr(T)) catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
    header.appendSlice(gpa, "', 'fortran_order': False, 'shape': (") catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
    var digits: [24]u8 = undefined;
    for (0..a.rank) |axis| {
        const printed: []const u8 = bufPrint(&digits, "{d}", .{a.shape[axis]}) catch
            return Error.OutOfMemory;
        header.appendSlice(gpa, printed) catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
        // A one-element tuple needs its trailing comma or Python reads it as a parenthesised
        // number. numpy writes `(3,)` and expects to read it back.
        if (a.rank == 1 or axis + 1 < a.rank) {
            header.appendSlice(gpa, ",") catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
        }
    }
    header.appendSlice(gpa, "), }") catch return Error.OutOfMemory;

    // 10 bytes of preamble, then the header, then padding, then a newline - all so the data
    // starts at a multiple of 64.
    const preamble: usize = 10;
    var padded: usize = header.items.len + 1;
    while ((preamble + padded) % 64 != 0) {
        padded += 1;
    }
    out.appendSlice(gpa, "\x93NUMPY") catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
    out.append(gpa, 1) catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
    out.append(gpa, 0) catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
    const header_len: u16 = @intCast(padded);
    out.append(gpa, @intCast(header_len & 0xFF)) catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
    out.append(gpa, @intCast(header_len >> 8)) catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
    out.appendSlice(gpa, header.items) catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
    for (header.items.len..padded - 1) |_| {
        out.append(gpa, ' ') catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
    }
    out.append(gpa, '\n') catch return Error.OutOfMemory;

    var walk: Walk = .over(a.shape[0..a.rank]);
    while (walk.next()) |at| {
        const value: T = try a.at(at);
        const bits: [@sizeOf(T)]u8 = @bitCast(value);
        out.appendSlice(gpa, &bits) catch return Error.OutOfMemory;
    }
}
loadNpy
/// Read a `.npy` array into `out`, whose shape must match what the header says.
///
/// The width in the file need not match `T`: a `<f4` file read as f64 is widened per element,
/// which is exact. The other direction narrows and is allowed, because refusing it would mean a
/// caller who knows their data fits in f32 cannot say so.
pub fn loadNpy(comptime T: type, out: Tensor(T), bytes: []const u8) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    const header: NpyHeader = try readNpyHeader(bytes);
    if (header.rank != out.rank) {
        return Error.ShapeMismatch;
    }
    var count: usize = 1;
    for (0..header.rank) |axis| {
        if (header.shape[axis] != out.shape[axis]) {
            return Error.ShapeMismatch;
        }
        count *= header.shape[axis];
    }
    if (bytes.len < header.data_at + count * header.width) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    const data: []const u8 = bytes[header.data_at..];
    var index: usize = 0;
    var walk: Walk = .over(out.shape[0..out.rank]);
    while (walk.next()) |at| : (index += 1) {
        const offset: usize = index * header.width;
        const value: T = switch (header.width) {
            4 => @floatCast(@as(f32, @bitCast(data[offset..][0..4].*))),
            8 => @floatCast(@as(f64, @bitCast(data[offset..][0..8].*))),
            else => unreachable, // readNpyHeader admits no other width
        };
        try out.setAt(at, value);
    }
}
readNpyHeader
/// Read a `.npy` header, refusing everything this library cannot represent.
///
/// WHAT IS REFUSED, AND WHY EACH ONE MATTERS
///
/// - **Big-endian** (`>f8`): the bytes would be read in the wrong order and produce plausible
///   nonsense rather than an error. Every value would be wrong and nothing would say so.
/// - **Fortran order**: the elements are all present and all in the wrong places. A reader that
///   ignored the flag would transpose the array silently.
/// - **Any dtype but `<f4` and `<f8`**: this library is float-only, and an integer array read as
///   floats is not a conversion, it is a reinterpretation.
///
/// Each of these is a case where CARRYING ON produces a result rather than a failure, which is
/// exactly when an explicit refusal is worth its lines.
pub fn readNpyHeader(bytes: []const u8) Error!NpyHeader {
    if (bytes.len < 10 or !eql(u8, bytes[0..6], "\x93NUMPY")) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    if (bytes[6] != 1) {
        return Error.DomainError; // version 2 and 3 use a wider length field
    }
    const header_len: usize = @as(usize, bytes[8]) | (@as(usize, bytes[9]) << 8);
    const header_end: usize = 10 + header_len;
    if (header_end > bytes.len) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    const header: []const u8 = bytes[10..header_end];

    const width: u8 = if (indexOf(u8, header, "'<f8'") != null)
        8
    else if (indexOf(u8, header, "'<f4'") != null)
        4
    else
        return Error.UnsupportedShape;
    if (indexOf(u8, header, "'fortran_order': False") == null) {
        return Error.UnsupportedShape;
    }

    const open_paren: usize = indexOfScalar(u8, header, '(') orelse
        return Error.DomainError;
    const close_paren: usize = indexOfScalarPos(u8, header, open_paren, ')') orelse
        return Error.DomainError;
    var out: NpyHeader = .{
        .shape = @splat(1),
        .rank = 0,
        .data_at = header_end,
        .width = width,
    };
    var cursor: usize = open_paren + 1;
    while (cursor < close_paren) {
        while (cursor < close_paren and !std.ascii.isDigit(header[cursor])) {
            cursor += 1;
        }
        if (cursor >= close_paren) {
            break;
        }
        var extent: usize = 0;
        while (cursor < close_paren and std.ascii.isDigit(header[cursor])) {
            extent = extent * 10 + (header[cursor] - '0');
            cursor += 1;
        }
        if (out.rank >= max_rank) {
            return Error.UnsupportedShape;
        }
        out.shape[out.rank] = extent;
        out.rank += 1;
    }
    return out;
}

saveTensors is zimrnum's own container and is better at what it does — several named tensors, a version byte, a self-describing dtype tag. But nothing else in the world reads it. .npy is what numpy, scipy, PyTorch and every notebook already understand, and it costs eighty lines.

The header is a Python dict literal in ASCII, padded with spaces so the data begins at a 64-byte boundary. That padding is not decoration: it exists so a reader can memory-map the array without copying, and getting it wrong produces a file that this library still reads and every other tool rejects. The test asserts the boundary directly, because a round trip through one implementation would never catch it.

Verified against real numpy, not just against itself. Files numpy wrote were read here — including a <f4 widened to f64, and a (1,) shape whose header carries the trailing comma Python needs — and bytes written here were handed back to numpy, which read them as a C-contiguous (3, 4) float64 array with the right values.

Three things are refused, and each is a case where carrying on produces a result rather than a failure:

RefusedWhat would happen otherwise
big-endian >f8every value read in the wrong byte order — plausible nonsense, no error
fortran_order: Trueevery element present, every one in the wrong place: a silent transpose
any dtype but <f4/<f8an integer array read as floats is not a conversion, it is a reinterpretation

15. Reinforcement learning#

This chapter is now chapters 2 to 8 of the zimrrl tutorial, arranged by topic, with the reinforcement-learning library it describes.

16. Autograd#

A Graph records operations as it performs them and walks the record backwards to produce gradients. The same XOR network as the previous section, differentiated automatically:

var graph: zn.Graph(f64) = .init(scope.allocator());

const gx  = try graph.constant(x);
const gt  = try graph.constant(target);
const gw1 = try graph.parameter(w1);
const gb1 = try graph.parameter(b1);
const gw2 = try graph.parameter(w2);
const gb2 = try graph.parameter(b2);

const pre1 = try graph.add(try graph.matmul(gx, gw1), gb1);
const h    = try graph.tanh(pre1);
const y    = try graph.add(try graph.matmul(h, gw2), gb2);
const loss = try graph.mseLoss(y, gt);

try graph.backward(loss);
const dw1 = try graph.gradOf(gw1);

16.1 Values are indices#

A Var is a u32 index into the graph, not a pointer. Keying gradients off the tensor would not work: a view shares data.ptr with its parent, so w and w.transpose(0,1) would collide, and a Tensor is copied by value throughout the library so it has no stable address at all. The graph owns the correspondence between a value, its tensor and its gradient, and Tensor needs no change to support it.

parameter allocates a gradient buffer; constant does not. gradOf on a constant is DomainError rather than a buffer of zeros that looks like an answer.

16.2 Eager forward, recorded backward#

Each operation computes its result immediately and appends a node describing how to push a gradient back through it. Computing eagerly means every shape is known when it is needed, so outputs are allocated as the graph is built and there is no separate shape-inference pass to disagree with the forward pass.

Nodes are appended in execution order, and a value can only depend on values recorded before it. Walking the list backwards therefore visits every consumer of a value before the value itself — a topological order by construction, with no sort, no visited set and no cycle check.

backward takes a value of a single element and seeds its gradient with 1. Differentiating a tensor with respect to parameters gives a Jacobian rather than a gradient; reverse mode answers how one number changes, so the entry point requires one. Anything else is UnsupportedShape. The pass zeroes every gradient before accumulating, so calling it twice gives the same answer rather than doubling.

16.3 Broadcasting is a sum on the way back#

A bias of shape (1, n) added to (m, n) is used m times in the forward pass, so its gradient is the sum of m contributions. Accumulation reduces along any axis that was broadcast:

if (dest.size() == contribution.size()) {
    return zimrnum.add(T, dest, dest, contribution);
}
// Broadcast along the leading axis: sum the contribution down to the bias's width.

Adding the raw gradient instead would be low by a factor of m, and the network would still train — with a bias moving m times too slowly. The test asserts the bias gradients specifically for that reason.

16.4 What is differentiable#

OperationBackward
addBoth inputs receive the gradient; a broadcast input receives its sum.
subThe left input receives the gradient, the right its negation.
mulEach side receives the other side's value times the incoming gradient.
matmuldA = g @ Bᵀ, dB = Aᵀ @ g
tanhtanhGrad(out, g), using the forward output
sigmoidsigmoidGrad(out, g), using the forward output
relureluGrad(in, g), using the forward input
mseLoss2(a − t)/n, scaled by the incoming gradient
crossEntropysoftmax − onehot, over the row count
softmaxRowsy · (g − ∑ g·y) per row; the Jacobian applied without being formed
layerNormRows(1/σ) · (g − mean(g) − y · mean(g·y)) per row
scaleThe gradient times the factor
dropoutThe gradient times the same mask as the forward pass
transposeThe transpose of the gradient. Materialised, because a value of the graph must own its storage.

The layer norm rule is checked against a finite difference on rows given very different scales and offsets, where a rule that dropped the variance term would be visibly wrong. Measured disagreement per operation, each alone: layer norm 9.7e-12, softmax 1.1e-11, scale 1.1e-9, dropout 7.1e-9.

dropout draws its mask once and stores it as a value of the graph. A dropout that redrew on every recompute would be a different function each time, and checkGradient would compare a derivative against a finite difference of something else. resampleDropout draws fresh masks, which a training loop calls once per step: each dropout node from its own split of the generator. A mask is a function of its generator and each element's index alone, so two dropout nodes of one shape fed the same generator would drop the same elements — two value heads would lose their independent noise — and every dropout a caller builds should likewise get a generator of its own. The scaling is inverted — kept elements are multiplied by 1/(1 − rate) — so removing the node at inference is exactly equivalent to rate = 0.

16.5 Replay and gradient checking#

try graph.recompute();
const worst = try graph.checkGradient(loss, gw1, 1.0e-5);

recompute replays the recorded operations forward, writing new results into the buffers already allocated. Leaves are skipped, so writing a new batch into an input tensor and calling recompute evaluates the same model on new data. Without it a graph would be single-use and a training loop would rebuild the whole tape every step.

checkGradient perturbs each element of a parameter, replays, and compares a central finite difference of the loss against the tape's gradient, returning the largest disagreement. It is the one check that does not repeat the derivation: a hand-written backward pass and a tape rule can be wrong in the same way, because the same person derived both, but a finite difference does not know the derivative at all.

Central rather than forward: (f(x+h) − f(x−h)) / 2h has error O(h²) where (f(x+h) − f(x)) / h has O(h). At h = 1e-5 in f64 that is the difference between agreeing to ten digits and to three, which decides whether a real error is visible above the noise. Every parameter of a graph exercising all eight operations agrees to better than 1e-8.

The routine restores every value and recomputes before returning, so checking a model leaves it exactly as it was found.

Convolution and embedding on the tape#

const l1: zn.Conv2d(f64) = try .init(a, rng, .{ 3, 3 }, .{ 1, 1 }, .{ 1, 1 }, .he);
const h1 = try l1.attach(&graph, input);       // .out, .kernel, .bias

const table: zn.Embedding(f64) = try .init(a, rng, vocabulary, width);
const e = try table.attach(&graph, &indices);   // .out, .table
Conv2d
/// A 2-D convolution layer: a learned kernel and a scalar bias, on `Dense`'s template.
///
/// SAME SHAPE AS `Dense`: own the parameters, `attach` to a graph, hand back the handles the
/// optimiser needs. That is the whole contract of a layer here, and it is why there is no
/// `Sequential` - a struct holding two of these IS the composition, and `attach` chains.
///
/// Single channel, rank 2. The kernel is initialised by fan-in, counting the window: a 3x3
/// kernel sees nine inputs per output, so `He` over 9 is the right scale and `He` over the whole
/// image is not.
pub fn Conv2d(comptime T: type) type {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    return struct {
        const Self = @This();

        kernel: Tensor(T),
        bias: Tensor(T),
        stride: [2]usize,
        pad: [2]usize,

        pub const Attached = struct {
            out: Var,
            kernel: Var,
            bias: Var,
        };

        pub fn init(
            gpa: Allocator,
            rng: Rng,
            size: [2]usize,
            stride: [2]usize,
            pad: [2]usize,
            scheme: InitScheme,
        ) Error!Self {
            const kernel: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(gpa, &size);
            const bias: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(gpa, &.{ 1, 1 });
            const fan_in: usize = size[0] * size[1];
            switch (scheme) {
                .xavier => try initXavier(T, kernel, rng, fan_in, fan_in),
                .he => try initHe(T, kernel, rng, fan_in),
                .small_normal => try initNormal(T, kernel, rng, small_normal_deviation),
            }
            bias.fill(0);
            return .{ .kernel = kernel, .bias = bias, .stride = stride, .pad = pad };
        }

        /// Convolve, then add the bias - which broadcasts from `(1, 1)` over the whole output.
        pub fn attach(self: Self, graph: *Graph(T), input: Var) Error!Attached {
            const k: Var = try graph.parameter(self.kernel);
            const b: Var = try graph.parameter(self.bias);
            const convolved: Var = try graph.conv2d(input, k, self.stride, self.pad);
            return .{ .out = try graph.add(convolved, b), .kernel = k, .bias = b };
        }
    };
}
Embedding
/// A lookup table of learned row vectors, indexed by whole numbers.
pub fn Embedding(comptime T: type) type {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    return struct {
        const Self = @This();

        table: Tensor(T),

        pub const Attached = struct {
            out: Var,
            table: Var,
        };

        /// Rows are drawn from the unit normal rather than by fan-in: an embedding row is not
        /// a projection of anything, so there is no fan to scale by. The usual choice.
        pub fn init(gpa: Allocator, rng: Rng, count: usize, width: usize) Error!Self {
            const table: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(gpa, &.{ count, width });
            rng.fillNormal(T, table.data);
            return .{ .table = table };
        }

        pub fn attach(self: Self, graph: *Graph(T), rows: []const usize) Error!Attached {
            const t: Var = try graph.parameter(self.table);
            return .{ .out = try graph.embedding(t, rows), .table = t };
        }
    };
}

The backward pass is the forward loop with the accumulation reversed. Forward, each output reads a window: y[i][j] += x[i·s+a−p][j·s+b−p] · k[a][b]. Both gradients fall out of that one line by moving what is read and what is written:

dx[i·s+a−p][j·s+b−p] += g[i][j] · k[a][b]
dk[a][b]                     += g[i][j] · x[i·s+a−p][j·s+b−p]

So it is written as one pass producing both, rather than as the "full correlation with a flipped kernel" the textbooks give. That form is correct and is a second thing to get right; this one cannot disagree with the forward pass about which taps are in range, because it asks the identical question.

An embedding's gradient is a scatter-add, and the += is the whole point: a token appearing three times in a batch must accumulate three contributions into one row. A scatter that assigned would train on the last occurrence and silently discard the rest. The test indexes row 2 three times and lets the finite difference — which perturbs the row and sees all three uses move — catch it.

16.6 Attention is not a primitive#

const q = try graph.matmul(gx, gq);
const k = try graph.matmul(gx, gk);
const v = try graph.matmul(gx, gv);
const scores = try graph.scale(
    try graph.matmul(q, try graph.transpose(k)),
    1.0 / @sqrt(@as(f64, @floatFromInt(width))),
);
const weights = try graph.softmaxRows(scores);
const attended = try graph.matmul(weights, v);

softmax(Q Kᵀ / √d) V is four operations the tape already has. Composing them is what shows the tape composes: a gradient error in any one, or in how gradients accumulate through a value used more than once, appears here. gx feeds all three projections, so its gradient is the sum of three paths — the accumulation a single-use test never exercises. All four parameters agree with a finite difference to better than 1e-8, and no backward rule was written for attention itself.

16.7 Initialisation and layers#

try zn.initXavier(f64, w, rng, fan_in, fan_out);   // uniform ±√(6/(in+out))
try zn.initHe(f64, w, rng, fan_in);                 // normal, deviation √(2/in)

const layer: zn.Dense(f64) = try .init(a, rng, 2, 16, .he);
const attached = try layer.attach(&graph, input);
// attached.out, attached.weight, attached.bias
initXavier
/// Fill `w` with Glorot/Xavier uniform values: `+/-sqrt(6 / (fan_in + fan_out))`.
///
/// WHY THE SCALE DEPENDS ON THE SHAPE
///
/// A layer's output variance is roughly `fan_in` times its weight variance. Fill every layer from
/// the same distribution and that factor compounds: after ten layers the activations are either
/// saturated or vanishing, and the network cannot train regardless of the optimiser. Scaling by
/// the fan sizes holds the variance constant from layer to layer.
///
/// Xavier balances the FORWARD and BACKWARD passes, which is why both fans appear - the
/// forward pass wants `1/fan_in` and the backward wants `1/fan_out`, and `2/(fan_in + fan_out)`
/// is their harmonic compromise. It suits `tanh` and `sigmoid`, whose useful range is symmetric
/// about zero.
pub fn initXavier(
    comptime T: type,
    w: Tensor(T),
    rng: Rng,
    fan_in: usize,
    fan_out: usize,
) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    if (fan_in == 0 or fan_out == 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    const total: T = @floatFromInt(fan_in + fan_out);
    const limit: T = @sqrt(@as(T, 6.0) / total);
    var i: usize = 0;
    while (i < w.size()) : (i += 1) {
        w.data[w.base + i] = rng.uniform(T, @intCast(i), -limit, limit);
    }
}
initHe
/// Fill `w` with He normal values: standard deviation `sqrt(2 / fan_in)`.
///
/// THE 2 IS THERE BECAUSE `relu` DISCARDS HALF ITS INPUT. A rectifier zeroes the negative
/// half, halving the variance that reaches the next layer; doubling the weight variance restores
/// it. Using Xavier with `relu` loses a factor of two per layer, which is a factor of a thousand
/// over ten layers.
pub fn initHe(comptime T: type, w: Tensor(T), rng: Rng, fan_in: usize) Error!void {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    if (fan_in == 0) {
        return Error.DomainError;
    }
    const deviation: T = @sqrt(@as(T, 2.0) / @as(T, @floatFromInt(fan_in)));
    var i: usize = 0;
    while (i < w.size()) : (i += 1) {
        w.data[w.base + i] = rng.normal(T, @intCast(i)) * deviation;
    }
}
Dense
pub fn Dense(comptime T: type) type {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    return struct {
        const Self = @This();

        weight: Tensor(T),
        bias: Tensor(T),

        /// Allocate and initialise. `He` for a layer feeding a rectifier, `Xavier` otherwise.
        pub fn init(
            gpa: Allocator,
            rng: Rng,
            fan_in: usize,
            fan_out: usize,
            scheme: InitScheme,
        ) Error!Self {
            const weight: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(gpa, &.{ fan_in, fan_out });
            errdefer gpa.free(weight.data);
            const bias: Tensor(T) = try .alloc(gpa, &.{ 1, fan_out });
            switch (scheme) {
                .xavier => try initXavier(T, weight, rng, fan_in, fan_out),
                .he => try initHe(T, weight, rng, fan_in),
                .small_normal => try initNormal(T, weight, rng, small_normal_deviation),
            }
            // Biases start at zero. A random bias adds nothing a random weight does not already
            // provide, and a non-zero one shifts every unit's activation before any data is seen.
            bias.fill(0);
            return .{ .weight = weight, .bias = bias };
        }

        /// What `attach` hands back: the output, and handles for the two parameters.
        ///
        /// RETURNING ONLY THE OUTPUT IS NOT ENOUGH, which a first attempt at a training loop
        /// showed immediately: the loop needs the parameter handles to read their gradients, and
        /// with the layer holding no `Var` there is nowhere else to get them. Returning all three
        /// keeps the layer graph-agnostic AND gives the caller what a step requires.
        pub const Attached = struct {
            out: Var,
            weight: Var,
            bias: Var,
        };

        /// Record `input @ weight + bias` onto `graph`, the weight and bias TRAINED (as parameters).
        pub fn attach(self: Self, graph: *Graph(T), input: Var) Error!Attached {
            return self.attachAs(graph, input, .trained);
        }

        /// Record `input @ weight + bias` onto `graph`, the weight and bias entering as `binding` says: `.trained`
        /// (parameters - what `attach` does) or `.frozen` (constants over the SAME tensors - the live weights, read at
        /// every `recompute`, never differentiated: how a planner or a target reads a network that another graph is
        /// training; `Params` tells the whole story).
        pub fn attachAs(
            self: Self,
            graph: *Graph(T),
            input: Var,
            binding: Binding,
        ) Error!Attached {
            const weight_value: Var = try bindTensor(T, graph, self.weight, binding);
            const bias_value: Var = try bindTensor(T, graph, self.bias, binding);
            return .{
                .out = try applyBound(graph, weight_value, bias_value, input),
                .weight = weight_value,
                .bias = bias_value,
            };
        }

        /// The layer's ARITHMETIC alone - `input @ weight + bias` - over handles already bound (`attachAs` binds, or a
        /// `Params.bind`). Binding once and applying many times is how ONE set of weights serves every step of a
        /// rollout: a tensor bound twice would be two parameters to the graph, each with half the gradient.
        pub fn applyBound(
            graph: *Graph(T),
            weight: Var,
            bias: Var,
            input: Var,
        ) Error!Var {
            const weighted_input: Var = try graph.matmul(input, weight);
            return graph.add(weighted_input, bias);
        }
    };
}

A layer's output variance is roughly fan_in times its weight variance. Filling every layer from the same distribution compounds that factor once per layer, and after ten layers the activations are saturated or vanishing regardless of the optimiser. Both schemes scale by the fan sizes to hold the variance constant.

Xavier balances the forward and backward passes — the forward wants 1/fan_in, the backward 1/fan_out, and 2/(fan_in + fan_out) is their compromise. It suits tanh and sigmoid, whose useful range is symmetric about zero.

He doubles that variance because relu discards its negative half, halving what reaches the next layer. Using Xavier with a rectifier loses a factor of two per layer — a factor of a thousand over ten.

Dense owns its weights as ordinary tensors and holds no Var. A Var is meaningful to one graph, so storing one would tie a layer to the first graph it met; keeping the layer graph-agnostic is what lets the same weights back two paths. attach therefore returns the parameter handles alongside the output, because a training loop needs them to read gradients and there is nowhere else to get them. Biases start at zero: a random bias adds nothing a random weight does not, and shifts every unit before any data is seen.

16.8 Optimiser#

var opt: zn.Optimizer(f64) = try .init(
    a, &graph,
    &.{ a1.weight, a1.bias, a2.weight, a2.bias },
    .{ .adam = .{ .rate = 0.02 } },      // or .{ .sgd = .{ .rate = 0.1 } }
);

while (step < 1000) : (step += 1) {
    try graph.recompute();
    try graph.backward(loss);
    try opt.step(&graph);
}
Optimizer
/// An optimiser bound to a set of a graph's parameters, owning whatever state the algorithm
/// needs per parameter.
///
/// THE STATE LIVES HERE, NOT WITH THE CALLER
///
/// `sgdMomentum` needs a velocity per parameter and `adamStep` needs two moments; without this,
/// a caller training four parameters with Adam allocates and threads eight extra tensors by
/// hand, and a mistake - one moment buffer shared between two parameters - trains silently
/// wrong. Binding the state to the parameter list at construction makes that mistake
/// unrepresentable.
///
/// ONE TYPE, THREE ALGORITHMS. The choice is a field, not a type parameter, so a training loop
/// can be written once and the algorithm changed at one call site. The state buffers for an
/// algorithm that does not use them are never allocated.
///
/// `step` reads gradients through the graph and writes updates into the graph's parameter
/// tensors, so the next `recompute` sees them with no further bookkeeping.
pub fn Optimizer(comptime T: type) type {
    comptime requireFloat(T);
    return struct {
        const Self = @This();

        pub const Kind = union(enum) {
            sgd: struct { rate: T },
            momentum: struct { rate: T, momentum: T },
            adam: Adam,
        };

        kind: Kind,
        params: []const Var,
        /// Per parameter: one buffer for momentum, two for Adam, none for SGD.
        state: []Tensor(T),
        /// Adam's 1-based step counter.
        steps: usize,

        pub fn init(
            gpa: Allocator,
            graph: *const Graph(T),
            params: []const Var,
            kind: Kind,
        ) Error!Self {
            const per: usize = switch (kind) {
                .sgd => 0,
                .momentum => 1,
                .adam => 2,
            };
            // THE PARAMETER LIST IS COPIED, NOT RETAINED
            //
            // The first version stored the caller's slice. Every test passed, because a test
            // writes `&.{ a, b, c }` in the same frame that calls `step`. The GPU training example
            // built its optimiser in `init` and stepped it from `update`, and the array literal
            // was gone - an out-of-bounds read inside `valueOf`, on the first frame. A type that
            // outlives the call that made it owns what it needs.
            const owned: []Var = try gpa.alloc(Var, params.len);
            @memcpy(owned, params);
            const state: []Tensor(T) = try gpa.alloc(Tensor(T), params.len * per);
            for (params, 0..) |v, i| {
                const shape: []const usize = graph.valueOf(v).shape[0..graph.valueOf(v).rank];
                var k: usize = 0;
                while (k < per) : (k += 1) {
                    state[i * per + k] = try Tensor(T).alloc(gpa, shape);
                    state[i * per + k].fill(0);
                }
            }
            return .{ .kind = kind, .params = owned, .state = state, .steps = 0 };
        }

        /// Apply one update to every bound parameter, from the gradients `backward` left.
        pub fn step(self: *Self, graph: *const Graph(T)) Error!void {
            self.steps += 1;
            for (self.params, 0..) |v, i| {
                const weight: Tensor(T) = graph.valueOf(v);
                const grad: Tensor(T) = try graph.gradOf(v);
                switch (self.kind) {
                    .sgd => |h| try sgdStep(T, weight, weight, grad, h.rate),
                    .momentum => |h| try sgdMomentum(
                        T,
                        weight,
                        weight,
                        grad,
                        self.state[i],
                        h.rate,
                        h.momentum,
                    ),
                    .adam => |h| try adamStep(
                        T,
                        weight,
                        weight,
                        grad,
                        self.state[i * 2],
                        self.state[i * 2 + 1],
                        h,
                        self.steps,
                    ),
                }
            }
        }
    };
}

An Optimizer is bound to a list of a graph's parameters at construction and owns whatever state the algorithm needs for each: nothing for SGD, a velocity for momentum, two moments for Adam. Without it a caller training four parameters with Adam threads eight extra tensors by hand, and a mistake — one moment buffer shared between two parameters — trains silently wrong. Binding the state to the parameter list makes that unrepresentable.

The algorithm is a field rather than a type parameter, so a loop is written once and the algorithm changed at one site. State for an algorithm that does not use it is never allocated. step reads gradients through the graph and writes updates into the graph's own parameter tensors, so the next recompute sees them.

SGD through the optimiser is asserted equal to sgdStep written by hand — the wrapper adds no arithmetic, so a difference would be a bookkeeping error in which parameter received which gradient. The three algorithms on the classifier of the previous section, from identical weights:

StepsSGDMomentumAdam
500.7690.5800.539
2000.6280.1770.043
10000.3540.00890.0012

The ordering holds at 200 steps. Adam's two buffers per parameter are a cost; the table is what they buy.

16.9 A training loop#

The graph is built once, outside the loop. Each step replays it, differentiates it, and steps the parameters in place:

while (step < 3000) : (step += 1) {
    try graph.recompute();
    try graph.backward(loss);
    try zn.sgdStep(f64, w1, w1, try graph.gradOf(gw1), 0.2);
    try zn.sgdStep(f64, b1, b1, try graph.gradOf(gb1), 0.2);
    try zn.sgdStep(f64, w2, w2, try graph.gradOf(gw2), 0.2);
    try zn.sgdStep(f64, b2, b2, try graph.gradOf(gb2), 0.2);
}

Nothing is allocated after the first iteration. sgdStep writes into the parameter tensors the graph already holds, so the next recompute sees the updated weights without any bookkeeping.

A three-class classifier on 32 points, labelled by quadrant sign, trained this way:

StepLossAccuracy
01.2820.22
2000.1260.97
30000.0211.00

The gradient check runs before and after: 3.8e-11 at the start and 9.7e-12 after training, at a point far from where it began. A model that trains is not by itself evidence that its gradients are right — a wrong but correlated gradient still reduces a loss — so the two are checked separately.

16.10 slice and concat, and why they were missing#

const top    = try graph.slice(x, 0, 0, 2);   // axis, start, len
const bottom = try graph.slice(x, 0, 2, 3);
const back   = try graph.concat(top, bottom, 0);

Tensor.slice gives a strided view for free, but a view carries no gradient, so slicing a computed value needs these graph ops: LstmCell slices its four gates out of one fused matmul with them, and Attention splits a projection into heads.

The backward of a slice is a scatter

The gradient lands in the rows the slice read, and every other row gets exactly zero — a row nobody read influenced nothing. concat's backward is the same thing read the other way: each input takes back the part of the gradient that came from its own rows.

A scatter that writes to the wrong offset still runs, still produces numbers of the right shape, and trains something adjacent to what you meant. So the comparison is against a central difference at every element, and separately asserts the zeros: slice the middle two rows of five, and rows 0, 3 and 4 must have no gradient — not small, zero.

It also checks that slicing and rejoining is the identity on values. That matters because it means a wrong offset in either backward shows up in the gradient while the forward pass still looks perfect.

16.11 Activations on the tape, and one that cannot be#

const h = try graph.silu(x);   // x * sigmoid(x)
const h = try graph.gelu(x);   // the tanh form

silu, gelu, softplus and elu all existed at tensor level with no tape node at all. A network using any of them could be evaluated and not trained — the forward works, the loss falls for the layers that do have nodes, and the activation simply never learns. Nothing reports it.

That is a worse failure than a missing gradient function, because it looks like training.

Two of the four are compositions of nodes that already exist, so they cost nothing and their gradients are the tape's.

exp, log and softplus — and why the third is not a composition

exp and log are tape nodes, so a ratio of exponentials, or the logarithm of one, trains like any other arithmetic.

But having the primitives does not mean composing them is safe. Written as log(1 + exp(x)), softplus overflows: measured at f32, exp(89) is infinity, so the composition returns inf from x = 89 upward where the true answer is 89 — softplus is very nearly the identity for large x.

So softplus is its own node. The identity behind its form:

log(1 + e^x) = max(x, 0) + log(1 + e^-|x|)

  for x > 0:  log(1 + e^x) = log(e^x (e^-x + 1)) = x + log(1 + e^-x)
  for x ≤ 0:  max is 0 and |x| = -x, leaving the original

The exponential is therefore only ever taken of a negative number and cannot overflow.

But overflow is not the only failure. At x = −50 the answer is 1.93e−22, and any form computing log(1 + e^-|x|) returns exactly zero — 1 + 1.9e-22 rounds to 1 in f64 and its logarithm is 0. A threshold form, if (x > 20) x else log(1 + e^x), also leaves a 1e−10 discontinuity just above 20.

log1p takes the small argument directly and never forms the 1:

x        log1p form        log(1 + ...) form
-50      1.929e-22         0
-700     9.860e-305        0
-745     4.941e-324        0

The tail survives to the smallest subnormal. It is the same trick logSumExp uses one screen away and the one log(softmax(x)) needed — three places in this library where forming the 1 loses everything.

The backward is what makes a dedicated node cheap: d/dx softplus(x) is exactly sigmoid(x) — no branch, nothing to derive.

The test probes all four gradients separately, because the three backwards read three different things: exp uses its own output, log needs the input, and softplus uses sigmoid of the input. Picking the wrong one is easy and gives plausible numbers. It also checks log(exp(x)) == x, which would fail if either node were wrong in a way the separate probes happened to miss.

ELU, and a probe that would have passed anyway

elu is a real node, not a composition: it switches on the sign, and there is no elementwise select to build that from. Its backward is 1 above zero and alpha * exp(x) below, read from the input — the output would give the same numbers, but only the input says which side of the branch a value was on.

The shared gradient probe above uses all-positive values, because log needs them. On positive input ELU is the identity, so that probe exercises one side of the branch and reports success. It gets its own spread straddling zero — {-3, -1, -0.1, 0, 0.1, 1, 3} — which is the only place the branch shows.

Two properties pin it beyond the derivative: above zero the output equals the input exactly, and below zero it saturates toward -alpha without reaching it.

Every activation in the library has a tape node — relu, sigmoid, tanh, silu, gelu, softplus, mish, elu — so a network built from any of them trains, and does not only evaluate.

Mish with one exponential. Mish, x · tanh(softplus(x)), is the activation of the TD-MPC family, in every hidden layer. Written out it takes an exponential, a logarithm and a hyperbolic tangent, but the three collapse into one. With e = ex, softplus(x) = log(1 + e), and for any u > 0, tanh(log u) = (u² − 1) / (u² + 1). At u = 1 + e:

tanh(softplus(x)) = ((1 + e)^2 - 1) / ((1 + e)^2 + 1) = n / (n + 2),      n = e (e + 2)

mish(x)  = x n / (n + 2)
mish'(x) = t + x (1 - t^2) sigmoid(x),       t = n / (n + 2),   sigmoid(x) = e / (1 + e)

x           -20        -1         0      1         20
mish(x)     -4.1e-8    -0.3034    0      0.8651    20
mish'(x)                          3/5

The slope is the product rule: tanh's slope 1 − t² times softplus's slope, the sigmoid. One exponential forward and one backward, in one tape node, where the composition took three nodes and five transcendental evaluations. It is the same function, accurate in both tails: for very negative x the ratio is formed directly, with nothing cancelling, and above about 19 (in f64), where the ratio rounds to exactly 1, mish returns x itself, with slope 1 (zm.mish, zm.mishSlope).

GELU is written x * sigmoid(2u) rather than 0.5x * (1 + tanh(u)). They are the same function:

(1 + tanh u)/2 = (1 + (e^u - e^-u)/(e^u + e^-u))/2
               = (2e^u / (e^u + e^-u))/2
               =  1 / (1 + e^-2u)
               =  sigmoid(2u)

The first form needs a tensor of ones to add — allocated on every call, and on a graph rebuilt each training step that is a per-step allocation for a constant. The second needs none and is two nodes shorter.

GELU is the tanh form, not the erf definition. The exact version needs erf; the approximation is what PyTorch, JAX and every published transformer actually run, so matching it matters more than matching the definition — weights were trained against it.

Two things worth stating

One might expect the tensor gelu was the erf definition and expected the two to differ by about 1e−3. They agree to 8e−13 — zimrnum's tensor version is the same approximation. The bar is set from that measurement rather than from an assumption about the code.

And the finite-difference probe mutates its input, so the input must be allocated. Every other test here builds tensors with @constCast(&[_]f64{...}), which is safe because none of them writes — a literal lives in read-only memory and @constCast only silences the type system. Writing through it aborts.

17. A network that learns#

Every piece above has its own test. None of those catches a mistake in how the pieces fit — a gradient with the wrong sign, a transpose on the wrong operand, a bias summed along the wrong axis. Each of those leaves every individual function correct and the network unable to learn.

The following is a test in src/zimrnum.zig. It trains a two-layer network on XOR, which is the smallest problem a linear model cannot solve: without a working hidden layer the loss stalls near 0.25.

// forward
try zn.matmul(f64, pre1, x, w1);
try zn.add(f64, pre1, pre1, try b1.broadcastTo(&.{ samples, hidden }));
try zn.tanh(f64, h, pre1);
try zn.matmul(f64, y, h, w2);
try zn.add(f64, y, y, try b2.broadcastTo(&.{ samples, 1 }));
const loss = try zn.mseLoss(f64, y, target);

// backward: d(mse)/dy is 2(y - t)/n
try zn.sub(f64, dy, y, target);
try zn.scale(f64, dy, dy, 2.0 / @as(f64, @floatFromInt(samples)));
try zn.matmul(f64, dw2, try h.transpose(0, 1), dy);
try zn.sumAxis(f64, db2, dy, 0);
try zn.matmul(f64, dh, dy, try w2.transpose(0, 1));
try zn.tanhGrad(f64, dpre, h, dh);
try zn.matmul(f64, dw1, try x.transpose(0, 1), dpre);
try zn.sumAxis(f64, db1, dpre, 0);

// update
try zn.sgdStep(f64, w1, w1, dw1, rate);
try zn.sgdStep(f64, b1, b1, db1, rate);
try zn.sgdStep(f64, w2, w2, dw2, rate);
try zn.sgdStep(f64, b2, b2, db2, rate);

Weights and intermediates come from an arena, so nothing in the loop is freed individually and the whole allocation goes when the scope closes. The transposes are stride swaps — no copy.

StepLoss
00.541
1006.2e-6
5004e-8
10000

Final outputs are −0.000000, 1.000000, 1.000000, −0.000000 against targets of 0, 1, 1, 0, and the weight gradients have fallen to about 2e-11.

One detail worth noting: tanhGrad takes h, the forward output, not pre1. Passing the input compiles, runs, and produces a network that learns far too slowly — the kind of error only an end-to-end check finds.

17b. Reinforcement learning#

This chapter is now chapters 2 to 8 of the zimrrl tutorial, arranged by topic, with the reinforcement-learning library it describes.

17c. Diffusion#

A diffusion model generates by learning to undo noise. Train it by destroying a real sample a little at a time; generate by running that backwards from pure noise. This section covers the arithmetic zimrnum provides — the schedules and the forward process — which is the part that has to be exactly right and is easy to get subtly wrong.

17c.1 The schedule decides where the model learns#

var betas: [1000]f64 = undefined;
var alpha_bar: [1000]f64 = undefined;

try zn.betaSchedule(f64, &betas, .cosine);
try zn.alphasCumprod(f64, &alpha_bar, &betas);
betaSchedule
/// Fill `betas` with a diffusion noise schedule over `betas.len` timesteps.
///
/// ---- WHAT A SCHEDULE IS ----
///
/// Diffusion trains a model to undo noise. The forward process adds a little at each of T steps
/// until the signal is gone; `beta[t]` is how much variance step `t` contributes. The schedule
/// is therefore a statement about WHERE the model spends its capacity: steps with small beta are
/// nearly clean and teach fine detail, steps with large beta are nearly pure noise and teach
/// coarse structure.
///
/// ---- LINEAR VERSUS COSINE IS NOT COSMETIC ----
///
